fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Pandita Ramabai
fields.subtitle: A Scholar of the Scriptures, the Widows of India, and a Treasure That Never Failed
fields.description: A Christian biography of Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), the Sanskrit scholar orphaned by famine who became a widow at twenty-three, a pioneer of women's rights in India, a Christian, and the founder of Mukti, where thousands of famine girls, child-widows and outcast women found a home. Built on her own writings and checked against the early lives and modern scholarship, it tells the whole story — the reformer and the saint, the 1893 storm with the Hindu reformers, her anger at British injustice, the 1905 revival and her Marathi Bible. All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of Pandita Ramabai about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922). It follows her from her birth in a forest in the Western Ghats and her childhood as a pilgrim, through the famine that killed her family, her honours as a Sanskrit scholar in Calcutta, her marriage and widowhood, England and America, her school for widows in Bombay and Poona, the famine rescues of 1896–1900, the founding of Mukti at Kedgaon, the 1905 revival, and her translation of the Bible into Marathi. It draws mainly on her own writings.

qa.question: Who was Pandita Ramabai?
qa.answer: She was a Brahman woman, taught Sanskrit by her parents, who was acclaimed by the pandits of Calcutta in 1878 and became one of the first Indian women to campaign publicly for women's education and the rights of widows. She became a Christian in England in 1883, founded the Sharada Sadan school for widows in 1889 and the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon in 1897, rescued thousands of girls from famine, and translated the Bible into everyday Marathi.

qa.question: Why does she say she found Christ eight years after her baptism?
qa.answer: In her 1907 Testimony she wrote that at her baptism in 1883 she had found 'the Christian religion' but 'had not found Christ, who is the Life of the religion.' About 1891, after reading the Bible itself rather than books about it, she came to an end of herself and surrendered to Christ, and found salvation as a free gift. The book takes that distinction seriously.

qa.question: What happened in the Sharada Sadan crisis of 1893?
qa.answer: Her school for widows had been promised as religiously neutral. When girls began attending her private prayers and some declared faith in Christ, the Hindu reformers on its advisory board, including M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar, resigned, and thirty-one pupils were withdrawn. The book gives both sides: the reformers' reasonable sense of a broken understanding, and Ramabai's refusal to shut the open door of her own room.

qa.question: Was the Mukti revival of 1905 the start of Pentecostalism?
qa.answer: The revival at Mukti began in June 1905, before the Azusa Street meetings of 1906, and it influenced Pentecostal movements elsewhere, including in Chile. But speaking in tongues at Mukti came later, in December 1906, after news of Azusa Street arrived. Ramabai herself taught that love, not tongues, was the one necessary sign of the Holy Spirit.

qa.question: Was she the first woman to translate the Bible?
qa.answer: No. Julia Smith had published a translation of the whole Bible into English in 1876, and Marathi Bibles existed before Ramabai's. Hers was the first translation of the Bible into colloquial Marathi, made for village women, and she was among the first women anywhere to translate the whole of Scripture from the original languages. The complete edition was published after her death.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme, from 'A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows' to 'there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus', and further passages are woven through the story, including verses Ramabai herself quoted. Every quotation was checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources and the three ways Ramabai has been remembered — as reformer, saint, and missionary; the chapters then follow her life in order. Appendix A gathers lessons from her life, Appendix B is a study guide for groups, Appendix C a chronology, and Appendix D a note on sources and on popular claims the book corrects.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, Is God in his holy habitation.”

— Psalm 68:5, ASV

The first five volumes of this series told the stories of Watchman Nee in China, John Hyde in the Punjab, Corrie ten Boom in Haarlem, Mary Slessor in south-eastern Nigeria, and Samuel Ajayi Crowther on the Niger. This sixth volume returns to India, to a woman who was born in a forest in the Western Ghats in 1858 and died at Mukti, her settlement at Kedgaon outside Poona, in 1922, and who in between became one of the most remarkable people of her century.

Pandita Ramabai was many things at once, and people have never agreed which of them mattered most. She was a scholar of Sanskrit, so learned that the pandits of Calcutta acclaimed her with the title Sarasvati, after the goddess of learning. She was a pioneer of women’s rights in India, who told a British commission in 1882 that the women of her country were “oppressed and cruelly treated” by the men, and who wrote a book that a modern scholar has called an Indian feminist manifesto. She was a widow and a single mother at twenty-three. She crossed the sea to England at a time when a high-caste Hindu woman who did so was thought to have lost her caste for ever. She became a Christian, argued with the Anglican sisters who had baptised her, lectured across America, and came home to found a school for child-widows that was attacked by the leading Hindu reformers of her day. She walked into the famine districts of Central India and brought back hundreds of starving girls. She built a community at Kedgaon that at its height fed and housed some two thousand women and children, without an endowment or a bank balance. She saw a revival there that spread across India. And in the last years of her life she translated the whole Bible, from Hebrew and Greek, into the everyday Marathi of the village women she loved.

She also called herself a sweeper. “I sweep into this compound as many as I can get,” she told a missionary who came to work with her in 1901, “child-widows, deserted wives, and orphans of every kind.”

Why Her

This series is called Portraits of Courage, and courage in Ramabai’s case took an unusual form. She was not a martyr. No one put her in prison. Her courage was the courage to think for herself and to act on what she thought, whatever it cost her. It cost her a great deal. When she was a girl it cost her family their standing among the Brahmins, because her father refused to marry her off as a child. When she married, it was across caste, to a man her world regarded as far beneath her. When she became a Christian, many of her own people counted her a traitor, and some still do. When she refused to be told what to believe by the Christians who had baptised her, they feared for her orthodoxy and rebuked her. When girls in a school she had promised would be neutral in religion began coming to her Christian prayers, and some of them asked to become Christians, the reformers who had supported her resigned in anger. And when she stood between the British government and the famine girls it had failed to protect, she warned that if the state again licensed vice, “British iniquity will reach its climax,” words that her British biographers do not quote.

She did all this as a woman, in a society that gave women almost no public voice, and she did much of it half-deaf, often ill, and always short of money. She did it, as she came to believe, in dependence on God. The verse at the head of this preface is one she would have recognised as a description of her own work. God is “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows.” She spent her life trying to be his hands.

Her Own Words

We are fortunate in having a good deal of Ramabai’s own writing in English. The High-Caste Hindu Woman, published in Philadelphia in 1887, is her own book. Famine Experiences in India, written in 1897, tells the story of her parents’ deaths in her own words. A Testimony, first printed at Kedgaon in 1907, is her account of her spiritual journey. Her letters to her American supporters were printed year by year in their reports. This book quotes her wherever it can, and marks the places where we depend instead on what others said about her.

Her biographers are a mixed blessing. The earliest were admirers who wanted to raise money for her work, and they told her story as a missionary romance, adding details she never gave and sometimes leaving out things she did say. The most careful of the older lives, by Nicol Macnicol in 1926, had access to sources in Marathi. Modern scholars in India and the West have written about her with great seriousness, some chiefly as a reformer and some chiefly as a Christian. The introduction that follows explains how this book has tried to find its way among them.

Her story is not always comfortable. She could be imperious and hard to work with. She changed her mind about important things, and said so. Her Christianity was not quite the Christianity of the missionaries who taught her, and she did not want it to be. Her faith grew in stages, and she was honest about them. For eight years after her baptism, she said, she had found “the Christian religion,” but not Christ. It is one of the most honest confessions any Christian has made, and it is part of why her testimony still rings true.

Like the Psalmist, she looked back at the end of her life and saw that she had been carried. “He upholdeth the fatherless and widow” (Psalm 146:9, ASV). She had been both, and she spent her life upholding others who were.

fields.title: Introduction: The Pandita and Her Biographers
fields.body_html:
“and ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”

— John 8:32, ASV

Three Ramabais

If you ask about Pandita Ramabai in India today, you may hear of three different women.

The first is a social reformer. She appears in school textbooks and on a postage stamp issued in 1989. She was one of the first Indian women to speak in public for the education of women, to found a women’s society, and to describe, in print and before government commissions, the lives of child-brides and widows. Historians such as Meera Kosambi and Uma Chakravarti have written about her chiefly in this light, as a pioneering thinker whose criticism of her own society was so sharp that the reformers of Maharashtra later preferred to forget her. In this telling, her Christianity is sometimes a footnote, sometimes a later and narrower phase.

The second woman is a Christian saint. She is remembered on 30 April in the calendar of the Church of England, under the name she took at her baptism, “Pandita Mary Ramabai, Translator of the Scriptures.” She founded Mukti, which still shelters women and children at Kedgaon. She prayed down a revival in 1905 that historians of Pentecostalism count among the sources of the movement. She translated the Bible. In this telling, her early life as a scholar and reformer is sometimes only a preparation for her real work.

The third woman, in the eyes of some Hindu nationalists, is a missionary who used her learning and her reputation to draw Hindu girls away from their faith. That charge was first made in her lifetime, and it has never quite gone away.

Each of these portraits leaves out something the others include. This book is written from a Christian point of view, and it will not pretend that her faith in Christ was a footnote. It was the centre of her life. But it will also try not to leave out the reformer, the feminist, the critic of her own church, or the Hindu critics who had reasons for their anger. The verse at the head of this introduction is Jesus’ promise: “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” Ramabai spent her life looking for the truth, and she was not afraid of it. Her story should not be told in a way she would have been afraid of either.

Her Own Words

The best guide to Ramabai is Ramabai. She wrote a great deal, in Marathi and in English, and much of her English writing survives.

The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887) is her own book, written in America. The edition of that year also contains a long introduction by her friend Dr. Rachel Bodley, the dean of the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, which includes many details of her early life that Ramabai told her. Some of these details do not agree with Ramabai’s own later accounts. When the book was reprinted in 1901, Ramabai asked for Bodley’s introduction to be left out.

Famine Experiences in India (1897) is a short pamphlet she wrote to raise help for the famine-stricken. It begins with the fullest account she ever gave of how her own parents died, twenty years earlier.

A Testimony, written at Mukti in 1907, is her account of her spiritual journey. We have not been able to find a copy of the original pamphlet. It survives in two later printings: a condensation made with her permission by the missionary J. J. Lucas in 1919, and a fuller text printed by Helen Dyer in a biography published soon after Ramabai’s death. The two do not quite agree. Dyer’s version, for reasons she does not explain, leaves out the names of the Hindu reformers who helped Ramabai in Poona, and the name of the Indian priest, Father Nehemiah Goreh, whose book, Ramabai said, convinced her of the truth of Christianity. This book uses both, and quotes Lucas where Dyer has cut.

Her letters to her American supporters were printed in the annual reports of the Ramabai Association in Boston between 1890 and 1898. Others were printed in Australia. They are among the most vivid things she wrote.

There are important gaps. Her letters to the Anglican sisters at Wantage, which record her arguments with them over doctrine and obedience in the 1880s, were collected and published in India in 1977, and that collection is still in copyright. We know their contents chiefly from what modern scholars have written about them. Her Marathi writings, including a book about America, are known to most English readers only through modern translations.

The Biographers

Three biographers who wrote during her lifetime or soon after it are in the public domain, and all three are useful.

Helen Dyer, an English writer who knew her and supported her work, published Pandita Ramabai: The Story of Her Life in 1900 and a longer book, Pandita Ramabai: Her Vision, Her Mission and Triumph of Faith, published after Ramabai’s death, in about 1923. Dyer wrote to inspire prayer and giving. She calls her first book “a record of answered prayers.” She sometimes adds colour that Ramabai’s own accounts do not contain, and she writes of Hinduism with a contempt that goes beyond even Ramabai’s own sharp later judgments, and without Ramabai’s lifelong respect for her parents’ sincerity.

Clementina Butler, an American Methodist and a member of the Ramabai Association, published a memorial biography in 1922, the year of Ramabai’s death. It is short, warm, and valuable for its American documents.

Nicol Macnicol, a Scottish missionary and scholar of Indian religion who worked for many years in western India, published Pandita Ramabai in 1926 in a series called Builders of Modern India. It is the most careful of the three. Macnicol used the Marathi biography by D. G. Vaidya and the recollections of Ramabai Ranade, and he warns his readers that Ramabai’s later descriptions of Hinduism were written “after she had been for many years a Christian,” so that “we cannot expect a balanced judgment from such a witness.” That is a fair warning for us as well.

Where these writers tell stories that do not appear in Ramabai’s own accounts, this book says so. Where they disagree with each other, or with her, the disagreement is noted. The end of the book has a fuller note on the sources, and a list of popular claims that turn out not to be true.

Two Conversions

One more thing needs to be said at the beginning, because it shapes the whole story.

Ramabai was baptised in the Church of England in September 1883. But she herself did not date her conversion to her baptism. In A Testimony she wrote: “I came to know, after eight years from the time of my baptism, that I had found the Christian religion, which was good enough for me; but I had not found Christ, who is the Life of the religion.”

The difference between finding the religion and finding Christ is at the heart of her testimony. For eight years she was a Christian by conviction. She believed that Christianity was true, and that it was better than anything she had known. She was baptised, she taught, she lectured. But something was missing, and in about 1891 she found it. This book takes her distinction seriously. It does not read her later evangelical faith back into her earlier years, nor does it dismiss those earlier years as unimportant. The woman who argued with the sisters at Wantage about the Trinity and the woman who knelt at Mukti in 1905 to pray for revival were the same woman. Both were looking for the truth. The second had found more of it.

Paul wrote that Christians “know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9, ASV). Ramabai would have agreed. Her life was a long discovery, and she was willing to be taught.

fields.title: The Forest School
fields.body_html:
“And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be upon thy heart; and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”

— Deuteronomy 6:6-7, ASV

A Boy in the Palace

Ramabai’s story begins with her father, and her father’s story begins with a woman reciting poetry.

Anant Shastri Dongre was a Brahman from a village in the Mangalore district, on the south-western coast of India, below the long wall of mountains called the Western Ghats. He was born, as far as we can tell, at the end of the eighteenth century. As a young man, already married according to the custom of his people, he went north to Poona to study Sanskrit with a famous scholar named Ramachandra Shastri. Poona was then the capital of the Peshwas, the Brahman rulers of the Maratha lands, and Ramachandra Shastri had been engaged to teach Sanskrit to one of the Peshwa’s wives. Anant went with his teacher to the palace, and sometimes he heard the lady reciting Sanskrit poetry.

It astonished him. The sacred language was not meant for women. The law-books of the Brahmans taught that women, like the lowest castes, could not study the Vedas, and most learned men held that they should not learn Sanskrit at all. Here was a queen who knew it well. Rachel Bodley, who heard the story from Ramabai, wrote that his astonishment turned to admiration, and that he resolved to teach his own wife as his teacher had taught the queen.

His wife refused. So did his mother and the elders of the family. The experiment was abandoned. Years passed, children were born, and at last his first wife died.

A Bride of Nine

What happened next Ramabai told herself, without naming anyone, in The High-Caste Hindu Woman. It is one of a number of examples she gives of how carelessly Hindu fathers married off their daughters.

I know of a most extraordinary marriage that took place in the following manner: the father was on a religious pilgrimage with his family, which consisted of his wife and two daughters, one nine and the other seven years of age, and they had stopped in a town to take rest for a day or two. One morning the father was bathing in the sacred river Godavari, near the town, when he saw a fine-looking man coming to bathe there also.

The stranger was a widower. On learning his caste and clan and where he lived, the father offered him his nine-year-old daughter in marriage. “All things were settled in an hour or so; next day the marriage was concluded, and the little girl placed in the possession of the stranger, who took her nearly nine hundred miles away from her home.” The father went on with his pilgrimage the next day, “with a light heart.” Fortunately, Ramabai adds, “the little girl had fallen in good hands, and was well and tenderly cared for beyond all expectation.”

The Forest

Anant began at once to teach his young wife Sanskrit, and once again his family objected. This time he did not give in. He took his wife away, up into the mountains, and made a home in a forest on the top of a peak of the Western Ghats. Ramabai described it in A Testimony:

It is worth being clear about what kind of reformer he was. Anant Shastri did not question the Hindu religion. He was, Ramabai says, “a very orthodox Hindu and strictly adhering to caste and other religious rules.” He kept the Vedas themselves from his wife, and taught her the Puranas, the great popular scriptures of Hinduism, not the most sacred texts. What he rejected was the rule that women must be kept ignorant. And she had them. “When I was about eight years old my mother began to teach me,” she wrote, “and continued to do so until I was about fifteen years of age. Her parents did not want their children to learn anything else. “Learning any other language except Sanskrit was out of the question. fields.title: Pilgrims
fields.body_html:
“Their idols are silver and gold, The work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they speak not; Eyes have they, but they see not;”

— Psalm 115:4-5, ASV

Puranikas

For the next fifteen years the Dongre family lived on the road. “Ever since I remember anything,” Ramabai wrote, “my father and mother were always travelling from one sacred place to another, staying in each place for some months, bathing in the sacred river or tank, visiting temples, worshipping household gods and the images of gods in the temples, and reading Puranas in temples or in some convenient place.”

They were Puranikas, public readers of the Puranas, the great Sanskrit collections of Hindu myth and legend. It was an honourable calling. A Puranika sat in a temple hall, under a tree, or on the bank of a sacred river, and read aloud from his manuscript in Sanskrit. Few of the hearers understood a word. That did not matter. The sound of the sacred text was believed to purify those who heard it, and those who stopped to listen gave the reader a present: a handful of rice, a coin, a flower, a few cowrie shells. “The reading and hearing of the sacred literature is in itself believed to be productive of great merit,” Ramabai explained. “We never had to beg or work to earn our livelihood. We used to get all the money and food we needed, and more; what remained over after meeting all necessary expenses was spent in performing pilgrimages and giving alms to the Brahmins.”

So the child grew up reciting the scriptures in public, with her father, her mother, her brother, and her sister, in towns and temples across the south and west of India. She learned to speak before crowds while she was still a child. It was an odd education, and a rich one. It gave her a memory stocked with poetry, a voice that did not fear an audience, and a first-hand knowledge of popular Hindu religion that few Indian women and almost no Europeans possessed.

What She Saw

It also gave her a great deal to think about. Many years later, after she had become a Christian, Ramabai wrote down her memories of the sacred places she had visited as a child. Macnicol, who read them, warns that they were written by a convert looking back, and that “we cannot expect a balanced judgment from such a witness.” That is fair, and we should read them in that light. But her memories are also specific and unsentimental, and they show a child who was watching closely.

Her earliest memory of religion, she said, was from about the age of four, at the hill shrine of Tirupati in the south. The priests there told the pilgrims “any number of lies.” “My parents knew all about these lies and laughingly made mention of them. But yet the priests were looked upon as very gods and worshipped accordingly.” The family bathed in a waterfall called Papanasini, the “destroyer of sin,” though, she says, they “knew in their own hearts that the sins remained where they were, as before.”

When she was about thirteen, the family spent a year at Dwarka, on the coast of Gujarat, the city of Krishna. According to legend, Krishna’s golden city had sunk beneath the sea, but on one rare day, which came only once in sixty years, Krishna would show it to the sinless. The day came while they were there. Pilgrims arrived in their thousands. The Dongres bathed in the sea, gave alms to the Brahmans, recited the sacred texts, and waited through a cloudy day for the vision. At sunset the clouds on the horizon glowed gold.

Many people did not dare to say that they did not see the city, for that would be confessing that they were sinners. They kept silence about it and so did we. But we were convinced in our inmost hearts that we saw no city but saw the ordinary clouds which we were accustomed to see, almost daily, at the time of sunset.

“The pockets of the priests were filled with money,” she added, “while the pilgrims went empty away.”

At Pandharpur, in the Maratha country, the great shrine of the god Vithoba, the family prostrated themselves at the first sight of the holy city, and drank the muddy water of the Bhima river to wash away their sins. Ramabai wrote that she went there first “as a Hindu fully believing in all that I heard,” but that “the seed of unbelief was planted in my young heart by the sight of the inconsistency of the priests and worshippers.”

The First Call

She saw other things, too, that she never forgot.

When she was about nine, the family was living on the banks of the Jumna, in the north. There she saw a young wife beaten by her husband and her mother-in-law. Nearly thirty years later she wrote: “Her cries went right to my heart and I seem to hear them now after nearly thirty years. … I suppose that was the first call I received to enter upon the sacred duty of helping my sisters according to the little strength that I had.”

When she was about thirteen, she went with her mother and sister to visit the women’s quarters of a prince who had four wives. The eldest had borne him two sons, and her rooms were bright with happiness. The other three had no children, and their faces, she remembered, were “sad and careworn; there seemed no hope for them in this world, since their lord was displeased with them, on account of their misfortune.” She never forgot that either. When she came to write her book about the women of India, it was one of the scenes she described.

She saw such things as a Hindu girl, and as a Hindu girl she did not yet know what to make of them. The teaching around her, as she later described it in The High-Caste Hindu Woman, did not tell her they were wrong. It told her that a woman’s suffering was the result of sins in a former life, and that her only hope lay in pleasing her husband. Her own parents had broken with that teaching in their own home. But the questions it raised were only beginning to take shape in her mind.

Stone and Silence

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from a psalm that mocks the idols of the nations. “They have mouths, but they speak not; Eyes have they, but they see not.” It is a hard verse to use about the religion of a family that was sincere, learned, and devout, and it should be used carefully. Anant Shastri and Lakshmibai were not fools. They knew, Ramabai later wrote, that they did not worship the stone images themselves, but the gods whom the images represented. “We knew the Vedanta, and knew, also, that we worshipped not the images, but some gods whom they represented.”

And yet, she went on, “all our learning and superior knowledge was of no avail. We bowed to the idols, as thousands of learned Brahmans do. We expected them to speak to us in wonderful oracles.” What she remembered, looking back, was not that the images were ugly or that her parents were foolish. It was the silence. “The stone images remained as hard as ever, and never answered our prayers.” She was writing of the last years before her parents died, when the family prayed day and night for wealth and help; but the silence was the same silence she had met at Dwarka.

When she wrote those words in 1897, she added a verse from the prophet Jeremiah, in the old version she knew. In the American Standard Version it reads: “every goldsmith is put to shame by his graven image; for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them” (Jeremiah 10:14, ASV). For the child at Dwarka, staring at the sunset clouds and seeing no golden city, there was no such verse. There was only the quiet suspicion that the promises were not true, and the knowledge that one must not say so.

Her family was not unusual in its questions. Many devout Hindus of that age, and many before and since, have looked beyond the images and the priests toward a God who could not be seen or bought. Ramabai was not yet looking for Christ. She did not know that he existed. But she was learning, as she stood among the silent pilgrims at Dwarka, that she would rather know the truth than pretend to see what was not there. That habit of mind would lead her, in the end, a very long way.

fields.title: The Famine
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.”

— Psalm 27:10, ASV

Twenty Years Later

In January 1897 Ramabai sat down in Poona to thank the friends who had helped her and to describe her first journey into the famine districts of Central India. Before she described their sufferings, she described her own. “I feel deeply for these poor dying people,” she wrote, “because I have myself [known] what it is to suffer from hunger and thirst, and have seen my dearest relatives die of starvation.” She said she would never have written the story down, “had not the necessity of my present situation obliged me to do so.” It is the fullest account we have of how her family died, and this chapter follows it closely.

She dated it “some twenty-two years ago,” in a famine that reached its height in the Madras Presidency in 1876-77 but had begun at least three years before. Later in the same pamphlet she calls herself “a girl of sixteen” at the time, and Rachel Bodley, who heard the story from her in 1887, gives the same age. That would place their deaths in about 1874 or 1875, in the early years of the famine, not at its peak. She gives no year.

A Famine of Their Own Making

Ramabai did not blame the weather for all of it. Her father, she explained, had once been a landholder and an honoured pandit who had earned wealth by his learning. But as he grew old and blind he lost it all “in one way or another.” His children had no secular education, and no trade.

We had all the sacred learning necessary to lead an honest religious life; but the pride of caste and superior learning and vanity of life prevented our stooping down to acquire some industry whereby we might have saved the precious lives of our parents.

In short we had no common sense, and foolishly spent all the money we had in hand in giving alms to Brahmans to please the gods, who, we thought, would send a shower of gold mohurs upon us and make us rich and happy.

In A Testimony she described it more simply. The sacred books promised that if people worshipped the gods in the prescribed ways, gave alms, fasted, and repeated the holy names, the gods would appear and give them what they asked. “We decided to take this course of meeting our temporal wants. For three years we did nothing but perform these religious acts. At last all the money which we had was spent, but the gods did not help us. We suffered from famine, which we had brought upon ourselves.”

Her brother Srinivas, “a stalwart young fellow of twenty-one,” ruined his health by fasting for months on end. When the money was gone, the family sold their jewellery, their good clothes, their silver, and at last their cooking pots of brass and copper, and gave the money to the Brahmans. They lived on a little coarse rice until the last grain was eaten. “Oh, the sorrow, the helplessness, and the disgrace of the situation!”

The Forest at Tirupati

They were staying at Tirupati, the hill shrine where Ramabai’s memories of religion began. There, after a long discussion, they decided that it would be better to go into the forest and die than bear the disgrace of poverty among their own people. That night they left their lodging and walked into the jungle. For eleven days and nights they lived on water, leaves, and a handful of wild dates.

At last her father, old, blind, and starving, could bear no more. He decided to drown himself in a sacred pool nearby, which in Hindu belief was not suicide but a holy death. It was suggested that the rest of the family should do the same. First he said goodbye to each of his children, one by one. Ramabai, the youngest, came last.

I shall never forget his last injunctions to me. His blind eyes could not see my face, but he held me tight in his arms; and, stroking my head and cheeks, he told me in a few words, broken with emotion, to remember how he loved me, and how he taught me to do right, and never depart from the way of righteousness. His last loving command to me was to lead an honorable life, if I lived at all, and serve God all my life.

“Remember, my child,” he said, “you are my youngest, my most beloved child. I have given you into the hands of our God. You are His, and to Him alone you must belong and serve all your life.”

She was too bewildered to answer. Twenty years later, as a Christian, she wrote: “He did not know the only true God, but served the, to him, unknown God with all his heart and strength.” She was thinking of Paul in Athens, who found an altar inscribed “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD,” and said to the Athenians, “What therefore ye worship in ignorance, this I set forth unto you” (Acts 17:23, ASV). “I can now say to the departed spirit of the loving parent, ‘Yes, dear father, I will serve the only true God to the last.’ But I could not say so when my father spoke to me for the last time.”

Her father asked for an hour alone to prepare for death. Then Srinivas stepped in. He could not bear to watch his father drown himself, he said. They would give up their pride of caste and go to work. He would carry their father down the mountain himself, and find work in the nearest village. Their father agreed. “Our hearts were gladdened,” Ramabai wrote, “and we prepared to start from the forest. And yet we wished very much that a tiger, a great snake, or some other wild animal would put an end to our lives. We were too weak to move, and too proud to beg or work to earn a livelihood.”

Sugar and Water

It took them nearly two days to drag themselves out of the forest to a village at the foot of the hill. They took shelter in a temple, but the Brahman priests turned them out. They moved into the ruins of an old temple outside the village, where nothing lived but wild animals. A young Brahman, seeing their helplessness, gave them some food.

On the day they reached the village her father fell ill with fever. “On the first day, at the beginning of his last illness, he asked for a little sugar and water. We gave him water, but could not give sugar.” He could not eat the coarse food they had. He became unconscious, and died on the morning of the third day.

No one in the village would help to carry his body. The young Brahman who had fed them paid for a grave to be dug, but he dared not touch the corpse himself, for fear of losing caste, since he was not sure they were Brahmans. Before his death Anant Shastri had taken the vows of a sannyasi, a holy man, and so he was to be buried, not burned. “As there was no one else who could help to carry the dead, my brother tied the body in his dhoti, like a bundle, and carried it alone over two miles to its last resting-place. We sadly followed to the river bank, and helped him a little.” They buried him outside the village, away from any house, and went back to the ruined temple.

Raichur

That same evening her mother fell ill with fever. There was no work and no food, and they could not stay. They walked for a time with their sick mother, and then some kind people gave them a little food and the fare to the town of Raichur. There they stayed for some weeks, too weak to go on. Srinivas could not work, and they could not bring themselves to beg. Now and then someone gave them something to eat.

One day her mother was so hungry that she sent Ramabai to a neighbour’s house to ask for a piece of bajri bread, the coarse millet bread of the poor.

I went there very reluctantly. The lady spoke kindly to me, but I could on no account open my mouth to beg that piece of bajree bread. With superhuman effort and a firm resolution to keep my feelings from that lady, I kept the tears back; but they poured out of my nose instead of my eyes, in spite of me, and the expression of my face told its own story.

The woman understood, and asked if she wanted some food. “So I said, ‘Yes, I want only a little piece of bajree bread.’ She gave me what I wanted; and I felt very grateful, but could not say a word to express my gratitude. I ran to my mother in great haste, and gave it to her. But she could not eat, she was too weak.” A few days later her mother died.

This time two Brahmans came to help, and with them Ramabai and her brother carried their mother’s body to the burning-ground, about three miles from the town. Bodley adds a detail that Ramabai must have told her: that because she was so short, she carried her share of the weight on her head.

Her sister Krishnabai died soon afterwards. “My elder sister also died of starvation, after suffering from illness and hunger. During those few months before our sister died, we three travelled on foot from place to place in search of food and work; but we could not get much of either.” We do not know where she died, or when.

Taken Up

Within a few months, then, Ramabai lost her father, her mother, and her sister. She was about sixteen. Only her brother was left.

The verse at the head of this chapter is David’s: “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” Ramabai’s parents had not forsaken her. They had loved her to the end, and her father’s last act had been to give her into the hands of God, the only God he knew. She did not yet know the God who would take her up. But she came to believe that he had already done so, in that forest above Tirupati. “My father’s prayers for me were, no doubt, heard by the Almighty, the all-merciful heavenly Father, whom the old Hindu did not know.”

She carried the memory for the rest of her life. “The memory of the last days of their life, full of sorrow, almost breaks my heart,” she wrote in 1897. And it shaped her work in a way she could not have foreseen. Years later, Ramabai told her daughter: “When you go to Raichur, think of my mother, and remember that it was there that I got my inspiration for famine work.”

fields.title: Four Thousand Miles
fields.body_html:
“They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way; They found no city of habitation. Hungry and thirsty, Their soul fainted in them. Then they cried unto Jehovah in their trouble, And he delivered them out of their distresses,”

— Psalm 107:4-6, ASV

Two Left

After their sister’s death, Ramabai and Srinivas were alone in the world. She was about sixteen. He was a few years older, the young man who had carried his father’s body two miles in a cloth. They had no home, no money, no relatives who would take them in, and no training for any work but the reading of Sanskrit scriptures in public places. For the next three years and more they walked.

“My brother and myself continued our sad pilgrimage,” she wrote in 1897, “to the northern boundary of India and back to the east as far as Calcutta.” In A Testimony she gave the distance:

We wandered from place to place, visiting many temples, bathing in many rivers, fasting and performing penances, worshipping gods, trees, animals, Brahmins, etc., for more than three years after the death of our parents and elder sister. We had walked more than four thousand miles on foot without any sort of comfort, sometimes eating what kind people gave us and sometimes going without food, with poor coarse clothing, and finding but little shelter except in dharma shalas (i.e., free lodging places for the poor), which are common to all pilgrims and travellers of all sorts except the low caste people. We wandered from the south to the north, as far as Cashmere, and then to the east, and went to Calcutta in 1878.

The figure of four thousand miles is her own, and there is no reason to doubt it. It is roughly the distance from the southern tip of India to Kashmir and across to Calcutta, with the detours that pilgrims make. Later retellings sometimes attach it to her whole childhood of pilgrimage, or inflate it. It belongs to these years, and to these two.

Four Rupees a Month

Srinivas found work where he could. “Brother got work here and there,” she wrote, “but most of the time we lived a wanderer’s life. Very often we had to go without food for days. Even when my brother had work to do, he got so little wages, only four rupees a month, and sometimes much less than that, that we were obliged to live on a handful of grain soaked in water and a little salt.”

They had no blankets or warm clothes. They walked barefoot, without umbrellas against the sun or the rain, and slept “either under the trees on the roadside or under the arches of bridges, or lie down on the ground in the open air.” Sometimes they were so hungry that they ate handfuls of wild berries, “swallowing the hard stones together with their coarse skins.”

One night in the far north, they stopped on the banks of the Jhelum river, in the Punjab.

Once on the banks of the Jhelum, a river in the Punjab, we were obliged to rest at night in the open air, and tried to keep off the intense cold by digging two gravelike pits, and putting ourselves into them and covering our bodies — except the heads — with dry sand of the river bank.

It is one of the most unforgettable pictures in her writings: a brother and sister, the children of a learned pandit, lying in two graves of their own digging on the river bank, with only their heads above the sand.

She did not dramatise it. “Four long years we suffered from scarcity. We did not mind it much, as we were young and strong. We could stand it much better than our poor old parents and weak sister.”

Losing Faith

They kept up their religious observances all the way. They bathed in the holy rivers, visited the temples, fasted, performed penances, and worshipped whatever the scriptures told them to worship. But their faith was draining away. “We had fulfilled all the conditions laid down in the sacred books and kept all the rules as far as our knowledge went, but the gods were not pleased with us and did not appear to us. After years of fruitless service we began to lose our faith in them and in the books which prescribed this course and held out the hope of a great reward to the worshippers of the gods.”

They did not abandon their religion. “We still continued to keep caste rules, and worshipped gods and studied sacred literature as usual.” But it no longer held them as it had. And as it loosened its grip, they became less strict about the rule that had cost their parents their lives: the rule against secular learning and ordinary work. “As our faith in our religion had grown cold we were not quite so strict with regard to obtaining secular education and finding some means of earning an honest livelihood.”

Some of her admirers later told stories of these years that she did not tell herself. One says that she worked as a cook in a high-caste household while her brother taught. Another describes Srinivas swimming out at dawn across a Himalayan lake to discover that the “floating mountains” the pilgrims came to see were rafts pushed by priests. Neither appears in any of her own accounts, and this book does not rely on them. Her own story is remarkable enough.

A Heart of Stone

What did these years do to her? It would be natural to say that her own hunger taught her compassion for the hungry, and that she learned on the roads of India to feel for the poor. Twenty years later, as she set out to rescue famine children, she herself warned against saying anything so simple.

Yet I must say that suffering alone is not able to produce sympathy for other sufferers. My own experience of the unconverted state of mind, and the present knowledge of my fellow country women and girls, whom I have ample opportunity to study, shows that suffering in itself has rather a hardening effect on the human heart. It takes away almost all delicate feelings from the soul, making it as hard as a stone.

It is a striking thing for her to have written, and a brave one. She did not claim that she had come out of the famine a better person. She said that, left to itself, suffering hardens the heart. She understood now, she went on, what God meant when he spoke through Ezekiel: “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26, ASV). What changed her heart, she believed, was not suffering but grace.

This is worth remembering as the story goes on. The woman who later walked into the famine camps of Central India was not simply acting out of memory. She had known hunger, and she had also known what hunger does to the soul. She knew that pity could die. She believed it had been brought back to life in her.

The Wilderness Way

The psalm at the head of this chapter describes wanderers in the desert, hungry and thirsty, who “found no city of habitation.” Ramabai and Srinivas had spent their childhood walking from one sacred city to another, and now they walked through city after city and found no home in any of them. The psalm goes on: “Then they cried unto Jehovah in their trouble, And he delivered them out of their distresses.”

They did not yet know to whom to cry. But as they turned east, towards Calcutta, the greatest city of British India, they were walking, without knowing it, towards the next turning of their lives. There, for the first time, people would listen to her. And there, for the first time, she would meet Christians.

After years of fruitless service we began to lose our faith in them and in the books which prescribed this course and held out the hope of a great reward to the worshippers of the gods.” They did not abandon their religion. “We still continued to keep caste rules, and worshipped gods and studied sacred literature as usual.” But it no longer held them as it had. What changed her heart, she believed, was not suffering but grace. This is worth remembering as the story goes on. The woman who later walked into the famine camps of Central India was not simply acting out of memory. She had known hunger, and she had also known what hunger does to the soul. She knew that pity could die. She believed it had been brought back to life in her. The Wilderness Way The psalm at the head of this chapter describes wanderers in the desert, hungry and thirsty, who “found no city of habitation.” Ramabai and Srinivas had spent their childhood walking from one sacred city to another, and now they walked through city after city and found no home in any of them. The psalm goes on: “Then they cried unto Jehovah in their trouble, And he delivered them out of their distresses.” They did not yet know to whom to cry. But as they turned east, towards Calcutta, the greatest city of British India, they were walking, without knowing it, towards the next turning of their lives. There, for the first time, people would listen to her. And there, for the first time, she would meet Christians.

fields.title: Pandita
fields.body_html:
“But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? Man knoweth not the price thereof; Neither is it found in the land of the living.”

— Job 28:12-13, ASV

Calcutta

In 1878 Ramabai and Srinivas reached Calcutta. It was the capital of British India, a city of great wealth and great poverty, of English offices and Bengali mansions, of colleges, printing presses, and newspapers, and it was in the middle of an intellectual ferment that historians would later call the Bengal Renaissance. Educated Bengalis were arguing about everything: religion, caste, the place of women, the relation between Indian tradition and European learning. Into this city walked a young woman of about twenty who could recite thousands of verses of Sanskrit poetry from memory, compose Sanskrit verse on the spot, and speak with authority about the Hindu scriptures. She caused a sensation.

“We stayed in Calcutta for about a year,” she wrote, “and became acquainted with the learned Brahmins.” By now she and her brother had moved a long way from the religion of their parents. By her own account, as Macnicol reports it, two years before Srinivas’s death they had given up much of their faith in the Hindu gods and adopted a simple belief in one God. But they still kept caste, and much of their thinking was still the thinking of devout Brahmans.

The Christians

In Calcutta, for the first time, they met Christians. They were invited to a Christian social gathering, and were shocked when they were offered refreshments. “We thought the Last Age, Kali Yuga, that is, the age of quarrels, darkness and irreligion had fully established its reign in Calcutta, since some of the Brahmans were so irreligious as to eat food with the English.” Then they watched the Christians pray.

We looked upon the proceedings of the assembly with curiosity, but did not understand what they were about. After a little while one of them opened a book and read something out of it, and then they all knelt down before their chairs and some said something with closed eyes. We were told that was the way they prayed to God. We did not see any image to which they paid their homage, but it seemed as though they were paying homage to the chairs before which they knelt.

Before they left, the Christians gave her a copy of the Bible in Sanskrit. Two of the men there, she remembered, were its translators, “grand old men,” whose names she had forgotten. “I liked the outward appearance of the book and tried to read it, but did not understand. The language was so different from the Sanskrit literature of the Hindus, the teaching so different, that I thought it quite a waste of time to read that Book; but I have never parted with it since then.”

Sarasvati

The learned men of Calcutta were fascinated by her. Macnicol records that she was welcomed at the Calcutta Senate House by three Sanskrit professors, two of them Englishmen, who chanted her praises in Sanskrit verse, and that she answered them at once in an extempore Sanskrit poem. “I am not worthy of the praise you have showered upon me,” she said. “I am only a humble worshipper in your temple of Saraswati.” Saraswati is the Hindu goddess of learning. Soon afterwards an assembly of the city’s pandits, after examining her, gave her the title Sarasvati itself.

The other title by which she has been known ever since, Pandita, the feminine of pandit, a learned scholar, seems to have come by popular acclaim rather than formal grant. From that time she was known as Pandita Ramabai. Her admirers later claimed that she was the first woman, or the only woman, ever to be given these honours. No one really knows whether that is true, and this book does not repeat it. It is enough that a young woman, orphaned and penniless, with no formal schooling, was hailed by the scholars of the capital as a master of the sacred learning.

Many years later, Macnicol noted, she counted all this as nothing. But at the time it mattered, and not only to her. A Bombay newspaper wrote that “the patriotic among us ought to feel proud that there is, even in our fallen condition, one such among their sisters who would do credit to the female sex in any country.” She had shown, in her own person, what an Indian woman could do if she were taught.

What the Books Said

Her fame brought an invitation that changed her life. Some of the pandits asked her to lecture to women in purdah, the high-caste women who lived secluded from the world, on the duties of women according to the Hindu scriptures. To prepare, she bought the Hindu law-books, the Dharma Shastras, and read them carefully for the first time. She had been taught the popular scriptures, not the law. Now she discovered what the law said about her.

She found, first of all, that the books contradicted each other on almost everything. “What one book said was most righteous, the other book declared as being unrighteous.” She quoted a line from the epic Mahabharata: “The Vedas differ from each other; Smritis do not agree with one another; the secret of religion is in some hidden place.” But on two things, she found, every authority was agreed.

There were two things on which all these books — the Dharma Shastras, the sacred epics, the Puranas and modern poets, the popular preachers of the present day, and orthodox high caste men, all were agreed — that women of high and low caste, as a class, were bad, very bad, worse than demons, as unholy as untruth; and that they could not get Moksha as men.

A woman, the books taught, could not attain moksha, liberation from the endless round of death and rebirth. Her only hope was to worship her husband as her god, however wicked he might be, and so earn the merit to be born again, in some later life, as a man. The same was true of the lowest castes, the Shudras and those beneath them, who were forbidden even to hear the Vedas.

She had known something of this all her life. Now it came home to her with overwhelming force.

My eyes were being gradually opened; I was waking up to my own hopeless condition as a woman, and it was becoming clearer and clearer to me that I had no place anywhere as far as religious consolation was concerned. I became quite dissatisfied with myself. I wanted something more than the Shastras could give me, but I did not know what it was that I wanted.

Her father had taught her mother Sanskrit because he believed that women could learn. He had defended himself before an assembly of pandits, and won. But the books he revered, she now found, held out no hope for the women he had taught. The books her family had followed into the forest had nothing to say to her, as a woman, except that she must wait to be born a man.

Keshab

Among the people who wanted to meet her was Keshab Chandra Sen, the most famous religious reformer in India. Keshab was the leader of the Brahmo Samaj of India, a movement that rejected image worship and caste and taught the worship of one God, drawing on the Upanishads, on other religions, and not least on the teaching of Jesus. He invited Ramabai and her brother to his house, took her into the inner rooms to meet his wife and daughters, and when she left he gave her a copy of one of the Vedas.

He asked if I had studied the Vedas. I answered in the negative, and said that women were not fit to read the Vedas, and they were not allowed to do so. I would be breaking the rules of religion if I were to study the Vedas. He could not but smile at my declaration of this Hindu doctrine. He said nothing in answer, but advised me to study the Vedas and Upanishads.

It was a small thing, a smile, but it was enough. “New thoughts were awakening in my heart. I questioned myself why I should not study the Vedas and Vedanta. Soon I persuaded myself into the belief that it was not wrong for a woman to read the Vedas. So I began first to read the Upanishads, then the Vedanta, and the Veda.”

Some of her early biographers later said that Keshab gave her a book of selections from the scriptures of all religions, including the Sermon on the Mount, as if the path to Christ had begun that day. Ramabai’s own account says only that he gave her a Veda. Hers is the account this book follows. What Keshab gave her was not the Gospel, but permission: the permission to read what she had been told she must not read, and to think for herself about it.

Where Wisdom Is Found

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Job, from a poem about the search for wisdom. Men dig for silver and gold, the poet says, and find precious stones in the depths of the earth. “But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?” It is not in the mines, not in the sea, and it cannot be bought with gold. Ramabai had more of the wisdom of her people than almost anyone of her age in India. She had just been honoured for it by the scholars of Calcutta. And she had found, at the bottom of it all, that it held no place for her.

The poem in Job ends with an answer: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; And to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28, ASV). She did not know that answer yet. The Sanskrit Bible lay half-read among her books. But she had begun to ask the right question.

fields.title: Nineteen Months
fields.body_html:
“Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed: neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth; and the reproach of thy widowhood shalt thou remember no more. For thy Maker is thy husband; Jehovah of hosts is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is thy Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called.”

— Isaiah 54:4-5, ASV

Srinivas

From Calcutta, Ramabai and her brother travelled on through Bengal and into Assam, lecturing and being received with honour. Then, in 1880, Srinivas fell ill and died. Macnicol places his death at Dacca in May 1880. Other early accounts say Calcutta. The details are uncertain, but what passed between them in his illness, as she wrote it for Rachel Bodley, is not.

His great thought during his brief illness was for me; what would become of me left alone in the world? When he spoke of his anxiety, I answered: “There is no one but God to care for you and me.” “Ah,” he answered, “then if God cares for us, I am afraid of nothing.” And, indeed, in my loneliness, it seemed as if God was near me; I felt His presence.

She was twenty-two. Her father, her mother, her sister, and now her brother were dead. Some of her admirers later retold the exchange in tidier words. In her own telling it is simpler and braver: there was no one but God to care for either of them, and her dying brother found that enough.

A Marriage Across Caste

Six months later she married. Her husband was Bipin Behari Medhavi, a Bengali lawyer with a master’s degree and a law degree from the University of Calcutta, who had been a friend of her brother’s. He was not a Brahman. Ramabai described him as “a Bengali gentleman of the Shudra caste.” He was in fact a Kayastha, a respected caste of scribes and officials, but orthodox Brahmans counted such men as Shudras, and for a Brahman woman to marry one was, in their eyes, a scandal and a pollution.

She married him knowing all this, and she said plainly why. “Having lost all faith in the religion of my ancestors I married a Bengali gentleman of the Shudra caste.” Neither of them wished to be married with Hindu or Christian rites. “We neither of us believed either in Hinduism or Christianity,” she told Bodley, “and so we were married with the civil marriage rite.” Modern scholars date the marriage to November 1880. In Poona, Mrs. Ramabai Ranade later recalled, orthodox women gossiped that the “horrid creature” had been married to Krishna at Dwarka by her father and had then gone and married a Bengali — a story Ramabai herself denounced as wholly false.

They made their home at Silchar, a small town in the Cachar district of Assam, where Bipin practised law. In the spring of 1881 a daughter was born. They had longed for a daughter, Bodley was told, and the name was waiting for her: Manorama, “heart’s joy.”

A Pamphlet in the Library

At Silchar something happened that seemed small at the time.

While living with my husband at Silchar, Assam, I had found a little pamphlet in my library. I do not know how it came there, but I picked it up and began to read it with great interest. It was Luke’s Gospel in the Bengali language.

There was a Baptist missionary in the town, a Mr. Allen, who sometimes visited them and spoke about the gospel. He explained to her the first chapter of Genesis. “The story of the creation of the world was so very unlike all the stories which I read in the Puranas and Shastras that I became greatly interested in it. It struck me as being a true story, but I could not give any reason for thinking so or believing in it.”

She read and asked questions, and she told her husband that she meant to become a Christian if she were fully satisfied that it was true. Bipin was not pleased.

My husband, who had studied in a mission school, was pretty well acquainted with the Bible, but did not like to be called a Christian. Much less did he like the idea of his wife being publicly baptised and joining the despised Christian community. He was very angry, and said he would tell Mr. Allen not to come to our house any more. I do not know just what would have happened had he lived.

It is a telling scene. The husband who had defied his caste to marry her was not prepared for her to defy it further. Crossing caste in marriage was radical, but a Hindu reformer could do it and remain respectable in progressive circles. Becoming a Christian meant joining a community that most Hindus regarded as outcast, “the despised Christian community,” and it would have cost him dearly.

Cholera

He did not live. Early in 1882, probably in February, Bipin Medhavi died of cholera. Ramabai remembered the marriage as “nineteen months of happy married life,” though the dates that modern scholars give suggest it was closer to fifteen months. Manorama was less than a year old.

“My husband died of cholera within two years of our marriage,” she wrote in A Testimony, “and I was left alone to face the world with one baby in my arms.”

To understand what this meant, we have to remember what it meant to be a widow in Hindu India. A widow was believed to be to blame for her husband’s death, through sins in this life or a former one. Among the higher castes she could not remarry. Her head was shaved, her jewellery taken away, and she wore coarse clothing for the rest of her life. She ate one meal a day and fasted often. She was kept away from weddings and festivals because her presence was unlucky. She was often treated as a servant by her husband’s family. And child-widows, girls who had been married as infants and widowed before they had ever lived with their husbands, suffered all this from childhood to old age.

Ramabai was spared most of it. She had married outside Hindu custom, and she did not follow its rules for widows. But she knew them from the inside, and she had seen what they did. Now she was twenty-three, alone, with no family, a baby daughter, and no home.

“He Must Himself Draw Me”

She did not despair. In the grief of those months, she said, God seemed nearer, not further away. “This great grief drew me nearer to God. I felt that He was teaching me, and that if I was to come to Him, He must Himself draw me.”

That is a remarkable sentence for someone who was not yet a Christian. She did not yet know who God was. She had lost her faith in the gods of her fathers, she was not satisfied with the religion of the Brahmos, and she had only begun to read the Christian scriptures. But she had grasped something that many Christians take years to understand: that she could not find her own way to God, and that if she was to come to him, he must bring her. Jesus said the same: “No man can come to me, except the Father that sent me draw him” (John 6:44, ASV).

Years later she described her state of mind at this time. “I was desperately in need of some religion. The Hindu religion held out no hope for me; the Brahmo religion was not a very definite one, for it is nothing but what a man makes for himself. … It could not and did not satisfy me; still I liked and believed a good deal of it that was better than what the orthodox Hindu religion taught.”

Thy Maker Is Thy Husband

The words at the head of this chapter were spoken by the prophet Isaiah to Israel in exile, pictured as a widow, forsaken and ashamed. “Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed … the reproach of thy widowhood shalt thou remember no more. For thy Maker is thy husband.”

Ramabai would come to know these words, and to see in them a promise for every widow of India. In the Hindu world, a woman’s husband was her god, and when he died her hope died with him. The Bible told her the opposite: that God himself would be a husband to the widow, that her widowhood was not her disgrace, and that she need not be ashamed. She would spend her life telling that to the widows of India. But first she had to learn it herself.

She did not go back to Calcutta. All her family were gone, and there was no one to go back to. She went first to Madras, meaning to learn English there, but found the language of the south wholly strange to her. So in 1882, with her baby, she went west, to the city where her father had studied as a young man and first heard a woman reciting Sanskrit: to Poona.
