They made their home at Silchar, a small town in the Cachar district of Assam, where Bipin practised law. In the spring of 1881 a daughter was born. They had longed for a daughter, Bodley was told, and the name was waiting for her: Manorama, “heart’s joy.” A Pamphlet in the Library At Silchar something happened that seemed small at the time. While living with my husband at Silchar, Assam, I had found a little pamphlet in my library. I do not know how it came there, but I picked it up and began to read it with great interest. It was Luke’s Gospel in the Bengali language. There was a Baptist missionary in the town, a Mr. Allen, who sometimes visited them and spoke about the gospel. He explained to her the first chapter of Genesis. “The story of the creation of the world was so very unlike all the stories which I read in the Puranas and Shastras that I became greatly interested in it. It struck me as being a true story, but I could not give any reason for thinking so or believing in it.” She read and asked questions, and she told her husband that she meant to become a Christian if she were fully satisfied that it was true. Bipin was not pleased. My husband, who had studied in a mission school, was pretty well acquainted with the Bible, but did not like to be called a Christian. Much less did he like the idea of his wife being publicly baptised and joining the despised Christian community. He was very angry, and said he would tell Mr. Allen not to come to our house any more. I do not know just what would have happened had he lived. It is a telling scene. The husband who had defied his caste to marry her was not prepared for her to defy it further. Crossing caste in marriage was radical, but a Hindu reformer could do it and remain respectable in progressive circles. Becoming a Christian meant joining a community that most Hindus regarded as outcast, “the despised Christian community,” and it would have cost him dearly. Cholera He did not live. Early in 1882, probably in February, Bipin Medhavi died of cholera. Ramabai remembered the marriage as “nineteen months of happy married life,” though the dates that modern scholars give suggest it was closer to fifteen months. Manorama was less than a year old. “My husband died of cholera within two years of our marriage,” she wrote in A Testimony, “and I was left alone to face the world with one baby in my arms.” To understand what this meant, we have to remember what it meant to be a widow in Hindu India. A widow was believed to be to blame for her husband’s death, through sins in this life or a former one. Among the higher castes she could not remarry. Her head was shaved, her jewellery taken away, and she wore coarse clothing for the rest of her life. She ate one meal a day and fasted often. She was kept away from weddings and festivals because her presence was unlucky. She was often treated as a servant by her husband’s family. And child-widows, girls who had been married as infants and widowed before they had ever lived with their husbands, suffered all this from childhood to old age. Ramabai was spared most of it. She had married outside Hindu custom, and she did not follow its rules for widows. But she knew them from the inside, and she had seen what they did. Now she was twenty-three, alone, with no family, a baby daughter, and no home. “He Must Himself Draw Me” She did not despair. In the grief of those months, she said, God seemed nearer, not further away. “This great grief drew me nearer to God. I felt that He was teaching me, and that if I was to come to Him, He must Himself draw me.” That is a remarkable sentence for someone who was not yet a Christian. She did not yet know who God was. She had lost her faith in the gods of her fathers, she was not satisfied with the religion of the Brahmos, and she had only begun to read the Christian scriptures. But she had grasped something that many Christians take years to understand: that she could not find her own way to God, and that if she was to come to him, he must bring her. Jesus said the same: “No man can come to me, except the Father that sent me draw him” (John 6:44, ASV). Years later she described her state of mind at this time. “I was desperately in need of some religion. The Hindu religion held out no hope for me; the Brahmo religion was not a very definite one, for it is nothing but what a man makes for himself. … It could not and did not satisfy me; still I liked and believed a good deal of it that was better than what the orthodox Hindu religion taught.” Thy Maker Is Thy Husband The words at the head of this chapter were spoken by the prophet Isaiah to Israel in exile, pictured as a widow, forsaken and ashamed. “Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed … the reproach of thy widowhood shalt thou remember no more. For thy Maker is thy husband.” Ramabai would come to know these words, and to see in them a promise for every widow of India. In the Hindu world, a woman’s husband was her god, and when he died her hope died with him. The Bible told her the opposite: that God himself would be a husband to the widow, that her widowhood was not her disgrace, and that she need not be ashamed. She would spend her life telling that to the widows of India. But first she had to learn it herself. She did not go back to Calcutta. All her family were gone, and there was no one to go back to. She went first to Madras, meaning to learn English there, but found the language of the south wholly strange to her. So in 1882, with her baby, she went west, to the city where her father had studied as a young man and first heard a woman reciting Sanskrit: to Poona.

fields.title: “Open Thy Mouth for the Dumb”
fields.body_html:
“Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, And minister justice to the poor and needy.”

— Proverbs 31:8-9, ASV

Poona

Poona in 1882 was the intellectual capital of western India, and it was divided. On one side stood the reformers, men such as Mahadev Govind Ranade, a judge, and R. G. Bhandarkar, a great Sanskrit scholar, members of a society called the Prarthana Samaj, the Prayer Society, which worshipped one God and worked cautiously for social change: the education of women, the raising of the age of marriage, the remarriage of widows. On the other side stood the orthodox, who saw in every such change an attack on Hindu society and on the Hindu nation, and whose leading voice in the coming years would be the brilliant young journalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

The reformers welcomed Ramabai. “The leaders of the reform party, and the members of the Prarthana Samaj treated me with great kindness and gave me some help,” she wrote. “Messrs. Ranade, Modak, Kelkar, and Dr. Bhandarkar were among the people who showed great kindness to me.” She gave readings from the Puranas at the Ranades’ house. Ranade’s young wife, also named Ramabai, who would become a pioneer of women’s education herself, never forgot her. “The sweet and musical flow of her speech and the manner in which she presented her subject were alike admirable,” Mrs. Ranade remembered. “In addition she had amazing skill in winning the hearts of her hearers for whatever she had to say.”

The Arya Mahila Samaj

Within a few months of her arrival, Ramabai founded a society of women. She called it the Arya Mahila Samaj, the Aryan Women’s Society. Its aims, as Macnicol records them, were “to work for the deliverance of women from the evil practices (e.g., child-marriage, the bondage of ignorance, etc.) which by tradition and custom have come down to India from the past,” and to work for the raising of women’s condition “in respect of religion, morality, etc.” It met on Saturdays, and she travelled from city to city in the Bombay Presidency founding branches of it.

It was one of the earliest organisations in India founded and led by a woman to work for women, and she did not mince her words. “Men look on us women as chattels,” she declared in June 1882. “We make every effort to deliver ourselves from this situation. But some will say that this is a rebellion against man, and that to do this is sin. To leave men’s evil acts unrebuked and remain unmoved before them is a great sin.”

That was more than orthodox Poona was ready to hear. The orthodox press attacked her almost at once. The Poona newspaper Kesari, which Tilak had helped to found, was criticising her by the summer of 1882.

She also wrote a small book in Marathi, Stri Dharma Niti, “Morals for Women,” a practical guide for women on how to improve their minds and manage their lives. It was, by later standards, a cautious book, which accepted a wife’s duties to her husband while urging women to educate themselves. But it contained one sentence that summed up her impatience with her country: “No spirit of daring, no ardour, no enterprise, no self-reliance, no anything — it is all No, no, no.” The sale of the book would help to pay for her voyage to England.

Before the Commission

In September 1882 the British government’s Education Commission, headed by Dr. W. W. Hunter, came to Poona to inquire into the state of education in India. The women of the Arya Mahila Samaj and others, some three hundred Brahman women with their children, gathered in the Town Hall to welcome the commissioners, to show them that the best families of the Maratha country wanted their daughters taught. Ramabai spoke for them. Then she gave evidence before the commission herself.

Hunter thought her evidence so important that he had it translated from Marathi and printed separately. She began by explaining who she was: the child of a man who had suffered for teaching women. “I consider it my duty,” she said, “to the very end of my life, to maintain this cause, and to advocate the proper position of women in this land.”

She asked for women teachers to be properly trained and properly paid, and for women inspectors of girls’ schools instead of men. Her reasons were blunt.

In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, the educated men of this country are opposed to Female Education and the proper position of woman. If they observe the slightest fault, they magnify the grain of mustard-seed into a mountain, and try to ruin the character of a woman. … Men being more able to reach the authorities are believed, while women go to the wall. … It is evident that women, being one-half of the people of this country, are oppressed and cruelly treated by the other half.

And she asked the government to train women doctors. “The women of this country are much more reserved than in other countries, and most of them would rather die than speak of their ailments to a man. The want of lady-doctors is, therefore, the cause of hundreds of thousands of women dying premature deaths.”

It was said at the time, on the authority of the Times of India, that her plea for women doctors reached the ears of Queen Victoria herself, and helped to inspire the movement later led by the Viceroy’s wife, Lady Dufferin, to provide medical care for Indian women. Rachel Bodley reported this as something that was “believed.” Whether or not it is true, the need Ramabai described was real, and she was among the first to describe it in public.

She was twenty-four. She had no degree, no position, and no family. But she had stood before a British commission and told it, in an answer the chairman later had printed, that the women of India were oppressed by the men. It was a courageous thing to do, and the verse at the head of this chapter describes it exactly: “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate.”

A Girl Who Had “Eaten Her Husband”

That same year, a Brahman child-widow of about twelve was brought to her. She had been married at five, and her boy husband had died a few days after the wedding. Her mother-in-law would not look at her. “She said the girl had eaten up her son and was a great demon.”

Ramabai took the girl to live with her. And as she looked at her, her plans began to take shape.

As I looked on that little figure my vague thoughts about doing something for my sisters in similar conditions began to take shape. … I began to place a plan for starting a Home for Hindu widows before my countrymen and to ask for their help. For six months or more I tried my best to get help, but could not. Then the thought came to me that I had better get a medical education and then do what I could to help widows. With that purpose I made up my mind to go to England, if the way opened for me.

She wrote those words many years later, as a Christian, and she added: “The unknown God, who was directing my steps toward the way of life, made it possible for me to carry out the purpose which He had put into my heart.”

Teachers

In Poona she met Christians again, and this time she listened more closely. A missionary of the Anglican High Church, Miss Hurford, came to teach her English and the New Testament in Marathi. “She used to teach me some lessons from the primary reading books, yet sometimes I was more interested in the study of the New Testament than in the reading books.”

Another visitor was Father Nehemiah Goreh. Goreh was, like Ramabai, a Chitpawan Brahman, a learned man who had become a Christian more than thirty years before and was now a priest of an Anglican religious order. He was gentle, humble, and a formidable scholar of Hindu philosophy. “The Rev. Father Goreh was another missionary who used to come and explain the difference between the Hindu and Christian religions,” she wrote. “I profited much by their teaching.” It was a book by Goreh that would later convince her of the truth of Christianity.

But she was not yet ready. Macnicol, citing Goreh’s biographer, records that she was said to have written to a vernacular newspaper around this time declaring that nothing would ever induce her to become a Christian. The letter itself has not been traced. If she said it, she had reason to. She had seen what becoming a Christian had cost others, and she knew what it would cost her in Poona.

The Sea

To go to England was itself an enormous step. For an orthodox Hindu of high caste, crossing the sea meant losing caste. For a woman, and a widow, to go alone with a small child to a country where she knew almost no one was almost unheard of. She knew it, and later wrote that a Hindu woman who crossed the sea cut herself off from her people for ever.

She went anyway. The Sisters of the Anglican Community of St. Mary the Virgin, at Wantage in Berkshire, to whom Miss Hurford had introduced her, agreed to receive her. In the spring of 1883, with Manorama, who was just two, and a young woman friend, Anandibai Bhagat, as her companion, she sailed from Bombay for England.

The Psalmist prayed that God would arise “To judge the fatherless and the oppressed, That man who is of the earth may be terrible no more” (Psalm 10:18, ASV). The girl who had “eaten up her son” was one of thousands, and Ramabai knew it. She was going to England to learn how to help them. God, as she later saw it, meant to teach her something more.

fields.title: As Abraham
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”

— Hebrews 11:8, ASV

Not Knowing Whither

Four years later, in Philadelphia, Ramabai tried to explain to Rachel Bodley what it had meant to leave India.

I could not have done this unless I had felt that my faith in God had become strong: it is such a great step for a Hindu woman to cross the sea; one cuts oneself always off from one’s people. But the voice came to me as to Abraham. … It seems to me now very strange how I could have started as I did with my friend and little child throwing myself on God’s protection. I went forth as Abraham, not knowing whither I went.

She was not yet a Christian. She had read some of the New Testament, and she had listened to Miss Hurford and Father Goreh. But she already knew the story of Abraham, and she already thought of her journey in its terms. The verse at the head of this chapter describes it: “he went out, not knowing whither he went.” God had said to Abram, “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto the land that I will show thee” (Genesis 12:1, ASV). Ramabai had no country, no kindred, and no father’s house left to leave. But she was leaving her caste and her people’s good opinion, and she knew she might never have them back.

Wantage

She landed in England in the spring of 1883, and the Sisters of the Community of St. Mary the Virgin met her at the ship and took her to their convent at Wantage, a market town at the foot of the Berkshire Downs, south-west of Oxford. The Wantage sisters were an Anglican religious order of the High Church kind, devoted to prayer, teaching, and works of mercy, with a house in Poona, where Miss Hurford had worked. One of them, almost certainly Sister Geraldine, took Ramabai under her care. “The Sisters took me to their Home,” Ramabai wrote, “and one of them who became my spiritual mother, began to teach me both secular and religious subjects.” She learned English there, and it was there that she spent her first year.

Her plan had been to study medicine. It did not work out. She was already partly deaf, whether from scarlet fever or from the hardships of her wandering years, and she was told that her deafness would make it impossible for her to train as a doctor. It was a hard blow. She had crossed the sea to become a doctor for the women of India, and now she could not.

A worse blow followed. Her friend and companion, Anandibai Bhagat, who had come with her from India, took her own life a few months after they arrived. The reasons have never been clear. Some people at the time, including the Oxford scholar Max Müller, suggested that the young woman had been terrified of being pressed to become a Christian. Others have seen other causes. None of her published accounts mentions it. She was twenty-five, and she had now lost her parents, her sister, her brother, her husband, and the friend who had come with her from India. For a time, it seems, she was badly shaken.

Fulham

Then something happened that she never forgot. The Mother Superior sent her for a change of air to one of the order’s houses in London, and there she was taken to see the rescue homes at Fulham, where the Sisters of the Cross worked among women who had been prostitutes.

The Sisters there took me to see the rescue work carried on by them. I met several of the women who had once been in their Rescue-Home, but who had so completely changed, and were so filled with the love of Christ and compassion for suffering humanity, that they had given their life for the service of the sick and infirm. Here for the first time in my life, I came to know that something should be done to reclaim the so-called fallen women, and that Christians, whom Hindus considered outcasts and cruel, were kind to these unfortunate women, degraded in the eyes of society.

She had never seen anything like it in India. “I had not heard anyone speaking kindly of them, nor seen any one making any effort to turn them from the evil path.” The Hindu law, she wrote, commanded that the king should cause such women “to be eaten by dogs in the outskirts of the town.” Here, the women whom society had cast out were nursing the sick in the name of Christ.

She asked the sister who was teaching her what it was that made Christians care for these women. The sister read to her the fourth chapter of John’s Gospel: the story of Jesus and the Samaritan woman at the well.

The Woman at the Well

It is not hard to see why that chapter struck her. The Samaritan woman belonged to a despised people, whom the Jews would not touch. She had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband. She came to the well at midday, alone, when the other women had gone. And Jesus, a Jewish teacher, spoke to her, asked her for a drink, told her the truth about her life without condemning her, and offered her “living water.” “Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4:14, ASV). She was the first person in John’s Gospel to whom Jesus plainly said that he was the Christ. And she went back to her town and told everyone.

Ramabai had spent months reading the Hindu law-books and discovering that they had nothing to say to a woman except that she was “worse than demons” and could hope for salvation only through her husband. Now she heard of a teacher who went out of his way to speak to a woman of the worst reputation, and offered her, directly, the gift of God.

She spoke of the Infinite Love of Christ for sinners. He did not despise them but came to save them. I had never read or heard anything like this in the religious books of the Hindus. I realized, after reading the fourth chapter of St. John’s Gospel, that Christ was truly the Divine Saviour He claimed to be, and no one but He could transform and uplift the downtrodden womanhood of India, and of every land.

“Thus my heart was drawn to the religion of Christ.”

Goreh’s Book

Her heart was drawn. Her mind still needed convincing, and she was not a woman who would believe anything without reasons. The reasons came, she said, from Father Goreh. “I was intellectually convinced of its truth on reading a book written by Father Goreh.” Goreh was the author of a searching critique of the Hindu philosophical systems from a Christian point of view. He also wrote to her from India, and she wrote of one of his letters: “His humble, sweet voice has pierced my heart. I think no one would have had the power of turning me from the Brahman religion but Father Goreh.”

It is worth noticing that the two voices that brought her to the point of faith were, one, a sister of an English order showing her Christians caring for outcast women, and, two, an Indian Brahman convert showing her, in her own intellectual tradition, why Christianity was true. She needed both. She was never satisfied with a faith that was only feeling, or with one that was only argument.

Baptism

On 29 September 1883, at Wantage, Ramabai was baptised in the Church of England, and Manorama with her. She took the baptismal name Mary. According to Macnicol, she was baptised in Wantage parish church by Canon William Butler, the founder of the order, with Sister Geraldine among the witnesses; later accounts call Geraldine her godmother. She was later confirmed.

She was calm about it, not ecstatic. “I was comparatively happy,” she wrote, “and felt a great joy in finding a new religion which was better than any other religion I had known before. I knew full well that it would displease my friends and my countrymen very much; but I have never regretted having taken the step. I was hungry for something better than what the Hindu Shastras gave. I found it in the Christian’s Bible and was satisfied.”

She was right about her countrymen. When the news reached Poona, the friends who had helped her there were dismayed, and the orthodox felt vindicated. The brilliant Brahman widow who had stood before the Education Commission had gone to England and been lost to the Christians. For some of her countrymen, she has never been forgiven.

But there is one more thing to say about this baptism, and Ramabai herself said it. What happened at Wantage, she came to believe, was real, but it was not the whole story. She had found the religion. She had not yet found the Person. That would take another eight years.
fields.body_text: “By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.” — Hebrews 11:8, ASV Not Knowing Whither Four years later, in Philadelphia, Ramabai tried to explain to Rachel Bodley what it had meant to leave India. I could not have done this unless I had felt that my faith in God had become strong: it is such a great step for a Hindu woman to cross the sea; one cuts oneself always off from one’s people. But the voice came to me as to Abraham. … It seems to me now very strange how I could have started as I did with my friend and little child throwing myself on God’s protection. I went forth as Abraham, not knowing whither I went. She was not yet a Christian. She had read some of the New Testament, and she had listened to Miss Hurford and Father Goreh. But she already knew the story of Abraham, and she already thought of her journey in its terms. The verse at the head of this chapter describes it: “he went out, not knowing whither he went.” God had said to Abram, “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto the land that I will show thee” (Genesis 12:1, ASV). Ramabai had no country, no kindred, and no father’s house left to leave. But she was leaving her caste and her people’s good opinion, and she knew she might never have them back. Wantage She landed in England in the spring of 1883, and the Sisters of the Community of St. Mary the Virgin met her at the ship and took her to their convent at Wantage, a market town at the foot of the Berkshire Downs, south-west of Oxford. The Wantage sisters were an Anglican religious order of the High Church kind, devoted to prayer, teaching, and works of mercy, with a house in Poona, where Miss Hurford had worked. One of them, almost certainly Sister Geraldine, took Ramabai under her care. “The Sisters took me to their Home,” Ramabai wrote, “and one of them who became my spiritual mother, began to teach me both secular and religious subjects.” She learned English there, and it was there that she spent her first year. Her plan had been to study medicine. It did not work out. She was already partly deaf, whether from scarlet fever or from the hardships of her wandering years, and she was told that her deafness would make it impossible for her to train as a doctor. It was a hard blow. She had crossed the sea to become a doctor for the women of India, and now she could not. A worse blow followed. Her friend and companion, Anandibai Bhagat, who had come with her from India, took her own life a few months after they arrived. The reasons have never been clear. Some people at the time, including the Oxford scholar Max Müller, suggested that the young woman had been terrified of being pressed to become a Christian. Others have seen other causes. None of her published accounts mentions it. She was twenty-five, and she had now lost her parents, her sister, her brother, her husband, and the friend who had come with her from India. For a time, it seems, she was badly shaken. Fulham Then something happened that she never forgot. The Mother Superior sent her for a change of air to one of the order’s houses in London, and there she was taken to see the rescue homes at Fulham, where the Sisters of the Cross worked among women who had been prostitutes. The Sisters there took me to see the rescue work carried on by them. I met several of the women who had once been in their Rescue-Home, but who had so completely changed, and were so filled with the love of Christ and compassion for suffering humanity, that they had given their life for the service of the sick and infirm. Here for the first time in my life, I came to know that something should be done to reclaim the so-called fallen women, and that Christians, whom Hindus considered outcasts and cruel, were kind to these unfortunate women, degraded in the eyes of society. She had never seen anything like it in India. “I had not heard anyone speaking kindly of them, nor seen any one making any effort to turn them from the evil path.” The Hindu law, she wrote, commanded that the king should cause such women “to be eaten by dogs in the outskirts of the town.” Here, the women whom society had cast out were nursing the sick in the name of Christ. She asked the sister who was teaching her what it was that made Christians care for these women. The sister read to her the fourth chapter of John’s Gospel: the story of Jesus and the Samaritan woman at the well. The Woman at the Well It is not hard to see why that chapter struck her. The Samaritan woman belonged to a despised people, whom the Jews would not touch. She had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband. She came to the well at midday, alone, when the other women had gone. And Jesus, a Jewish teacher, spoke to her, asked her for a drink, told her the truth about her life without condemning her, and offered her “living water.” “Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4:14, ASV). She was the first person in John’s Gospel to whom Jesus plainly said that he was the Christ. And she went back to her town and told everyone. Ramabai had spent months reading the Hindu law-books and discovering that they had nothing to say to a woman except that she was “worse than demons” and could hope for salvation only through her husband. Now she heard of a teacher who went out of his way to speak to a woman of the worst reputation, and offered her, directly, the gift of God. She spoke of the Infinite Love of Christ for sinners. He did not despise them but came to save them. I had never read or heard anything like this in the religious books of the Hindus. I realized, after reading the fourth chapter of St. John’s Gospel, that Christ was truly the Divine Saviour He claimed to be, and no one but He could transform and uplift the downtrodden womanhood of India, and of every land. “Thus my heart was drawn to the religion of Christ.” Goreh’s Book Her heart was drawn. Her mind still needed convincing, and she was not a woman who would believe anything without reasons. The reasons came, she said, from Father Goreh. “I was intellectually convinced of its truth on reading a book written by Father Goreh.” Goreh was the author of a searching critique of the Hindu philosophical systems from a Christian point of view. He also wrote to her from India, and she wrote of one of his letters: “His humble, sweet voice has pierced my heart. I think no one would have had the power of turning me from the Brahman religion but Father Goreh.” It is worth noticing that the two voices that brought her to the point of faith were, one, a sister of an English order showing her Christians caring for outcast women, and, two, an Indian Brahman convert showing her, in her own intellectual tradition, why Christianity was true. She needed both. She was never satisfied with a faith that was only feeling, or with one that was only argument. According to Macnicol, she was baptised in Wantage parish church by Canon William Butler, the founder of the order, with Sister Geraldine among the witnesses; later accounts call Geraldine her godmother. She was later confirmed. She was calm about it, not ecstatic. “I was comparatively happy,” she wrote, “and felt a great joy in finding a new religion which was better than any other religion I had known before. I knew full well that it would displease my friends and my countrymen very much; but I have never regretted having taken the step. I was hungry for something better than what the Hindu Shastras gave. I found it in the Christian’s Bible and was satisfied.” She was right about her countrymen. When the news reached Poona, the friends who had helped her there were dismayed, and the orthodox felt vindicated. The brilliant Brahman widow who had stood before the Education Commission had gone to England and been lost to the Christians. For some of her countrymen, she has never been forgiven. She had found the religion. She had not yet found the Person. That would take another eight years.

fields.title: The Religion Without Christ
fields.body_html:
“prove all things; hold fast that which is good;”

— 1 Thessalonians 5:21, ASV

Cheltenham

In September 1884 Ramabai moved from Wantage to Cheltenham, the spa town in Gloucestershire, to the Ladies’ College founded and run by Dorothea Beale. Miss Beale was one of the great pioneers of women’s education in England, a devout Anglican, a thinker, and a formidable personality. At Cheltenham Ramabai taught Sanskrit and studied mathematics, natural science, and English literature. It was the first formal schooling she had ever had.

A student at the college remembered her at Miss Beale’s Saturday Scripture classes, where they studied the opening verses of John’s Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word.” Ramabai, already troubled with deafness, sat on a high stool beside the Principal “with her aurophone touching her teeth,” following every word. She was not an easy pupil. Another woman at the college remembered that her mind became clouded with religious doubt, and that she went away to fight the battle alone, and came back joyfully to tell Miss Beale “of faith restored.”

She owed Miss Beale, and the sister at Wantage, almost certainly Sister Geraldine, who became her “spiritual mother,” a great deal, and she said so. “I owe an everlasting debt of gratitude to her and to Miss Beale,” she wrote of her “spiritual mother.” “Both of these ladies took great pains with me and taught me the subjects which would help me in my life. … Their motherly kindness and deeply spiritual influence have greatly helped in building up my character.”

But gratitude did not mean agreement. The years at Wantage and Cheltenham were years of argument.

The Quarrels

Ramabai’s letters from these years, and those of Sister Geraldine and others about her, were preserved by the sisters and published in India in 1977. That collection is still in copyright, and this book knows it chiefly through the work of modern scholars who have studied it. What they describe is a long struggle.

Ramabai had been baptised as an Anglican, but she did not accept everything the Anglicans taught. She questioned the doctrine of the Trinity, and whether Christ was fully God. She questioned eternal punishment. She objected to the Athanasian Creed, with its warnings that those who did not believe it would perish. She would not give up her vegetarian diet, which she had kept all her life. She wanted her cross inscribed in Sanskrit. She asked why she should accept the teaching of one church over another, when the Christians she met disagreed so much among themselves. And she refused to let the sisters, or the Canon who had founded their order, or the Bishop of Bombay, direct her life and work.

Sister Geraldine, who loved her and considered herself responsible for her soul, treated much of this as pride and heresy. The sisters wanted Ramabai to return to India as a teacher in their own Anglican mission. Ramabai wanted to be free. The historian Antoinette Burton has described the relationship as “less a question of sisterhood than a struggle for authority.” When the sisters warned her about her doubts and her independence, she answered, in a letter preserved in the 1977 edition of her correspondence and often quoted by modern scholars, that “the door of the Universal Church of God is not shut against me.”

It is easy to take sides in this quarrel. Some modern historians admire Ramabai as a free thinker resisting the authority of a colonial church. Some Christian writers see a proud young convert who had not yet learned humility. Both are partly right. She was proud, in a way; she had been honoured by pandits, and she was not used to being told what to think. She was also right to refuse to be governed by people who, however kind, did not understand her country and assumed they knew best. And the sisters, however possessive, loved her and prayed for her, and she knew it. Years later, it is said, she still kept Sister Geraldine’s photograph on her wall.

No Special Sect

In 1895, looking back, she described her faith in these years in a little tract published in Bombay.

I believed the Apostles’ Creed, and all the essential doctrines of Christianity. My mind was at rest; and I trusted in God, believed on Christ, and prayed in His name. I did not adhere to any special sect, nor do I now. It was enough for me to be called a Christian, on the ground of my belief in Christ as the Saviour of mankind.

She went on:

I had many doubts and many difficulties in the matter of belief. So many sects, so many opinions, so much want of spirituality and much shallow talk in the name of religion. All these troubled me very much, and I began to see much the same in the picture of Christianity as I have been accustomed to see in that of the Hindu religion. But all this time I was conscious that God was leading me; and I determined not to take the opinion of men as my ground of belief, and went on reading the Bible only and trusted in God’s mercy.

That is a significant confession. She had left the Hindu religion partly because its authorities contradicted each other, and because they told her things about women she could not believe. Now she found the Christian authorities contradicting each other too. Her answer was not to abandon Christianity, nor to submit to whichever church had baptised her. It was to go to the Bible itself. “I determined not to take the opinion of men as my ground of belief.”

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s instruction to the Thessalonians: “prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” Ramabai was proving all things. She was not being contrary for its own sake. She was a scholar trained in a tradition of argument, and a woman who had learned at great cost not to accept what she was told without examining it. The Bereans in Acts were praised because they “received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the scriptures daily, whether these things were so” (Acts 17:11, ASV). That was what she was trying to do.

What Was Missing

Later she came to see these years differently. It was not that her questions were wrong, she thought, but that she had been looking in the wrong place. In A Testimony she wrote that for years after her baptism she had studied “other books about the Bible,” and had not studied “the Bible itself as I should have done.” She had also held on, without realising it, to ideas she had brought with her from Hinduism.

I thought that repentance of sin, and the determination to give it up, was what was necessary for forgiveness of sin: that the rite of baptism was the means of regeneration: that my sins were truly washed away, when I was baptized in the name of Christ. These and such other ideas, which are akin to Hindu mode of religious thought, stuck to me. For some years after my baptism, I was comparatively happy to think that I had found a religion which gave its privileges equally to men and women; there was no distinction of caste, colour, or sex made in it. All this was very beautiful, no doubt.

“All this was very beautiful, no doubt.” But something was missing. She had found a religion that treated women and men as equal before God. She believed its creed. She had been washed in its water. What she did not yet have, she came to believe, was a personal trust in Christ himself as her Saviour.

It is worth hearing, too, how a sympathetic outsider saw her. Max Müller, the Oxford scholar of Sanskrit, who admired her, wrote to her American supporters in 1895, when she was under attack, that “in all essentials she had been a Christian even while she was still a Brahman,” and that she had joined a church chiefly because “she felt the necessity of belonging to some communion, to be one with her friends.” It was a kind judgement, and a mistaken one. It explained her conversion as a matter of sympathy and loneliness. Ramabai herself would have said that it was neither. It was, at this stage, a matter of conviction without life. The life came later.

To America

Late in 1885 or early in 1886 a letter came from America. Anandibai Joshee, a young Brahman woman from the Maratha country, a relative of Ramabai’s, was about to graduate in medicine from the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, the first Indian woman to do so. She invited Ramabai to her graduation.

The sisters did not want her to go. Nor did Miss Beale. There was talk of a government educational post for her in India. But after some weeks of painful indecision Ramabai accepted. In February 1886 she sailed for America. Manorama, not yet five, went with her at first, but was soon sent back to England, to live with the sisters at Wantage, who cared for her for the next three years.

It was, in its way, one more act of independence. And it would change her life again.

fields.title: The High-Caste Hindu Woman
fields.body_html:
“learn to do well; seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”

— Isaiah 1:17, ASV

Philadelphia

Ramabai reached Philadelphia in the first days of March 1886. On 6 March, in the house of Dr. Rachel Bodley, dean of the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, she met her relative Anandibai Joshee for the first time, and five days later she watched her graduate as a doctor of medicine, the first Indian woman to do so. Anandibai wrote of her admiringly, as a woman “delicate and flowerlike” who had yet, by her courage, “caused great yogis to quail before her.” It was a proud moment for both of them. It was also a short-lived triumph. Anandibai went home to India that year to take up a hospital post, fell ill with tuberculosis, and died early in 1887, at the age of twenty-one.

Ramabai had meant to stay in America a few weeks. She stayed nearly three years. Rachel Bodley’s house became her home, and Bodley herself became one of her closest friends. What held her was what she saw. “I am deeply impressed by and am interested in the work of Western women,” she wrote that summer, “who seem to have one common aim, namely, the good of their fellow-beings. It is my dream some day to tell my countrywomen in their own languages this wonderful story, in the hope that the recital may awaken in their hearts a desire to do likewise.”

She studied everything that might be useful to her in India. A Philadelphia woman showed her the city’s kindergartens, and in the autumn she enrolled in a course to train as a kindergarten teacher. She began to prepare a series of reading books for Marathi children, and when she found that illustrations were too expensive to have drawn in India, she bought hundreds of electrotype printing plates to take home. She visited schools and colleges. And she wrote.

The Book

The High-Caste Hindu Woman was published in Philadelphia in June 1887. Ramabai had it printed at her own risk to raise money, and by the time she left America some seven thousand copies had been sold, ten thousand within a few years. It is a short book, and an angry one.

She described the life of a high-caste Hindu woman from birth to death: the disappointment that greeted the birth of a daughter, the marriage of girls as young children to men they had never seen, the wife’s life in her husband’s family as the servant of her mother-in-law, and above all the life of the widow. She quoted the Hindu law-books against themselves. She described what she had seen herself. “A child of thirteen,” she wrote, “was cruelly beaten by her husband in my presence for telling the simple truth, that she did not like so well to be in his house as at her own home.”

She did not spare the British. English law in India, she pointed out, enforced child marriages through the courts. “Now, under the so-called Christian British rule, the woman is in no better condition than of old.” It was a line her Western admirers did not always quote.

Modern Indian scholars have called the book a feminist manifesto, and it is not hard to see why. It argued that women were half the nation, that the nation could not rise while they were kept down, and that the reform of Indian society must begin with the education of its women. Above all it pleaded for the child-widows, and it ended with a practical proposal. She would go home and start a school for high-caste widows, where they could be trained as teachers and so earn their own living with dignity. It would need help for about ten years, after which, she hoped, it could be supported by Indians alone.

I am fully aware of the great responsibility the trial — and it may be the failure — will involve; but as some one must make a beginning, I am resolved to try, trusting that God, who knows the need of my countrywomen, will raise up able workers to forward this cause, whether I succeed in it or not.

“Out of Nazareth”

The school she proposed would not be a Christian school. It would receive Hindu widows as Hindus, and leave them free in matters of religion. Bodley described the plan in her introduction: Ramabai “would make no condition as to reading the Bible or studying Christianity,” but would put on the shelves of the school library, “side by side, the Bible and the Sacred books of the East, and for the rest, earnestly pray that God will guide them to His saving truth.” That promise of neutrality would cause her great trouble later.

Bodley closed her introduction with a scene. Ramabai came into her library to say goodbye before a journey, and Bodley asked her if she had a last message for her readers.

“Remind them,” she replied, with animated countenance and rapid speech, as she clasped my hand, “that it was ‘out of Nazareth’ that the blessed Redeemer of mankind came; that great reforms have again and again been wrought by instrumentalities that the world despised. Tell them to help me educate the high-caste child-widows; for I solemnly believe that this hated and despised class of women, educated and enlightened, are, by God’s grace, to redeem India!”

When Nathanael first heard of Jesus, he asked, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46, ASV). The despised town produced the Saviour of the world. Ramabai believed that the most despised people in India, the child-widows, whom their own families considered cursed, could be the means of its renewal. It was a vision grounded in the gospel, and it would govern the rest of her life.

Boston

She took her cause to Boston, and Boston responded. In May 1887 a public meeting was held at Channing Hall. Because the school was to be non-sectarian, the leaders of the different churches could not sponsor it without dispute, and so the meeting was held under Unitarian auspices, with the support of Episcopalians such as the great preacher Phillips Brooks. On 13 December 1887 the Ramabai Association was formed. Its president was the writer Edward Everett Hale. Among its officers were Phillips Brooks, the Congregationalist Lyman Abbott, the temperance leader Frances Willard, and Rachel Bodley. It promised to support her school for ten years.

That night, it was later reported, she could not sleep for joy. “I am crying for joy,” she said, “that my dream of years has become a reality.”

For the rest of her time in America she travelled and spoke. She went as far as Canada in the north and the Pacific coast in the west. She gave more than a hundred lectures for the Association and many more on her own account, to pay her debts in England and America, and she insisted on repaying the sisters at Wantage for all they had spent on her. More than fifty local circles were formed to support her work. She also wrote a book in Marathi about America, describing to her own people the country she had come to admire, its schools, its women, and its freedoms, as well as its faults. It was published in Bombay in 1889.

Home

In November 1888 she sailed from San Francisco for India, by way of Japan and Hong Kong. As she set sail for home she was afraid. “I felt as if I were going to a strange country and to a strange people. I fell on my knees, committed myself to the care of our loving heavenly Father and sailed.” She had left India as a Hindu widow and was coming back as a Christian. She knew the welcome she could expect.

She landed at Bombay on 1 February 1889. She had been away nearly six years.

The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s command to his people through Isaiah: “seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.” For three years in America she had pleaded for the widow, in lecture halls and churches and in a book that thousands read. Now she had to do what she had asked others to support. In less than six weeks, she would open her school.

On 6 March, in the house of Dr. Rachel Bodley, dean of the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, she met her relative Anandibai Joshee for the first time, and five days later she watched her graduate as a doctor of medicine, the first Indian woman to do so. Anandibai wrote of her admiringly, as a woman “delicate and flowerlike” who had yet, by her courage, “caused great yogis to quail before her.” It was a proud moment for both of them. It was also a short-lived triumph. Anandibai went home to India that year to take up a hospital post, fell ill with tuberculosis, and died early in 1887, at the age of twenty-one. Ramabai had meant to stay in America a few weeks. She stayed nearly three years. Rachel Bodley’s house became her home, and Bodley herself became one of her closest friends. What held her was what she saw. “I am deeply impressed by and am interested in the work of Western women,” she wrote that summer, “who seem to have one common aim, namely, the good of their fellow-beings. It is my dream some day to tell my countrywomen in their own languages this wonderful story, in the hope that the recital may awaken in their hearts a desire to do likewise.” She studied everything that might be useful to her in India. A Philadelphia woman showed her the city’s kindergartens, and in the autumn she enrolled in a course to train as a kindergarten teacher. She began to prepare a series of reading books for Marathi children, and when she found that illustrations were too expensive to have drawn in India, she bought hundreds of electrotype printing plates to take home. She visited schools and colleges. And she wrote. The Book The High-Caste Hindu Woman was published in Philadelphia in June 1887. Ramabai had it printed at her own risk to raise money, and by the time she left America some seven thousand copies had been sold, ten thousand within a few years. It is a short book, and an angry one. She described the life of a high-caste Hindu woman from birth to death: the disappointment that greeted the birth of a daughter, the marriage of girls as young children to men they had never seen, the wife’s life in her husband’s family as the servant of her mother-in-law, and above all the life of the widow. She quoted the Hindu law-books against themselves. She described what she had seen herself. “A child of thirteen,” she wrote, “was cruelly beaten by her husband in my presence for telling the simple truth, that she did not like so well to be in his house as at her own home.” She did not spare the British. English law in India, she pointed out, enforced child marriages through the courts. “Now, under the so-called Christian British rule, the woman is in no better condition than of old.” It was a line her Western admirers did not always quote. Modern Indian scholars have called the book a feminist manifesto, and it is not hard to see why. It argued that women were half the nation, that the nation could not rise while they were kept down, and that the reform of Indian society must begin with the education of its women. Above all it pleaded for the child-widows, and it ended with a practical proposal. She would go home and start a school for high-caste widows, where they could be trained as teachers and so earn their own living with dignity. It would need help for about ten years, after which, she hoped, it could be supported by Indians alone. I am fully aware of the great responsibility the trial — and it may be the failure — will involve; but as some one must make a beginning, I am resolved to try, trusting that God, who knows the need of my countrywomen, will raise up able workers to forward this cause, whether I succeed in it or not. “Out of Nazareth” The school she proposed would not be a Christian school. Bodley described the plan in her introduction: Ramabai “would make no condition as to reading the Bible or studying Christianity,” but would put on the shelves of the school library, “side by side, the Bible and the Sacred books of the East, and for the rest, earnestly pray that God will guide them to His saving truth.” That promise of neutrality would cause her great trouble later. Bodley closed her introduction with a scene. Ramabai came into her library to say goodbye before a journey, and Bodley asked her if she had a last message for her readers. “Remind them,” she replied, with animated countenance and rapid speech, as she clasped my hand, “that it was ‘out of Nazareth’ that the blessed Redeemer of mankind came; that great reforms have again and again been wrought by instrumentalities that the world despised. The despised town produced the Saviour of the world. It was a vision grounded in the gospel, and it would govern the rest of her life. Boston She took her cause to Boston, and Boston responded. In May 1887 a public meeting was held at Channing Hall. She went as far as Canada in the north and the Pacific coast in the west. She gave more than a hundred lectures for the Association and many more on her own account, to pay her debts in England and America, and she insisted on repaying the sisters at Wantage for all they had spent on her. More than fifty local circles were formed to support her work. She also wrote a book in Marathi about America, describing to her own people the country she had come to admire, its schools, its women, and its freedoms, as well as its faults. It was published in Bombay in 1889. Home In November 1888 she sailed from San Francisco for India, by way of Japan and Hong Kong. As she set sail for home she was afraid. “I felt as if I were going to a strange country and to a strange people. She knew the welcome she could expect. She landed at Bombay on 1 February 1889. She had been away nearly six years. Now she had to do what she had asked others to support. In less than six weeks, she would open her school.

fields.title: Sharada Sadan
fields.body_html:
“Wisdom hath builded her house; She hath hewn out her seven pillars:”

— Proverbs 9:1, ASV

The Home of Wisdom

Ramabai spent the six weeks after her return preparing, and on 11 March 1889 she opened her school in a rented house at Chowpatty, on the seafront in Bombay. She called it Sharada Sadan, the Home of Sharada, which is another name for Sarasvati, the goddess of learning. The name was a deliberate choice. It told the Hindu families of Bombay that this was not a mission school, and that it honoured learning in their own terms. It can be translated simply as “the Home of Wisdom.”

The opening meeting was chaired by a Hindu woman, Mrs. Kashibai Kanitkar, and a leading Marathi paper called it the first time an Indian woman had presided over such an occasion. Ramabai spoke about her travels and her plans, and she did not flatter the men in the audience.

Let the newspapers and the general public say what they will, there is not the least doubt that the condition of the women of our country is heart-rending in the extreme. It is we, and we only, who can ever have a real knowledge of the welfare of our people. Foreigners can never know. … Gentlemen, in your parliament no one has allowed one of us sisters to plead the cause of India’s unfortunate women; I am fully convinced that you men have no better idea of the oppression and woe suffered by Hindu women than the British Parliament has of the misfortunes of Hindustan.

It is worth noticing what she was saying. Indian nationalists complained that the British Parliament could not understand India because no Indian sat in it. Ramabai turned the argument on the nationalists themselves. They could not understand the women of India, because no woman was allowed to speak among them.

Two Pupils

When the meeting ended and the guests went home, the school had two pupils. One was a young widow, whose name was Godubai. She had suffered greatly in her husband’s family and had more than once tried to take her own life. She was not quick to learn, and teaching her needed patience on both sides. Four years later she married a widowed professor at Fergusson College in Poona, Dhondo Keshav Karve, who became one of the great pioneers of women’s education in India. The other was a girl named Sharada, not a widow, who came as a paying day-pupil.

By the end of the first three months there were twenty-two. By the end of the first year there were twenty-seven, twelve of them widows. The aim was to train them, above all, to become teachers themselves, so that they could earn their own living with dignity. And the girls were allowed to keep the rules of their caste, so that no Hindu family need fear that a daughter would be polluted by living there.

The girls were also allowed to sing, which in orthodox homes was thought unbecoming for a respectable woman. “We have happy times in the evening,” Ramabai wrote, “when all the girls come into my room and we sing together as best we can. We have no love songs to sing, no comic bits to say; but we sing hymns, and feel quite content. You see, they do not allow women to sing; they think it is a bad thing in a housewife. But we are getting unruly in this school of ours. We are going to turn the tide, and make it a good and honourable taste.”

The Open Door

Sharada Sadan was not a Christian school. Ramabai had promised her American supporters and her Indian advisers that it would be neutral in religion. The Bible was not taught in class. The girls were free to follow their own religion. But she did not pretend not to be a Christian. Every morning, in her own room, she read the Bible and prayed with Manorama. And she left the door open.

One of her American friends, Miss Sarah Hamlin, described what happened. Going to Ramabai’s room one morning, she found eight of the older girls sitting on the lounge, listening intently to the Marathi Bible. When Ramabai knelt to pray, they knelt with her. Afterwards each girl came up to her, and she spoke a kind word to each, and kissed them.

“These are my own private prayers,” explained Pandita Ramabai. “No girl is compelled to come in; but one by one they have come of their own accord. At first, when they heard me with Manorama, they peeped in the door: then, one by one, they ventured a little farther. Occasionally, one would sit, but all would leave when I knelt: now all remain.”

It is a lovely scene. The Association in Boston, worried by newspaper talk of “converts,” warned that more had been made of it than it deserved. But it contains the whole of the conflict that was coming. To Ramabai, the open door was a matter of simple honesty. She would not force her faith on anyone, but she would not hide it either, and she would not shut out a girl who wanted to hear. To her Hindu advisers, the open door was a breach of trust. The parents who sent their daughters to Sharada Sadan had been promised a neutral school. What went on in the Principal’s room, they felt, was part of the school, whatever the timetable said.

A Voice Too Small

That December the Indian National Congress met in Bombay. Among the delegates were a handful of women, largely because of Ramabai’s influence. She spoke in support of two resolutions about widows. She denounced the custom of shaving widows’ heads, and the belief that if a widow kept her hair it would bind her dead husband in hell, and asked the men how they would like to have their own heads shaved on the death of a wife. When she stood up to speak there was a crush of men trying to hear her. She began, according to the Indian Magazine’s report: “It is not strange, my countrymen, that my voice is small, for you have never given a woman the chance to make her voice strong!”

The next hot season, in 1890, she went back to the forest of her birth for the first time. “The whole ground,” she wrote to a friend, “seemed hallowed with the association of my beloved parents.”

Poona and the Board

In November 1890 the school moved to Poona, where living was cheaper and the climate healthier. The move brought it under the eyes of the Poona reformers, and also of their opponents.

At first a new managing board was formed in Poona, which claimed full control of the admission of pupils and the funds, and gave Ramabai one vote in twelve. Under it, according to the Association’s chairman, the school was run as strictly Hindu, and Ramabai herself was forbidden to enter the dining-room, the kitchen, or the corridor while the girls were eating. The American Association refused to accept these terms, and the board was dissolved in the summer of 1891.

That summer and autumn the Poona papers attacked her fiercely. She was accused of disloyalty to her own people, of taking money from Americans under false pretences, of interfering with her pupils’ religion, and of getting rid of the managing board so that she could teach Christianity openly. Some of the attacks were indecent. One editor later withdrew his charges and apologised. Worn out, Ramabai offered to hand over the school and its funds, and to let someone “wiser than herself” be put at its head. The Association in Boston cabled back: “Be firm. The Association supports you. Funds and letters coming.”

“Those were the darkest days in the stormy time,” she wrote. “I was in great doubt, and was at a loss to know what would be the best course to follow. When this cablegram came, I was sure you would support me, and I went on in the usual way.”

But the storm left its mark. “Although we are living in our own country, and among our own people,” she wrote, “we are continually made to feel that we are among a strange and hostile people in a strange land. We are utterly defenceless, and almost friendless, in this beloved land of ours.”

In July 1892 the school moved into a compound of its own in Poona, bought by the Association, with two bungalows on nearly three acres of bare ground, which she soon turned into a garden. Within a year it had sixty-two pupils. The Home of Wisdom had its house. The verse at the head of this chapter describes Wisdom building her house and hewing out its pillars, and then sending out her maidens to call to anyone who would come: “Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither” (Proverbs 9:4, ASV). Ramabai’s house was open to any widow who would come. The question that was about to tear it apart was how open its mistress’s own door should be.

fields.title: The Storm of 1893
fields.body_html:
“What time I am afraid, I will put my trust in thee. In God (I will praise his word), In God have I put my trust, I will not be afraid; What can flesh do unto me?”

— Psalm 56:3-4, ASV

The Morning Prayers

By the spring of 1893 the school in Poona had more than sixty pupils, most of them widows. And more and more of them were coming to Ramabai’s room in the early morning.

Soonderbai Powar, an Indian Christian teacher who had become Ramabai’s close friend and colleague, returned from a visit to England that spring and found “all the girls attending Ramabai’s prayer-meetings.” Helen Dyer, who knew the school well, estimated that fully half the widows were by then coming to the morning prayers. Some of the girls in the school were not widows but orphans or poor girls whom Ramabai had taken in and supported herself, and a few she had adopted outright. These girls, Dyer wrote, she felt it her duty to instruct in the Christian faith.

That May, on a Hindu festival day during the hot-weather holiday, Ramabai offered the girls a choice between a picnic and a day of prayer. According to Dyer, about thirty of the sixty-odd girls chose to stay for prayer, and more than twenty of them said they wished to learn about Christ.

Nothing was done in secret. And that was precisely the problem.

The Resignation

On 13 August 1893 the three Hindu gentlemen whose names appeared on the school’s reports as its advisory board in Poona wrote to the Ramabai Association in Boston. They were R. G. Bhandarkar, the Sanskrit scholar; M. G. Ranade, the judge and reformer who had welcomed Ramabai to Poona eleven years before; and C. N. Bhat. Their letter is worth quoting at length, because it put their case fairly and it was the case that most educated Hindus believed.

Encouraged, apparently, by some expressions contained in your Committee’s communications, Pundita Ramabai has during the past year or so departed from the lines of strict neutrality on which the institution was started and managed for some time. We have strong reasons to believe that many of the girls are induced to attend her private prayers regularly, and read the Bible, and that Christian doctrines are taught to them. Pundita Ramabai has also shown her active missionary tendencies by asking the parents and guardians of girls to allow them to attend her prayers, and in one case at least, to become Christians themselves; and we are assured that two of the girls have declared to their elders that they have accepted Christ. Such a departure from the original understanding cannot fail, in our opinion, to shake the stability of the institution, and alienate public sympathy from this work. We are sorry our individual remonstrances with the Pundita Bai have proved of no avail. If the Sadana is to be conducted as an avowed proselytizing institution, we must disavow all connection with it.

According to the Association, they published their resignation in the newspapers before it reached Boston; according to Ramabai, they sent a circular to parents and guardians asking them not to send their girls to the school.

The effect was immediate. The Poona papers, already hostile, grew fiercer. Anonymous letters threatened Ramabai’s life. Parents came and took their girls home. Ramabai’s own register records that thirty-one pupils were withdrawn: twenty-six widows and five others. She kept track of every one. Twelve went to the Poona High School for girls, where some of her former advisers paid fees for some of them. Nine later came back. One remarried. One went to train as a nurse. Four, she wrote, were “kept at home in a miserable condition,” and one “went to her destruction.”

Two Sides

It would be easy to tell this story as a simple conflict between a faithful Christian and her persecutors. It was not. Ranade and Bhandarkar were not bigots. They were among the most liberal Hindus of their day, men who had risked their own standing to support women’s education and widow remarriage. They had supported Ramabai when few others would. They had lent their names to her school on the understanding that it would not be used to make converts. And they believed, with reason, that the understanding had been broken.

They were not wrong about the facts. Girls were attending Ramabai’s prayers and reading the Bible, and she did not deny it. She did deny that there had been any conversions or baptisms, though rumour said that two of the widows had privately professed faith in Christ. In an interview published in a Madras newspaper she told her side of the story.

They had nothing practically to do with the internal management of the Sadan. … We went on satisfactorily for some time, but when the number of girls attending my private prayers rose to about twenty, the matter was reported to them. We did nothing in secret. My room was always open. They asked me whether some of the girls attended my private prayers. I replied that they did. They then asked me to prevent them from doing so. I told them I could not conscientiously do that — I could not restrict my intercourse with the pupils. As a Christian was at the head of the institution, the girls must be more or less under Christian influences.

Some time earlier, according to Macnicol (drawing on Kelkar’s life of Tilak), she had told one of her leading critics plainly that she could not undertake that a Hindu girl entering her school would always remain a Hindu.

Where does the truth lie? Both sides were honest, and both had a point. The reformers were right that the school had been presented as neutral, and that a school run by a devout and persuasive Christian, whose room was always open, could not in practice be neutral in the way Hindu parents understood. Ramabai was right that she had never compelled anyone, that she had never made the Bible a school subject, that the girls who came to her prayers came freely, and that no one could reasonably ask her to shut her door against a girl who wanted to pray. The underlying problem was that the promise of neutrality had been made in America, in good faith, by people who did not fully understand what it would mean in Poona. Even in America the message had been double: her own book had told Christian readers that such a school would “prepare the way for the spread of the gospel,” and Boston had soon been embarrassed by newspaper talk of “converts.” Ramabai herself had helped to make it. Now she could not keep it in the way her critics understood it, and she would not pretend to.

The Americans sided with her. Mrs. Judith Andrews, chair of the Association’s executive committee (the very committee whose letters the advisers had blamed), reached Bombay on Christmas Day 1893 and stayed more than six months. She concluded that Ramabai had kept faith with her promises as she understood them, that no girl had been compelled, and that many of the charges against her were baseless. The Association stood by her. But the school was badly damaged. “The last and greatest of all storms,” Ramabai wrote, “in 1893 did us a great deal of harm, — we have not yet recovered.”

The Girl Who Was Hidden

There was another episode that year, less creditable to Ramabai’s friends, and it should be told. One of the girls she had taken in was not a widow but the young daughter of a Bombay woman attached to a temple, placed with Ramabai by a Hindu reformer. When the storm broke, the reformer turned against the school and urged the mother to reclaim her daughter. The girl did not want to go back. The girl was first sent into a Bombay hospital to gain time. Then Helen Dyer and a friend living in her house moved her out of the city to a missionary, and kept Ramabai herself in ignorance of where she was. The case came before the police. The mother did not appear. The missionary then baptised the girl, at the girl’s own wish but without Ramabai’s knowledge or consent.

Dyer, who used the phrase “justifiable expedients” for the steps Ramabai took to keep girls from being carried off, plainly approved. Ramabai, by Dyer’s own account, had begged for the girl to be produced, fearing that otherwise the school would be ruined. The episode added fuel to the fire, and it showed how difficult it was for Ramabai to control what others did in her name. It also shows why Hindu parents feared her school. It is to her credit that she wanted the girl returned. It is to the discredit of some of her friends that they did not listen.

Not Afraid

What kept her going? According to Helen Dyer, in that terrible year three promises from the Bible came to her. One was from Isaiah: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” (Isaiah 54:17, ASV). Another was Jesus’ word to his disciples: “In the world ye have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” The third was from the prophet Malachi: “prove me now herewith.” That last one would matter greatly in the years ahead.

The psalm at the head of this chapter was written, its title says, when David was a fugitive in the hands of his enemies. “What time I am afraid, I will put my trust in thee.” Ramabai was afraid, in 1893. She was a woman alone, attacked by the leading men of her own people, threatened with death, abandoned by friends, her school half empty, her work in danger of collapse. She did not pretend not to be afraid. She trusted anyway. And she came out of that year freer than she went in.

Looking back, she wrote that she had been delivered twice: “I have been first delivered from the slavery of man’s opinions, from the fear of man which holds so many of my dear people, and a second time from the bondage of sin.” It is hard not to think that the first deliverance was won in the storm of 1893.
