In God (I will praise his word), In God have I put my trust, I will not be afraid; What can flesh do unto me?” — Psalm 56:3-4, ASV The Morning Prayers By the spring of 1893 the school in Poona had more than sixty pupils, most of them widows. And more and more of them were coming to Ramabai’s room in the early morning. Soonderbai Powar, an Indian Christian teacher who had become Ramabai’s close friend and colleague, returned from a visit to England that spring and found “all the girls attending Ramabai’s prayer-meetings.” Helen Dyer, who knew the school well, estimated that fully half the widows were by then coming to the morning prayers. Some of the girls in the school were not widows but orphans or poor girls whom Ramabai had taken in and supported herself, and a few she had adopted outright. These girls, Dyer wrote, she felt it her duty to instruct in the Christian faith. That May, on a Hindu festival day during the hot-weather holiday, Ramabai offered the girls a choice between a picnic and a day of prayer. According to Dyer, about thirty of the sixty-odd girls chose to stay for prayer, and more than twenty of them said they wished to learn about Christ. Nothing was done in secret. And that was precisely the problem. The Resignation On 13 August 1893 the three Hindu gentlemen whose names appeared on the school’s reports as its advisory board in Poona wrote to the Ramabai Association in Boston. They were R. G. Bhandarkar, the Sanskrit scholar; M. G. Ranade, the judge and reformer who had welcomed Ramabai to Poona eleven years before; and C. N. Bhat. Their letter is worth quoting at length, because it put their case fairly and it was the case that most educated Hindus believed. Encouraged, apparently, by some expressions contained in your Committee’s communications, Pundita Ramabai has during the past year or so departed from the lines of strict neutrality on which the institution was started and managed for some time. We have strong reasons to believe that many of the girls are induced to attend her private prayers regularly, and read the Bible, and that Christian doctrines are taught to them. Pundita Ramabai has also shown her active missionary tendencies by asking the parents and guardians of girls to allow them to attend her prayers, and in one case at least, to become Christians themselves; and we are assured that two of the girls have declared to their elders that they have accepted Christ. Such a departure from the original understanding cannot fail, in our opinion, to shake the stability of the institution, and alienate public sympathy from this work. We are sorry our individual remonstrances with the Pundita Bai have proved of no avail. If the Sadana is to be conducted as an avowed proselytizing institution, we must disavow all connection with it. According to the Association, they published their resignation in the newspapers before it reached Boston; according to Ramabai, they sent a circular to parents and guardians asking them not to send their girls to the school. The effect was immediate. The Poona papers, already hostile, grew fiercer. Anonymous letters threatened Ramabai’s life. Parents came and took their girls home. Ramabai’s own register records that thirty-one pupils were withdrawn: twenty-six widows and five others. She kept track of every one. Twelve went to the Poona High School for girls, where some of her former advisers paid fees for some of them. Nine later came back. One remarried. One went to train as a nurse. Four, she wrote, were “kept at home in a miserable condition,” and one “went to her destruction.” Two Sides It would be easy to tell this story as a simple conflict between a faithful Christian and her persecutors. It was not. Ranade and Bhandarkar were not bigots. They were among the most liberal Hindus of their day, men who had risked their own standing to support women’s education and widow remarriage. They had supported Ramabai when few others would. They had lent their names to her school on the understanding that it would not be used to make converts. And they believed, with reason, that the understanding had been broken. They were not wrong about the facts. Girls were attending Ramabai’s prayers and reading the Bible, and she did not deny it. She did deny that there had been any conversions or baptisms, though rumour said that two of the widows had privately professed faith in Christ. In an interview published in a Madras newspaper she told her side of the story. They had nothing practically to do with the internal management of the Sadan. … We went on satisfactorily for some time, but when the number of girls attending my private prayers rose to about twenty, the matter was reported to them. We did nothing in secret. My room was always open. They asked me whether some of the girls attended my private prayers. I replied that they did. They then asked me to prevent them from doing so. I told them I could not conscientiously do that — I could not restrict my intercourse with the pupils. As a Christian was at the head of the institution, the girls must be more or less under Christian influences. Some time earlier, according to Macnicol (drawing on Kelkar’s life of Tilak), she had told one of her leading critics plainly that she could not undertake that a Hindu girl entering her school would always remain a Hindu. Where does the truth lie? Both sides were honest, and both had a point. The reformers were right that the school had been presented as neutral, and that a school run by a devout and persuasive Christian, whose room was always open, could not in practice be neutral in the way Hindu parents understood. Ramabai was right that she had never compelled anyone, that she had never made the Bible a school subject, that the girls who came to her prayers came freely, and that no one could reasonably ask her to shut her door against a girl who wanted to pray. The underlying problem was that the promise of neutrality had been made in America, in good faith, by people who did not fully understand what it would mean in Poona. Even in America the message had been double: her own book had told Christian readers that such a school would “prepare the way for the spread of the gospel,” and Boston had soon been embarrassed by newspaper talk of “converts.” Ramabai herself had helped to make it. Now she could not keep it in the way her critics understood it, and she would not pretend to. The Americans sided with her. Mrs. Judith Andrews, chair of the Association’s executive committee (the very committee whose letters the advisers had blamed), reached Bombay on Christmas Day 1893 and stayed more than six months. She concluded that Ramabai had kept faith with her promises as she understood them, that no girl had been compelled, and that many of the charges against her were baseless. The Association stood by her. But the school was badly damaged. “The last and greatest of all storms,” Ramabai wrote, “in 1893 did us a great deal of harm, — we have not yet recovered.” The Girl Who Was Hidden There was another episode that year, less creditable to Ramabai’s friends, and it should be told. One of the girls she had taken in was not a widow but the young daughter of a Bombay woman attached to a temple, placed with Ramabai by a Hindu reformer. When the storm broke, the reformer turned against the school and urged the mother to reclaim her daughter. The girl did not want to go back. The girl was first sent into a Bombay hospital to gain time. Then Helen Dyer and a friend living in her house moved her out of the city to a missionary, and kept Ramabai herself in ignorance of where she was. The case came before the police. The mother did not appear. The missionary then baptised the girl, at the girl’s own wish but without Ramabai’s knowledge or consent. Dyer, who used the phrase “justifiable expedients” for the steps Ramabai took to keep girls from being carried off, plainly approved. Ramabai, by Dyer’s own account, had begged for the girl to be produced, fearing that otherwise the school would be ruined. The episode added fuel to the fire, and it showed how difficult it was for Ramabai to control what others did in her name. It also shows why Hindu parents feared her school. It is to her credit that she wanted the girl returned. It is to the discredit of some of her friends that they did not listen. Not Afraid What kept her going? According to Helen Dyer, in that terrible year three promises from the Bible came to her. One was from Isaiah: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” (Isaiah 54:17, ASV). Another was Jesus’ word to his disciples: “In the world ye have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” The third was from the prophet Malachi: “prove me now herewith.” That last one would matter greatly in the years ahead. The psalm at the head of this chapter was written, its title says, when David was a fugitive in the hands of his enemies. “What time I am afraid, I will put my trust in thee.” Ramabai was afraid, in 1893. The second had already begun, quietly, two years before.

fields.title: “I Had Not Found Christ”
fields.body_html:
“The people that sat in darkness Saw a great light, And to them that sat in the region and shadow of death, To them did light spring up.”

— Matthew 4:16, ASV

A Quieter Story

While the storms of the Sharada Sadan were raging in public, a quieter story was unfolding in private, and Ramabai later came to see it as the most important thing that happened to her in those years. She told it in A Testimony in 1907. It is the heart of that pamphlet, and it deserves to be heard in her own words.

It began, she said, when she came home from America. For years she had studied “other books about the Bible,” and not the Bible itself. Now she put them aside. “I gave up the study of other books about the Bible after my return home from America and took to reading the Bible regularly.”

It did not make her happy. It made her miserable. “Following this course for about two years I became very unhappy in my mind. I was dissatisfied with my spiritual condition.”

Building from the Top

One day she went on business to the Bombay Guardian Mission Press, and picked up a book called From Death into Life. Its author, William Haslam, had been a clergyman of the Church of England with a good parish, busy with every kind of church activity. One day a woman of his congregation told him that he was “trying to build from the top.” She meant, Ramabai explained, that he had never been converted. He had the religion without the life. It was the beginning of his conversion.

It changed Ramabai’s understanding of herself. “I read his account of his conversion and work for Christ, then I began to consider where I stood and what my actual need was. I took the Bible and read portions of it, meditating on the messages which God gave me. There were so many things I did not understand intellectually. One thing I knew by this time, that I needed Christ, and not merely His religion.”

That sentence is the key to her whole testimony. She had believed the creed. She had been baptised and confirmed. She had argued with Anglican sisters about the Trinity. She had lectured on Christian love to American audiences, and founded a school that was attacked for being too Christian. And she knew, when she looked honestly at herself, that something was missing. “I realised that I was not prepared to meet God, that sin had dominion over me.” She had not received, as Paul put it, “the Spirit of adoption,” and had “no witness of the Spirit” that she was a child of God.

The Burden

“What was to be done? My thoughts could not, and did not, help me.”

I had at last come to an end of myself, and unconditionally surrendered myself to the Saviour, and asked Him to be merciful to me and to become my Righteousness and Redemption, and to take away all my sin.

Only those who have been convicted of sin and have seen themselves as God sees them under similar circumstances can understand what one feels when a great and unbearable burden is rolled away from one’s heart.

In a tract she published in Bombay in 1895 or 1896, she described the same experience with more physical detail. She had been brought to see, she wrote there, that hers was “only an intellectual belief — a belief in which there was no life.” “I repented long; I became very restless and almost ill, and passed many sleepless nights.” Then the burden rolled away.

She dated it, in 1907, to “sixteen years ago,” which is 1891, eight years after her baptism. It happened, then, in the same year as the first great storm over the Sharada Sadan in Poona, when the papers were accusing her of deceit and disloyalty. We do not know the exact day. She did not want us to. “I shall not attempt to describe how and what I felt at the time,” she wrote. What mattered was not the moment but the result.

Sitting in Darkness

She tried to describe it with an image from the Gospels.

I do not know if any one of my readers has ever had the experience of being shut up in a room where there was nothing but thick darkness, and then groping in it to find something of which he or she was in dire need. I can think of no one but the blind man, whose story is given in John 9. … I can give only a faint idea of what I felt when my mental eyes were opened, and when I, who was “sitting in darkness, saw great light,” and when I felt sure that to me who, but a few moments ago, “sat in the region and shadow of death, light had sprung up.”

She was quoting the words at the head of this chapter, Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah’s prophecy of the dawn in Galilee. She could have chosen a hundred verses. She chose one about people who had been sitting in darkness, which is what she believed she had been doing, first as a devout Hindu and then as a Christian without Christ.

Good News for a Woman

What struck her most was that salvation was free, and that it was for women.

All her life she had been taught that happiness had to be earned by merit, through rituals, pilgrimages, and gifts to Brahmans. As a woman, she had been taught that liberation was simply not available to her. She might, by serving her husband as a god, earn a better birth, and in some distant future life be born a Brahman man, and only then begin the long work of attaining release. And the Christianity she had first embraced had not really changed that picture. She had thought, she said, that forgiveness depended on repentance and resolution, and that baptism itself washed sin away. These, she wrote, were ideas “akin to Hindu mode of religious thought.”

Now she read the Bible differently. “The Bible says that God does not wait for me to merit His love, but heaps it upon me without my deserving it.” She quoted Paul: “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8, ASV).

How good, how indescribably good! What good news — for me, a woman; a woman born in India among Brahmins, who hold out no hope for me and the like of me. The Bible declares that Christ did not reserve this great salvation for a particular caste or sex. …

No caste, no sex, no work, and no man was to be depended upon to get salvation, this everlasting life; but God gave it freely to any one and every one who believed on His Son.

There is a direct line between this discovery and everything she did afterwards. The famine children she rescued, the widows she sheltered, the women she took from the streets, did not have to earn anything. Neither had she.

The Holy Spirit

In the years that followed, her faith deepened again. In about 1895 she read the life of Amanda Smith, an African American evangelist who had been born a slave. When Amanda Smith was converted, she said she had been delivered twice: once from slavery and once from sin. Ramabai wrote that she too had been delivered twice: “first delivered from the slavery of man’s opinions, from the fear of man which holds so many of my dear people, and a second time from the bondage of sin.”

Reading Amanda Smith’s account of her spiritual life, Ramabai felt her need of “the abiding presence of the Holy Spirit.” She heard an English evangelist, Gelson Gregson, preach in Bombay on the text “I am crucified with Christ,” as her Bible put it, and in April 1895, at a camp meeting at Lonavla in the hills above Bombay, she asked him to pray with her. Later that day, she wrote, she became conscious of the Spirit’s presence in her. A year later she brought fifteen of her own girls to the same camp meeting.

The First Baptisms

In the summer of 1895, a group of girls at the Sharada Sadan asked to be baptised. Ramabai was in an impossible position. She had promised her American supporters that the school would not make converts, Her biographer Helen Dyer says she would have preferred them to wait while they were pupils. By her own account to Boston, she gave the permission they asked for, but told them that she could not keep them in the school after baptism unless her American friends consented. Some twelve girls were baptised, in the Methodist church in Poona. On 26 July 1895 six of them wrote to the Association in Boston.

We are very glad to be able to tell you that our hearts have been quite changed and made new by the gracious Lord, and we came out and confessed our faith in Christ. This we have done out of our own free choice. No human being could have wrought this change in us, and no one could have induced us to become Christians. To God alone we give the glory, and hold no one except ourselves responsible for our change of faith.

They offered to stay on as servants, and did. They signed themselves “your grateful children.” Their names were Vittiabai, Sarasvatibai, Sukhadabai, Manikarnikabai, Rukminibai, and Bhimabai. They were the first fruits. There would be many more.

fields.title: Remember the Days of Old
fields.body_html:
“Remember the days of old, Consider the years of many generations: Ask thy father, and he will show thee; Thine elders, and they will tell thee.”

— Deuteronomy 32:7, ASV

A Voice from Within

In 1896 the rains failed across much of India, and famine spread through the Central Provinces, north-east of Poona. Ramabai read the reports and felt the old memories stir. She did not want to go. Her school was still recovering from the storm of 1893. Money from America was barely enough for the girls she already had. She was thirty-eight, partly deaf, and tired. She argued with herself, and later wrote the argument down.

The human common sense said: “You had better stop here; and ‘Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it,’ here. You have no means and no strength to do what you wish. Your powers are limited, and you will not be held responsible for not doing anything to help those famished people. Indeed, what can a weak woman do to help the dying thousands? Besides, the government of India and other benevolent people are doing what they can to relieve the poor and the needy. There is nothing for you to do.”

“I tried to quiet my conscience in this manner,” she wrote, “but louder and louder spoke the voice of God from within my heart: ‘Remember the days of old’; ‘Thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondsman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee’; and ‘Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?’ I could no longer keep still.”

The first of those verses is the one at the head of this chapter. Moses, near the end of his life, told Israel to remember where they had come from. Ramabai remembered. She remembered her father in the forest above Tirupati, and her mother at Raichur, and the bajri bread, and the sand-pits by the Jhelum. She had been a famine child herself. She could not now sit in a good house in Poona while other famine children died.

Sohagpur

At the end of 1896, having sent two workers ahead, she set out for the Central Provinces with a missionary friend. At the first town they visited, Sohagpur, they went early to the hospital to ask the doctor for permission to take orphan children. He was not there yet. Outside the hospital, three small children were walking.

Right before that hospital were walking three little famished, skeleton-like forms, and this first sight of their distress I shall never forget. … The eldest was a girl of about seven, the second a boy of five, and the youngest a baby-boy three years of age. The girl was protecting herself from the intense cold with a covering of rags, but the two boys had nothing on their bodies.

Their mother had died the day before. The youngest was desperately ill. They were crying for food, and Ramabai and her companion had none with them. Believing that they needed official permission before they could take the children, they went on to find the officer in charge of the poorhouse. When they came back, the children had gone. She searched the town and the country round it, and never found them.

“The memory of the three little ones, especially of the youngest child, who, I am sure, could not have lived many days after that, haunts me to this day. … The Lord have mercy upon us all, and give us repentance for not going to help such innocent little sufferers.”

It is characteristic of her that she did not blame the officials, or the doctor who was late, or the rules. She blamed herself.

The Poorhouses

She visited the government poorhouses and relief camps, and she described them without softening anything.

The first poorhouse we saw was no house at all. It was a grove in the outskirts of the town. Groups of famished people were seen sitting all round the grove. Some were lying down in heaps or sitting or lying in ashes on the dirty ground. … The food was nothing but dry flour and some salt. An accustomed eye could at once see that the grain was adulterated with earth before it was ground into flour.

She was fair to the government. “The government officials are kind, and are doing what they can,” she wrote. But the officials were few, and the thousands in their care were in the hands of overseers, cooks, and guards, many of whom stole the food and abused the people. Above all, she saw what happened to girls. Young women, widows, and orphans were being enticed away from the camps with sweets and promises and sold into prostitution. The traffickers, she wrote, were “carrying on a wholesale trade in young girls.”

At Itarsi she met a girl of fourteen in the street, an orphan held by a man who had taken possession of her and her little sister. The girl was afraid to leave him. Ramabai could not take her that day, but a week later, with the help of a young missionary and the police, the girl was freed, snatched back by her captor, and freed again. That night Ramabai took her to Jabalpur. She was already, Ramabai wrote, “ruined for life, and is suffering from horrible disease.”

“Hell has become a horrible reality to me,” she wrote, “and my heart is bleeding for those daughters of fond parents who have died, leaving them orphans. Who with a mother’s heart and a sister’s love can rest without doing everything in her power to save at least a few of the girls who can yet be saved from the hands of the evil ones?”

Three Hundred

From that first journey she brought back some sixty young widows to Poona. It cost more than eight hundred rupees, and most of her own school’s funds were already spoken for. In it she told, in her own words and at length, the story of her parents’ deaths, and she announced a decision.

The Lord has put it into my mind to save three hundred girls out of the famine districts, and I shall go to work in His name. The funds sent to me by my friends in America are barely enough to feed and educate fifty girls, and several people are asking me how I am going to support all these girls who may come from Central India. … I do not know, but the Lord knows what I need.

“It seems a sin,” she added, “to live in this good house, and eat plenty of good food, and be warmly clothed, while thousands of our fellow-creatures are dying of hunger and are without shelter.” She and her girls, she promised, would live on one meal a day if necessary.

“It is a bold step I am taking without your permission,” she wrote to Boston before leaving again. Within days she was back in the Central Provinces.

Girija

On the second journey she brought back more than a hundred widows, and helped to place many more orphans with other missions. One story from that journey she told at length, because it had taught her something about God.

They were travelling back from Damoh in a line of seven bullock carts, and stopped one morning to rest beside the river Herna, west of Jabalpur. One of the famine girls, still hungry, slipped into a field and picked some green gram. Ramabai made her give it back to the owner, gave the girls a lecture on honesty, and thought no more of it, until the ringleader ran away. A cart driver went after her and brought her back. Ramabai decided to make an example of her. She told the girl that she might go her own way, since she did not wish to stay, and that she would not be taken back. That evening, when the carts moved off, the girl said she was sorry and begged to come. Ramabai did not believe her, and ordered the carts to start without her.

The poor girl stood there for some moments; and then, her thin legs seeming not able to carry the weight of the body, she sat down on the ground and looked on the starting procession of carts in silence. … It was getting dark, the sky was clouded and looked as though it was going to rain. The dark mountain range and the river bank, now deserted by people, formed the background of that living picture of misery and helplessness. The world seemed very, very wide; and on it was thrown one little girl, friendless, homeless, and helpless. The picture is everlastingly engraved on my heart. … The sad picture was too much, too much for me. I ordered the driver to stop the cart, for I could not move an inch from that place.

As she sat in the cart, she thought of how often she herself had rebelled against God and gone her own way, and how often he had called her back. “The Lord taught me a precious object-lesson of His love in that desert place; and His Holy Spirit took Rom. v. 8 for a text, and showed me that, just as I was the object of His love, so ought the poor wandering girl to be an object of my love.” That verse reads: “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8, ASV).

She motioned the girl to come. The girl was too far away to hear, but she saw the hand, “and at once bounded and ran toward me, looking as though a new life had been put into her dead soul.” Her name was Girija, “a child of the mountain.”

It is a story about a hard woman learning to be soft, and Ramabai told it against herself. She had been right, by every rule of discipline, to leave the girl behind. She had also been wrong. The God who had waited for her had not waited until her repentance was genuine. He had called her while she was still a sinner. fields.title: “My Great Sin”
fields.body_html:
“Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back. If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it? And he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it? And shall not he render to every man according to his work?”

— Proverbs 24:11-12, ASV

A Different Kind of Letter

Ramabai’s first famine letter, written in January 1897, was an appeal: sad, humble, full of Scripture. Her second, written in May, after she had been back to the famine districts and home again to a new disaster, was angrier. It is worth reading carefully, because it shows a side of her that many of her admirers preferred not to show. She was not only a gentle saint gathering orphans. She was also a fierce critic of injustice, and she did not exempt the British rulers of India from her criticism, or even her Christian friends.

“Kept”

On her second journey she went back to the government poorhouses looking for young widows and girls. In one of them she asked a girl of about fourteen whether she would like to come with her.

She said she would, but that she was “kept” there by some one. I did not understand her at first. So I asked her three times over, to know if she was detained there against her wish; but I understood the dreadful meaning of that word “kept,” when an old woman sitting beside her explained it to me. This was in a government poorhouse, where the government officers are supposed to protect the virtue of young women detained under some pretence or other. I told the deputy commissioner of that district about it. He was staying in the same town. He nodded his head, and said that it is quite possible that such things are happening in the poorhouses, but he cannot help it.

The women who worked in the relief camps, she wrote, were paid so little, and had to pay so much to the overseers who hired them, that young women “have either to starve or sell their virtue. There is no other alternative for them.”

Then she turned to the British army. In the princely states of Central India, she had learned, British soldiers and officers were among the chief opponents of missionaries living near them. When some American women missionaries had tried to settle near a military camp, the soldiers had refused to have them. The reason, she said, was plain: many of the soldiers wanted no witnesses to what they did. They took the daughters of the local people, kept them as long as they wished, and turned them out when they were tired of them. The parents, many of them respectable people of high caste, were powerless. “These devils in human shape keep the girls so long as they want, and turn them away when they get tired of them.”

The Contagious Diseases Acts

For years the British government in India had run a system of licensed prostitution for its soldiers, under laws known as the Contagious Diseases Acts. Women in the cantonments were registered, inspected, and confined if found to be diseased. Christian reformers in Britain and America had fought the system for years, and two American women, Kate Bushnell and Elizabeth Andrew, had recently exposed how it worked in India. The laws had been repealed, but there was pressure to bring them back.

Ramabai wrote without restraint.

Christians in India and England must wake up at this time, and try their best not to allow the dreadful demon, the C. D. act, to come into existence again. The birthright of Indian women had been trampled down long enough. If the C. D. act comes into existence again, British iniquity will reach its climax, and God’s vengeance is sure to come down on the ruling nation. The wicked must not think that the poor, ignorant women of this country have no defender; for “their Redeemer is strong, the Lord of hosts is His name: He shall thoroughly plead their cause.”

“British iniquity.” “God’s vengeance … on the ruling nation.” These were not words that a colonial subject wrote lightly, and they are not words that appear in the admiring biographies written by her British friends. But they are hers, and they belong in her story. She had written ten years earlier that “under the so-called Christian British rule, the woman is in no better condition than of old.” She had not changed her mind. She was grateful to the British for many things, and she supported the government when she thought it was right. She did not think that being a Christian meant excusing a Christian nation’s sins against the women of her country.

The Magistrate

When she came back to Poona early in 1897, she found that bubonic plague had reached the city. The authorities, terrified of its spread, were imposing drastic measures, and many of them fell hardest on the poor.

The city magistrate, a Mr. Plunkett, ordered her to remove more than a hundred of her famine girls from Poona within forty-eight hours. She had nowhere to take them and no money to move them. He told her, in effect, that she had brought them there, and she could take them away again, or send them to the segregation camp. “To have brought the girls here to save them from starvation and death,” she wrote, “was my great sin.” She would not be allowed to keep any famine girls in Poona, even in hired houses, nor to enlarge her school. Her compound of nearly three acres was to hold only thirty people.

She was furious, and her letter shows it. She wrote that “the reign of terror had begun in Poona,” and that the magistrate had come under the influence of the Poona men, “of all men in India … famous for their disregard of women’s feelings.” She added a sharp reminder that he too had once had a woman “to nurse him and rock his cradle when he was a helpless little baby.”

It is not a saintly letter. It is a very human one. She had brought starving children out of the famine and was being treated as if she had brought the plague. And the consequences were real. She sent the girls to camp in the open at Telegaon, some twenty miles away. The water was bad and the sun intense. Within a week one of the school’s own pupils, “a nice, healthy child, the only child of her old father,” died of sunstroke. Two others died later.

Kedgaon

There was one place left. In 1894 or early 1895 the school had bought a farm at Kedgaon, a village on the railway some thirty-five or forty miles from Poona, as a source of fruit and income. There was no shade, no proper building, and no water supply fit for hundreds of people. But there was land, and it was outside the municipality.

“A little over five weeks ago I took all my girls to dwell at Kedgaum,” she wrote in May. They lived in sheds fenced with thorn bushes. The heat was intense, and the girls fell ill with fever and sore eyes. Her own eyes were so strained that she could hardly write. A cattle-shed was being built, and when the rains came, she said, they would have to live in it with the cows and bullocks. She was planning small houses where the famine girls could live in families, each in the care of one of the trained pupils of the Sharada Sadan.

It was a dismal beginning. Out of it came Mukti.

“We Knew Not This”

The verse at the head of this chapter is a warning. “Deliver them that are carried away unto death,” it commands, “And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back. If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it?” The deputy commissioner who said “he cannot help it” knew. So did the soldiers, and the overseers, and the magistrate who told her to take the girls away. So, she said, did she, and she blamed herself for the three children at Sohagpur.

She did not claim to be better than they were. But she would not say, “We knew not this.” She had seen, and she would act, and she would tell others what she had seen whether they wanted to hear it or not. Moses had said of the Lord: “He doth execute justice for the fatherless and widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18, ASV). She intended, in her own small way, to do the same.

fields.title: Prove Me Now
fields.body_html:
“Bring ye the whole tithe into the store-house, that there may be food in my house, and prove me now herewith, saith Jehovah of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.”

— Malachi 3:10, ASV

Three Books

Some time around 1895, Ramabai read three books that changed the way she thought about money. One was the story of the China Inland Mission, founded by Hudson Taylor, who had gone into the interior of China without guaranteed support, trusting God to provide. One was The Lord’s Dealings with George Müller, the journal of the Bristol pastor who had fed and housed thousands of orphans for decades without ever asking anyone but God for money. The third was the life of John G. Paton, missionary to the New Hebrides in the South Pacific.

I was greatly impressed with the experiences of these three great men. … I wondered, after reading their lives, if it were not possible to trust the Lord in India as in other countries. I wished very much that there were some missions founded in this country which would be a testimony to the Lord’s faithfulness to His people and the truthfulness of what the Bible says in a practical way.

Why, she asked herself, did no missionary come forward to start such a “faith mission” in India? The answer, she said, came from God himself.

Then the Lord said to me, “Why don’t you begin to do this yourself, instead of wishing for others to do it? How easy it is for any one to wish that some one else would do a difficult thing instead of doing it himself.” I was greatly rebuked by the “still, small voice” which spoke to me.

It is one of the most practical rebukes in Christian autobiography, and one of the most widely applicable. She took it to heart. “At the end of 1896, when the great famine came on this country, I was led by the Lord to step forward and start new work, trusting Him for both temporal and spiritual blessings.”

Mukti

The new work was the farm at Kedgaon. The school had bought about a hundred acres there in 1894 or 1895, as a fruit farm to help support the Sharada Sadan. In the spring of 1897, driven out of Poona by the plague regulations, Ramabai took her famine girls there, to live in sheds fenced with thorns. It was meant to be a temporary refuge. It became her life’s work.

That autumn help arrived. Minnie Abrams, an American Methodist missionary who had been working as a village evangelist, woke one morning with a strong sense that she was called to Kedgaon. When she told Soonderbai Powar, Soonderbai said that she and Ramabai had been praying for months for such a helper. On 15 October Abrams moved to Kedgaon. Abrams became one of her closest co-workers.

Many of the famine girls now asked to be baptised. On 6 November 1897 seventeen bullock carts full of them went six miles to the Bhima river, the girls singing all the way, and were baptised in the stream. One who was there remembered each girl clasping her hands as she was presented, and joining in the words of the baptismal formula “with beaming face.” At Christmas, Ramabai gathered all the girls and told them how God had led her in finding them. The following Sunday she and Abrams and the missionary W. W. Bruere organised a church at Kedgaon, “taking the Bible only as our creed.”

In December 1897 Ramabai held a camp meeting of her own at Kedgaon, with missionaries and Indian Christians camping in grass huts and meeting in the barn. There, according to Dyer, she dedicated the new settlement to God and gave it a name. (The finished buildings were dedicated on 24 September 1898.) She called it Mukti. It was the perfect name. The liberation that the Shastras had denied to women was here offered freely to thousands of them.

Mukti was run on Müller’s principles. It had no endowment, no guaranteed income, and no support from any missionary society. The American Association continued to support the Sharada Sadan, but the funds for Mukti came, as Ramabai believed, directly from God, through the gifts of people who heard of the work and gave without being asked for money. The verse at the head of this chapter is God’s challenge to his people through the prophet Malachi. They had been robbing God, the prophet said, by withholding their tithes. If they would bring them in, God promised to open the windows of heaven. “Prove me now herewith, saith Jehovah of hosts.”

I have responded to the Lord’s challenge, “Prove Me now” (Mal. 3. 10), and have found Him faithful and true. I know He is a prayer-hearing and prayer-answering God. … I entreat you, my readers, to prove the Lord as I have proved Him.

fields.title: The Sweeper
fields.body_html:
“He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, And lifteth up the needy from the dunghill; That he may set him with princes, Even with the princes of his people. He maketh the barren woman to keep house, And to be a joyful mother of children. Praise ye Jehovah.”

— Psalm 113:7-9, ASV

The House of Grace

Mukti grew faster than anyone had planned. Among the girls brought out of the famine districts were some who, in the words of the time, had been “sinned against by wicked men.” Around the turn of 1898-99 two American women came to Kedgaon to work among them, and Ramabai decided to build a separate home for such women and girls, where they could be cared for without shame. She called it Kripa Sadan, the House of Grace.

There was no money for it. On the evening of 20 March 1899 the foundation stone was laid anyway, at a service with missionaries and nearly a hundred workmen standing by. Ramabai, or one of her workers (the accounts differ), explained to the workmen that “although there was not a single pice in hand to build this new house, yet the foundation stone was laid in obedience to God’s order.” No debt would be incurred. They would look to God alone. The house was built, and in the years that followed it sheltered hundreds of women whom most of society would have treated as beyond help.

It was a remarkable thing for a woman of her background to do. In the Hindu law-books she had studied, a “fallen” woman deserved no pity; a king might have her thrown to the dogs. At Fulham, sixteen years before, she had first seen Christians caring for such women, and had been told the story of the woman at the well. Now she built them a house and gave it the name of grace.

The Second Famine

In 1899 the rains failed again, and a terrible famine struck western India, especially Gujarat. It was one of the worst of the century. This time Ramabai could not leave Mukti herself, and she sent out others in her place: nearly twenty helpers, eight of whom, she noted with evident joy, were women who had themselves been rescued from starvation in 1896. They brought back girls by the hundred.

By August 1900 there were more than thirteen hundred and fifty Gujarati girls at Mukti. Ramabai listed them by age: about a hundred and fifty under seven, five hundred between seven and fourteen, some six hundred between fourteen and twenty, and the rest under thirty. Most could not read. She prayed for teachers, and chose fifty of the older Christian girls to train as teachers themselves. A school of more than fifty classes was planned.

There were other problems. At one point more than nineteen hundred people, and over a hundred cattle, depended on the wells at Mukti for water. Many of the famine children were ill, and many died. The Mukti cemetery, one of her colleagues wrote, was “very full of those who have died from the effects of famine.” A missionary who visited at the end of 1901 found some two thousand women and girls living in stone buildings with tiled roofs, with dormitories, kitchens, kitchens and dining rooms in a building four hundred and twenty-five feet long, a hospital, schools, workrooms, gardens, five wells, and a great church. “Five years ago,” he wrote, “there was nothing here but an open field.”

Work

Ramabai did not believe in charity that left people idle. The girls were taught to read and to earn a living. They worked in the fields and the gardens, cooked and cleaned, wove cloth, made clothes, and later printed books on the mission’s own press, set up about 1900. Older Christian girls helped the matrons care for the newcomers. Many were trained as teachers and Bible-women, and went out to work in villages and other missions. A home for boys was opened in 1902.

She had not forgotten what had destroyed her own family: “the pride of caste and superior learning,” which had kept them from “stooping down to acquire some industry.” She meant her girls to be able to work with their hands.

A Day at Mukti

What was it like to run such a place? Around 1901 she kept a diary for a few days, and part of it was printed. It is one of the few places where we see her ordinary life. A girl who did not like to be corrected cursed her and called her names. “I smile at it,” she wrote, “for I am so well used to hearing them curse me and speak dirty words about me.” The storekeeper reminded her that blankets and other things were needed, not knowing that there was no money to order grain. People came with their wants and their grievances all day. The last complaint of the evening was from a girl who said she did not get enough oil for her hair. Ramabai quieted her, kissed a few girls standing near her door, said goodnight, and shut it.

My feet were aching and my head was tired. Before going to bed, at half-past eight, I opened my Bible and began to read. The Holy Spirit brought one special verse to my mind to comfort me. “And the Government shall be upon His shoulders.” “What a blessing,” I said to myself, “all this burden does not fall on me, but He bears it on His shoulders.”

The verse is from Isaiah’s prophecy of the child who would be born: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6, ASV). She had two thousand people depending on her, and that night, at least, she went to bed knowing that the weight was not hers to carry.

“I Am a Sweeper”

In 1901 a missionary named Mary Macdonald came to work at Mukti. Ramabai, as Helen Dyer later reported, told her what she wanted.

Now I want you to go through this institution and teach them all about the Lord Jesus Christ. I am a sweeper; that is all I am. I sweep into this compound as many as I can get; child-widows, deserted wives, and orphans of every kind, and I want you missionaries to preach to them.

In India a sweeper was one of the lowest occupations there was, the work of the untouchable castes who cleaned what others would not touch. That a Brahman woman, a pandita honoured by the scholars of Calcutta, should call herself a sweeper was a deliberate reversal of everything she had been brought up to believe about purity and rank. It was also exactly what she did. She swept up the people their families and their society had thrown away.

The verse at the head of this chapter says that God “raiseth up the poor out of the dust, And lifteth up the needy from the dunghill; That he may set him with princes.” It ends with a promise to the barren woman, who in the ancient world was a figure of shame: God “maketh the barren woman to keep house, And to be a joyful mother of children.” Ramabai had only one child of her own. By 1901 she was mother to two thousand.

Christian Outcasts

Not everyone saw it that way. To many Hindus, Mukti was a place where famine children, who could not choose for themselves, were made into Christians. Some families came and took their girls back, and the government returned about thirty to relatives who claimed them. When two of her former pupils were gathering widows and children from a princely state, an official of the Raja asked them bluntly: “How many more women and children are you going to turn into Christian outcasts, and when do you intend to stop this work?”

The young women answered that their Saviour had commanded them to make disciples, and they would go on until the world was his. Ramabai would have given the same answer. But the question was a fair one from where the official stood, and it was asked again and again, and is still asked today. The famine girls did not come to Mukti because they wanted to become Christians. They came because they were starving. Most of them did become Christians. Ramabai never hid that she hoped they would, and never pretended that Mukti was anything but a Christian community. What she would not accept was that the gospel made them outcasts. In her eyes, they had been outcasts already. Now they had a home.

fields.title: “Ramabai Is Dead”
fields.body_html:
“For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? or am I striving to please men? if I were still pleasing men, I should not be a servant of Christ.”

— Galatians 1:10, ASV

A Hard Question in Boston

The Ramabai Association in Boston had been formed in 1887 to support a secular school for high-caste Hindu widows for ten years. By 1897 it found itself the patron of something it had not planned: a school where the bell was rung for morning prayers, where nearly half the pupils were now famine children, and where the number of avowed Christians had almost doubled in a year. Before the year was out, Ramabai would bring three hundred more famine girls out of the Central Provinces.

At its annual meeting in March 1897 the Association’s officers faced the question openly. One of them, the Rev. Dr. E. W. Donald, who presided, put it with painful honesty. Ramabai, he said, had begun gathering the pupils for morning prayer, and the school bell had been rung to call them. “There has been no coercion,” he admitted. But when the head of the school rang the official bell and presided at the prayers, many girls would come who would not have come to a private room. And Ramabai “very frankly discloses the fact that she has not attempted to conceal from her pupils her desire that they should become Christians.”

Now, of course, we have to admit that this is a reversion of the past method of the school; and it is apparently — nay, really — a contradiction of the elementary principle of our Association. Secularity has been displaced by religion.

Should the Association, he asked, send Ramabai a mandate that she must give up her prayers, stop ringing the bell, “and cease her efforts to bring these women to the feet of Christ”?

Donald was not hostile. She had not, he granted, “proselyted or publicly preached,” and he wondered aloud whether a frankly Christian school might do the work as well, “and certainly with more permanent and beautiful results.” The difficulty was the promise that had been made.

The executive committee was just as frank. A visitor had reported Ramabai saying, “I have asked God to send only those girls who will become Christians.” Whether or not she had put it so bluntly, the committee wrote, the school had plainly changed. “The Sadan has become a Christian institution.” If the change came from the indirect influence of her Christian life, it was God’s work, and they rejoiced. But if any direct influence had crept in, “then the pledge to the people is broken.” They were also alarmed by her famine rescues, undertaken without their consent, and by her debts, and by her health.

They were not wrong. They had raised money from Unitarians and Episcopalians, Methodists, Baptists and Congregationalists, on the understanding that the school would not try to convert its pupils. They had defended her in 1893 on exactly that basis. And now she had, in their view, quietly changed the terms.

“Ramabai Is Dead”

In early 1898, as the ten years drew to an end, she came to Boston herself. On 16 March she spoke to the tenth annual meeting at Channing Hall. She did not apologise. She explained.

Her Hindu friends, she said, had wanted her to shut the door of her room when she read the Bible and prayed. “I said, No, I have the same freedom to practise Christianity which these girls have to practise their religion. Why should I shut the door of my room, which I do not shut at any other time during the twenty-four hours of the day?” She insisted that the school was still what she had promised: “No kind of religious training is compulsory. We do not teach the Bible or the Vedas to the girls.” The girls could keep their caste and their customs, and some still wore their gods around their necks. The girls who had come had read the Bible for themselves and compared it with their own religion. “Forty-eight of our girls have been brave enough to be publicly baptized and become Christians; and glory be to God for that! I think this is the best result of the school. We started an unsectarian school, and an unsectarian school it shall be to the end; but such must be the result of the shining light that comes from Heaven.”

She gave an account of the money. Out of about ninety-five thousand dollars the Association had sent her over ten years, she said, the school buildings and the farm were worth sixty thousand. That much she was giving back, and the rest had been spent “in raising up this family to rise up and call you blessed.”

Then she said something startling.

Now what shall be the future of the school? … The first thing I have to tell you in this connection is that Ramabai is dead. The person who went in your stead is dead and gone. What will you do with the property? … Do not concentrate your interest in one person, for that person will die and be gone, as many have gone before.

She meant that the work must not depend on her. People die; the Association must not. She asked them to found a new body “to go on working in the same old way.” She proposed a new association, a “Faith, Hope, and Love Association,” and asked for twenty thousand dollars a year. “Last year God told me I must go into the Central Provinces of my country for the rescue of three hundred girls. I had eighty cents in my hand; and I said, Where shall I get the money? But He said, ‘Go on, and money will come.’ … The Father sent thirty thousand dollars in that year.”

The Parting

The Association did what its charter required. It resolved to dissolve itself once a new body was formed. The Association’s land and buildings in Poona were conveyed to Ramabai outright, though she soon transferred it to the new Association, not wishing to hold it in her own name, “absolute, and not to create any legal trust.” And she was given formal notice that she was no longer authorised to contract any debt in the Association’s name. A new American Ramabai Association was then formed to continue supporting the school without the old charter’s restrictions. It supported her for the rest of her life.

It was not a bitter parting, but it was not an easy one. The old Executive Committee’s final report captured both their exasperation and their admiration. If they had sometimes thought her unwise in “letting her heart mislead her judgment,” and had seen in her “the impatience of a child under restraining advice,” they had also recognised “the simple, absolute faith of a child, the courage of the martyr, the spirit of the true reformer, and the glory of womanhood.”

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s, written to churches that wanted him to soften his message. “Am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? … if I were still pleasing men, I should not be a servant of Christ.” Ramabai had depended on the favour of Hindu reformers, and lost it in 1893. She had depended on the favour of her American supporters, and in 1898 she risked losing it too. She did not court either. She told them the truth about what she was doing, and left the consequences to God.

It is fair to ask whether she had been entirely straightforward. The honest answer is that she had changed, and so had her work, and she had not asked permission before changing it. She had promised a neutral school in good faith in 1887, when she herself had not yet found Christ in the way she later did. The strain of the American visit wore her out, and for a day she lay in her room, crying to God. Two friends heard of it and gave her what was needed to meet Mukti’s wants for a time. Nearly four thousand people were there, she later recalled, in words Helen Dyer preserved.

At that time the Lord led me to ask those present to pray for an outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all Indian Christians. Five minutes were given me to speak, and I made the very best use of them. I requested God’s people to pray that 100,000 men and 100,000 women from among the Indian Christians may be led to preach the Gospel to their country people.

fields.title: Fire
fields.body_html:
“And it shall be in the last days, saith God, I will pour forth of my Spirit upon all flesh: And your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, And your young men shall see visions, And your old men shall dream dreams: Yea and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days Will I pour forth of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy.”

— Acts 2:17-18, ASV

News from Wales

In the last weeks of 1904, news reached India of a revival in Wales. In chapels across the Welsh valleys, ordinary people, many of them young, were praying for hours, confessing their sins publicly, and being converted in their thousands. Ramabai read the reports with joy. She had prayed at Keswick for an outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the Christians of India, and she wondered whether this might be the beginning of an answer.

In January 1905 she told the girls at Mukti about Wales and asked for volunteers to meet with her every morning to pray for revival in India. About seventy came forward. In A Testimony she described what they prayed for.

I was led by the Lord to start a special prayer circle at the beginning of 1905. There were about seventy of us who met together each morning and prayed for the true conversion of all the Indian Christians, including ourselves, and for a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all Christians of every land.

Note the words “including ourselves.” They did not pray for revival as something for other people. They prayed for themselves first.

The circle grew. By June, Dyer records, five hundred and fifty were meeting twice a day. Ramabai asked for volunteers from the Bible school to give up their ordinary studies and go out to preach in the villages, and thirty young women offered themselves. They were meeting daily to pray for power for their work when the revival came.

Fire

Minnie Abrams had been teaching the girls about the baptism of the Holy Spirit as “power for service.” One morning, late in June 1905, she was woken by one of the older girls. “Come over and rejoice with us,” the girl said. One of the young women had received the Holy Spirit. “I saw the fire, ran across the room for a pail of water, and was about to pour it over her when I discovered she was not on fire.”

When Abrams arrived, all the girls in that compound were on their knees, weeping, praying, and confessing their sins. The next evening, as Ramabai was teaching from the eighth chapter of John’s Gospel “in her usual quiet way,” the whole congregation broke into prayer, so loudly that she had to stop. Girls of every age wept and confessed their sins. Some saw visions. Some prayed for hours.

“From that time,” Minnie Abrams wrote, “our Bible school was turned into an inquiry room. Girls, stricken down under conviction of sin while in school, or in the industrial school, or at their work, were brought to us. Lessons were suspended, and we all, teachers and students, entered the school conducted by the Holy Spirit.”

For days, and then weeks, Mukti was transformed. There was prayer all night in the compounds. Girls who had come out of famine and abuse confessed thefts and lies and hatreds, and made restitution, and were filled with joy. The girls called it a “baptism of fire,” a burning sensation that the girls said was almost unbearable, followed by peace. Hundreds prayed aloud together, the sound rising and falling “like the rolling thunder.” One of the workers wrote of a twelve-year-old girl whose plain face had become radiant, and who did not know it: “She is occupied with Jesus.”

Ramabai’s Part

It is worth noticing what Ramabai herself did, and did not do. According to Macnicol, she took little part in the more dramatic experiences. She once felt the Holy Spirit like a burning flame within her, and once, praying alone, she found herself speaking some sentences in Hebrew. When the girls prayed with loud crying, she prayed with them, but quietly. She did not lead the way in the ecstatic side of the revival, and she did not discourage it.

At first she did not want it publicised. About a month after the revival began she was asked for permission to publish an account of it, and refused, fearing that publicity would spoil the work. She fell into a time of depression. When the workers prayed together about it, she came to believe that she had been wrong to withhold the glory from God. She allowed the story to be told, and accounts were printed in the Bombay Guardian and elsewhere.

Then she did something characteristic. She took a band of her girls to Poona, and there, before Europeans and Indians, Christian and Hindu, she confessed that she had “neglected her opportunities of preaching Christ boldly.” After that, praying bands went out from Mukti to orphanages, schools, and mission stations across western India, led by Minnie Abrams, by Manorama, and by others. Their purpose, Ramabai said, was “prayer for the Christian people living in the places to which the bands go.” “Our work will bear lasting fruit,” she told them, “if we pray more and work less.” Before long, some seven hundred girls and women were involved in the praying bands, and about sixty went out every day. A circular letter asked Christians everywhere to pray by name for others, and in time more than twenty-nine thousand people were being prayed for by name at Mukti. “When we were Hindus,” she explained, “we used to repeat one or two thousand names of the gods daily. … Why should we not, as Christians, be able to pray for many hundreds of people by name?”

In November 1905 she closed the school and all ordinary work for ten days of prayer. It ended, a worker wrote, in a “tremendous time of ‘house-cleaning,’” when things that had been stolen were returned to their owners.

Tongues

The revival at Mukti began in June 1905. That was nearly a year before the famous meetings at Azusa Street in Los Angeles in April 1906, which are often counted as the beginning of the Pentecostal movement. For that reason Mukti is sometimes called one of the sources of Pentecostalism, and historians of the movement have written about it at length.

But it is important to be accurate. The revival of 1905 was marked by repentance, confession, prayer, visions, and joy. Speaking in tongues, which Pentecostals came to see as the sign of the baptism of the Spirit, did not appear at Mukti until December 1906, after reports of Azusa Street had reached India. The historian Gary McGee has traced this carefully. Minnie Abrams’s little book The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire, printed at Mukti in 1906, was later read by missionaries in Chile and helped to begin a Pentecostal movement there.

Ramabai herself never made tongues a test of anything. When the revival’s physical features were criticised by Christians who watched from outside, she defended them in the Mukti Prayer Bell in 1907, but she put them firmly in their place.

Love, perfect divine love, is the only and most necessary sign of the baptism of the Holy Spirit. But other gifts, such as the power to heal, to speak with tongues, to prophesy, are not to be discarded. Indeed we should seek from God such gifts as will enable us to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ with power and draw men unto Him. I have to learn a great deal more than I know at present. So I shall wait upon the Lord and ask Him to teach me and lead me as He will.

“I looked upon these features with much concern for some time,” she admitted, “but did not try to interfere with God’s work in any way.”

Not everyone was convinced. An Anglican missionary who studied the revival concluded that its physical accompaniments were largely “to be explained physiologically rather than as due to the direct influence of the Holy Spirit.” But he also concluded that Ramabai had “showed herself wonderfully wise in the way she fostered and guided the entire movement,” and that its permanent results were real: “the true conversion of hundreds of women.” Paul had written to the Corinthians, who also prized spiritual gifts, that without love they were nothing: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1, ASV). Ramabai had learned the same lesson.

Daughters and Handmaidens

The words at the head of this chapter are from Peter’s sermon on the day of Pentecost, quoting the prophet Joel. God’s Spirit would be poured out on everyone, “your sons and your daughters,” and even on servants: “on my servants and on my handmaidens.” In the Hindu world Ramabai grew up in, a woman was forbidden to study the Vedas, and was taught that she could not attain liberation as a woman. At Mukti in 1905, the Spirit of God fell first on famine orphans and former child-widows and outcast girls, and they went out across India to pray and to preach. It was, she believed, exactly what Joel had promised. The handmaidens were prophesying.

fields.title: A Famine of the Word
fields.body_html:
“Behold, the days come, saith the Lord Jehovah, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of Jehovah.”

— Amos 8:11, ASV

The Book She Had Been Given

Ramabai owed her faith, as she saw it, to a book. In Calcutta in 1878 some Christians had given her a Sanskrit Bible, which she thought a waste of time to read and never parted with. At Silchar she had found Luke’s Gospel in Bengali in her library. In Poona she had read the New Testament in Marathi with Miss Hurford. In England she had heard John 4 read aloud. And around 1891, by her own account, she had come to Christ only when she gave up reading books about the Bible and read the Bible itself.

So it is not surprising that in the last part of her life she gave more and more of her time to giving the Bible to others. Her great project was a new translation of the whole Bible into Marathi. It was not the first Marathi Bible. Missionaries, beginning with William Carey at Serampore early in the nineteenth century, had translated the Scriptures into Marathi long before, and a revised version was in use in her day. But she believed that a new one was needed, for two reasons.

Two Reasons

The first was that the existing Marathi Bible was written in a high, literary language, full of Sanskrit words. Educated men could read it. The village women she loved could not. She wanted a Bible in the plain everyday Marathi of ordinary people, a translation, as Helen Dyer put it, in “the simplest form of Marathi speech, so that the women of the country with no mental training and a limited vocabulary could easily understand it.” The Psalmist had said: “The opening of thy words giveth light; It giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psalm 119:130, ASV). She wanted the simple to understand.

The second reason was theological. Many of the Sanskrit words in the older translations, she believed, carried Hindu ideas that would mislead those who heard them. As a scholar of Sanskrit and of Hindu philosophy, she knew those associations as few missionaries could. About 1909, five years into her own work, she wrote a strong letter to the revisers of the Marathi Bible. She thanked the missionaries for giving India the Scriptures, but protested:

Almost all the vernacular translations of the Bible were made with the help of Hindu pundits for the sake of putting the translations into correct language, so they have many words which teach pure Hindu ideas of religion. There are some words which cannot be separated from idolatrous ideas. They make wrong impressions on non-Christian hearers, and if done knowingly it is dangerous and sinful to use them.

She gave a long list of examples. “Supposing in each chapter of the Bible there are five mistakes, or mistranslated words, then we have no less than 5945 mistakes or mistranslations in the whole Marathi Bible. Ought we to teach and preach the Bible with so many mistakes?”

She was also alarmed by the influence of what was then called the “higher criticism,” the critical study of the Bible that was spreading from German universities into the missions. She believed it undermined the authority of Scripture, and she wrote bitterly about preachers who had “determined to know everything, save Jesus Christ.” In one letter she used the words of the prophet at the head of this chapter: “We are living in a strange time. There is famine, not of food and water, but of the Word of God.” She had lived through two famines of bread. She feared this one more.

How She Worked

The work began, according to Dyer, in 1904, with a Marathi concordance giving the Greek and Hebrew meaning of each word. Ramabai believed that God had given her the plan, with the words: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith Jehovah of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6, ASV).

She learned Greek and Hebrew for the work. For the Old Testament she spent years preparing an interlinear comparison of five different versions of its words and idioms, and her preparation for the New was as thorough. Some of her students made a special study of Greek and of Hebrew to help her, and she had the help of members of the ancient Jewish community of western India, the Bene Israel, who knew the Hebrew Scriptures. How much of the final translation was her own work and how much she supervised is not entirely clear. Macnicol, the most careful of her biographers, says that she acquired “some knowledge” of the languages so that she might supervise the translation with intelligence. Others give her a greater share. She would not have cared which. It was the Bible that mattered, not the translator.

She thought it would take seven years. It took fourteen, and more. It was done in the midst of everything else: running a community of two thousand, praying through the revival, rescuing girls from famine, raising money by prayer. The press at Mukti, worked by the girls themselves, set the type in Marathi, Greek, Hebrew, and Roman letters. A tentative edition of the New Testament as far as Acts was printed in 1912. She never allowed it to be sold. She had received the Bible as a gift, she said, and she must give it freely. Jesus had said to his disciples: “freely ye received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8, ASV).

A Narrowing?

Macnicol, who admired her greatly, also thought that something was lost in these years. In her early years in Poona, he says, a translation of the Bhagavad Gita had gone on alongside her plans for the Bible. Now she saw only darkness in the religion of her fathers. For many years she would not allow Sanskrit to be taught in her schools, for fear of “the subtle poison of Vedanta,” and she would not let her own daughter learn the language of her mother and grandfather. Macnicol wondered whether the danger of Hindu words in the Bible was as great as she feared. After all, he pointed out, the very name of her settlement, Mukti, was a Sanskrit word with a Hindu meaning, and every Christian who used it understood it to mean the salvation of Christ.

It is a fair point, and a reminder that great Christians can have blind spots. A woman who had once defended her parents’ faith against those who called it worthless came, in later life, to see almost nothing good in it. But it is also fair to remember why. She had seen what the Hindu law-books taught about women, and what she had seen done to widows at Brindaban and Pandharpur. She knew, as Macnicol did not, what it was to be a Brahman woman. And Sanskrit did eventually come back into her schools, once she had prepared textbooks of her own.

The translation of the whole Bible was finished shortly before her death in 1922, and the complete edition was published after it. It is often said that she was the first woman ever to translate the whole Bible. That is not quite right. An American woman, Julia Smith, had published her own translation of the whole Bible into English in 1876. What can be said is that hers is generally regarded as the first translation of the whole Bible into colloquial Marathi, the language of ordinary people, and that she was among the first women anywhere to undertake the translation of the whole of Scripture from the original languages.

In the Church of England’s calendar, where she is remembered on 30 April, she is described simply as “Translator of the Scriptures.” Of all the things she did, it was perhaps the one that she would have chosen to be remembered by.

fields.title: Manorama
fields.body_html:
“and he said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah.”

— Job 1:21, ASV

Heart’s Joy

Of all the people in Ramabai’s story, the one who appears most often and is known least is her daughter.

Manorama was born in Assam in the spring of 1881, the daughter her parents had longed for. Her name means “Heart’s Joy.” Before she was a year old her father was dead. She sailed to England with her mother at the age of two, was baptised with her at Wantage in 1883, went with her to America at nearly five, and was sent back to England to be cared for by the Wantage sisters while her mother travelled and lectured. For about three years she did not see her mother at all. She was brought back to India by one of the sisters, and was about eight when her mother opened the Sharada Sadan.

She was a Christian from childhood, and said so. Not long after the school opened, Soonderbai Powar visited and read the Bible to the pupils while Ramabai was out of the room. Little Manorama announced that she was a Christian, and that the Bible was her Shastra.

It cannot have been an easy childhood. She grew up shared with hundreds of other girls, first widows and then famine orphans, and her mother’s attention was always divided. She was sent away again for her education, to England and then to a seminary in New York State, and she was preparing to enter Mount Holyoke College when she was called home. Her mother, Macnicol tells us, would not allow her to learn Sanskrit, the language of her mother and grandfather, for fear of its Hindu associations. Whatever she felt about any of this, she did not record it. What she did was to give her life to her mother’s work.

Her Mother’s Right Hand

She came back to India in 1900, when the second famine had filled Mukti with more than a thousand new girls, and she took charge of the Sharada Sadan and the high school. She was nineteen. From then on she was her mother’s right hand. She taught, organised, edited the Mukti Prayer Bell, wrote reports and appeals, and travelled. In 1903 she went with Minnie Abrams to Australia and New Zealand, where she spoke about the work and helped to found circles of supporters who prayed by name for the girls at Mukti. In 1905 she led praying bands out from Mukti during the revival, and A visitor quoted by Macnicol, Canon Butcher, later heard her pray aloud in tongues at Mukti. She wrote a sequel to the Australian edition of her mother’s life, bringing the story up to 1902, and it is one of the sources on which this book depends.

In 1912 she was invited, and in 1912 or 1913 she started, a work of her own, a Christian school for girls at Gulbarga, in the Muslim-ruled state of Hyderabad to the south-east. She called it Shanti Sadan, the Home of Peace, and she was entirely responsible for it, raising its money separately from Mukti and spending a few days there every month. It was hard. The school taught the Bible, and the city was soon in a ferment because several pupils had confessed Christ in their own homes.

One episode from Gulbarga should be told plainly, because it shows the spirit of the time and the cost of it. When a plot of land was bought for the school, an idol stood in the middle of it, with a shrine where the farmers of the neighbourhood had worshipped every year at the start of the rains. Manorama wrote that “this we pulled down,” and dedicated the land to God standing on the spot where the shrine had been. To her it was an act of faith. To the people of Gulbarga, who were already angry, it can only have seemed an act of contempt. “This caused an uproar again,” Helen Dyer wrote, and the school fell from seventy pupils to two, though it slowly recovered to nearly forty. Manorama acted as most missionaries of her day would have acted, and probably as her mother would have approved. A modern reader, Christian or not, may still wish that it had been done differently.

In 1917 Manorama took her degree at the University of Bombay, so that the Mukti schools could be recognised to train teachers. She was by then her mother’s chosen successor, and everyone expected her to carry the work on after Ramabai’s death.

July 1921

Her health had long been fragile. In the summer of 1921 she was taken to the mission hospital at Miraj, south of Poona. An operation was attempted, but, as Clementina Butler wrote, “her heart was not equal to the strain.” She died there in July 1921. She was forty.

Ramabai was sixty-three, growing deaf, worn out by thirty years of labour, and dependent on her daughter for almost everything. The blow was terrible. Her letter to the officers of the American Association is short and restrained.

Let me thank you for your loving sympathy. All I have to say is “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away, Blessed be the name of the Lord.” There are 360 pupils studying in the Sharada Sadan, the Primary and the Kindergarten. This work shall be continued as long as God gives us grace and strength. The school was well organized and brought to its present state by my daughter, who has gone to the next world before me!

One of Manorama’s last acts, her mother added, had been to draw up the timetables for the school year.

The Lord Gave

The words Ramabai quoted, in the older translation she knew, are Job’s, spoken when he heard that his children were dead. They are the words at the head of this chapter: “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah.” Job said them in the first shock of his loss, before his long argument with God began, and they have been said by grieving Christians ever since. Ramabai did not argue. She had lost her father, her mother, her sister, her brother, her husband, and the friend who had come with her to England, all before she was twenty-six. Now, near the end of her own life, she had lost her only child. She blessed the name of the Lord.

Butler, who knew both of them, believed that the loss of her daughter, and of the support Manorama had given her, was more than her mother’s body could bear. It is very likely true. Ramabai lived less than nine months longer. But she did not stop working. When her old friend Ramabai Ranade, the widow of the judge who had resigned from her board in 1893, came to visit her in her grief, Mrs. Ranade later said that Ramabai preached the gospel to her.

Paul told the Thessalonians not to grieve over those who had died in Christ “even as the rest, who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13, ASV). Ramabai believed that her daughter had gone ahead of her to the country they had both been travelling towards, and that she would follow soon. She was right about that.
