fields.title: Having Nothing
fields.body_html:
“as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.”

— 2 Corinthians 6:10, ASV

The Later Years

In the last decade of her life, Ramabai seldom left Kedgaon. She was growing deafer, and in the end could hardly hear at all. She worked at the Bible translation for as many hours as she could spare, ran the community through her daughter and her helpers, wrote letters, prayed, and received visitors. Her own voice becomes harder to hear in these years. She had resolved, she wrote, that nothing should be “sown in my name,” and she wrote less and less about herself. Most of what we know comes from others.

The visitors came from everywhere. A young American, Howard Walter, spent three days at Mukti in 1918 and wrote that he had not been prepared for the impression she made on him. She was translating the Bible, and supervising the printing of a Marathi life of Christ of which 23,000 copies were already in Hindu homes. In 1919, when famine came again, Mukti fed some eight hundred starving people every day.

In the New Year’s honours of 1919 the British government awarded her the Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal, an award for public service in India, for distinguished service to Indian education. She was too weak to travel to Bombay to receive it from the Governor. Macnicol says that she chose to receive it instead from the hand of Mrs. R. A. Adams, the wife of the secretary of the Bible Society in Bombay, because of her love for the society’s work; Butler says that Manorama received it for her. Helen Dyer remarked that they had “heard nothing from her concerning it.” It is easy to believe. She had been given titles before, in Calcutta, forty years earlier. She had long since counted such things as nothing.

Setting Her House in Order

After Manorama’s death in July 1921, she knew that her own time was short. She appointed as her successor Lissa Hastie, an English friend who had worked beside her for twelve years, on condition, as Dyer’s book put it, that the work be “continued on exactly the same lines,” that is, as a work of faith. She signed a call for a Bible League to defend the authority of Scripture. She made her will. According to a friend, she set her house in order weeks before the end, and on the very day before she died wrote a letter about the care of some of the children.

A few days before her death, the secretary of the Bible Society in Bombay came to Mukti. She was too weak to speak, and too deaf to hear him. She sent for him to her room, and wrote with a trembling hand:

I want to say that I greatly appreciate your Society’s work. I have been a Christian for thirty-eight years. I have found a great salvation through the Society’s work. God bless you and yours.

Thirty-eight years took her back to her baptism at Wantage in 1883. Over the last ten years of her life, Macnicol records, she had given more than eleven thousand rupees to the Bible Society, and for years the girls at Mukti had set aside a fifteenth part of their daily grain for it. The Bible had been given to her freely. She gave it freely to others, and she gave to those who gave it to others.

5 April 1922

She died early in the morning of 5 April 1922, at Mukti. “She slipped away quietly in her sleep as the day broke,” Macnicol wrote. She was sixty-three, less than three weeks short of her sixty-fourth birthday. No source records a medical cause of death. Butler, who knew her, believed that her grief for her daughter, and the loss of all that Manorama had carried for her, had been too much for a body long weakened by the hardships of her youth. That is as near as we can come.

The cable to the American Association read: “Ramabai Promoted.”

The Funeral

The funeral service was conducted by her old friend Robert Hume of Ahmednagar, representing the American Association, with W. W. Bruere, who had helped to found the church at Mukti in 1897. Her plain coffin was carried on the shoulders of the young women of Mukti, and a thousand girls followed it to the cemetery. Over it was laid a white cloth inscribed with Paul’s words: “We shall all be changed, the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” On the lid were the words: “The Pundita Ramabai Medhavi — born April 23, 1858; slept April 5, 1922.”

All day, one of the Mukti workers wrote, people came from the villages around Mukti, people whom “Bai” had fed in every famine since 1896, to pay their respects. High castes, low castes, and outcastes stood together and folded their hands before the body of a Brahman woman who, in her youth, would have been polluted by the touch of most of them. One old Brahman widow, bent with age and with a lifetime of the fasting and hardship that were the lot of Brahman widows, leaned over the bed and cried out: “O, Great Mother, Great Mother, whom now shall I call Mother? Who will care for me?”

There was no money. Because all the gifts for Mukti had been sent in Ramabai’s name, none of them could be drawn until her will had been proved, and the courts were on holiday. “Here we were with a thousand people to feed,” Hastie wrote in June, “to say nothing of other expenses, and no money.” They prayed, and from day to day, she wrote, enough came to keep them going. Mukti was carrying on as its founder had intended.

Remembered

Across India, people gathered to honour her. At a memorial meeting in Poona, the British Collector of the district imagined her deaf ears “wakened to hear her Master say to her, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant.’” In Bombay, the poet and nationalist leader Sarojini Naidu, who was not a Christian, claimed her for India as “the first Christian to be enrolled in the calendar of Hindu saints.” It was meant as the highest praise a Hindu could give, and it was a sign that some of her countrymen, who had once called her a traitor, were ready to claim her as their own.

Having Nothing

The words at the head of this chapter are Paul’s description of the apostolic life: “as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” They describe Ramabai’s life as well as any words could. She had been born into wealth and lost it in a famine. She had been honoured by the scholars of Calcutta and lost her honour in the eyes of her people. She had founded a great work and would not hold its property in her own name. She owned, as she said, nothing on earth but a few clothes and her Bible, and the Bible she translated she gave away, never allowing it to be sold. And she left behind her a community of more than a thousand people, a Bible in the language of the village women of Maharashtra, and a multitude of women and girls who had been given back their lives.

“I have fought the good fight,” Paul wrote at the end of his life, “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7, ASV). Ramabai would not have claimed so much. She would have said, as she had said all her life, that God was faithful, and that she had proved him.

A few days before her death, the secretary of the Bible Society in Bombay came to Mukti. She was too weak to speak, and too deaf to hear him. She sent for him to her room, and wrote with a trembling hand: I want to say that I greatly appreciate your Society’s work. I have been a Christian for thirty-eight years. I have found a great salvation through the Society’s work. God bless you and yours. Thirty-eight years took her back to her baptism at Wantage in 1883. Over the last ten years of her life, Macnicol records, she had given more than eleven thousand rupees to the Bible Society, and for years the girls at Mukti had set aside a fifteenth part of their daily grain for it. The Bible had been given to her freely. She gave it freely to others, and she gave to those who gave it to others. 5 April 1922 She died early in the morning of 5 April 1922, at Mukti. “She slipped away quietly in her sleep as the day broke,” Macnicol wrote. She was sixty-three, less than three weeks short of her sixty-fourth birthday. No source records a medical cause of death. Butler, who knew her, believed that her grief for her daughter, and the loss of all that Manorama had carried for her, had been too much for a body long weakened by the hardships of her youth. That is as near as we can come. The cable to the American Association read: “Ramabai Promoted.” The Funeral The funeral service was conducted by her old friend Robert Hume of Ahmednagar, representing the American Association, with W. W. Bruere, who had helped to found the church at Mukti in 1897. Her plain coffin was carried on the shoulders of the young women of Mukti, and a thousand girls followed it to the cemetery. Over it was laid a white cloth inscribed with Paul’s words: “We shall all be changed, the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” On the lid were the words: “The Pundita Ramabai Medhavi — born April 23, 1858; slept April 5, 1922.” All day, one of the Mukti workers wrote, people came from the villages around Mukti, people whom “Bai” had fed in every famine since 1896, to pay their respects. High castes, low castes, and outcastes stood together and folded their hands before the body of a Brahman woman who, in her youth, would have been polluted by the touch of most of them. One old Brahman widow, bent with age and with a lifetime of the fasting and hardship that were the lot of Brahman widows, leaned over the bed and cried out: “O, Great Mother, Great Mother, whom now shall I call Mother? Who will care for me?” There was no money. Because all the gifts for Mukti had been sent in Ramabai’s name, none of them could be drawn until her will had been proved, and the courts were on holiday. “Here we were with a thousand people to feed,” Hastie wrote in June, “to say nothing of other expenses, and no money.” They prayed, and from day to day, she wrote, enough came to keep them going. Mukti was carrying on as its founder had intended. Remembered Across India, people gathered to honour her. At a memorial meeting in Poona, the British Collector of the district imagined her deaf ears “wakened to hear her Master say to her, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant.’” In Bombay, the poet and nationalist leader Sarojini Naidu, who was not a Christian, claimed her for India as “the first Christian to be enrolled in the calendar of Hindu saints.” It was meant as the highest praise a Hindu could give, and it was a sign that some of her countrymen, who had once called her a traitor, were ready to claim her as their own. Having Nothing The words at the head of this chapter are Paul’s description of the apostolic life: “as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” They describe Ramabai’s life as well as any words could. She had been born into wealth and lost it in a famine. She had been honoured by the scholars of Calcutta and lost her honour in the eyes of her people. She had founded a great work and would not hold its property in her own name. She owned, as she said, nothing on earth but a few clothes and her Bible, and the Bible she translated she gave away, never allowing it to be sold. And she left behind her a community of more than a thousand people, a Bible in the language of the village women of Maharashtra, and a multitude of women and girls who had been given back their lives. “I have fought the good fight,” Paul wrote at the end of his life, “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7, ASV). Ramabai would not have claimed so much. She would have said, as she had said all her life, that God was faithful, and that she had proved him.

fields.title: No Caste, No Sex
fields.body_html:
“There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus.”

— Galatians 3:28, ASV

Three Women Again

The introduction to this book described three Ramabais: the reformer, the saint, and, to some of her critics, the missionary who drew Hindu girls away from their faith. Having followed her life to its end, we can see why each portrait exists, and why none of them is enough.

The reformer is real. Ramabai was one of the first Indian women to speak in public for the rights of women, to found a women’s organisation, to give evidence before a government commission, and to write a book arguing that the women of India were oppressed and must be educated and set free. She did it in her twenties, as a widow, against the united opposition of orthodox Hindu society. The historian Meera Kosambi has argued that her disappearance from the standard histories of Maharashtrian reform was caused as much by her being an outspoken woman as by her being a Christian. The Indian government recognised her contribution in 1989 by issuing a postage stamp in her honour.

The saint is real too. She gave away everything she had. She rescued thousands of women and girls from starvation and from prostitution. She founded a community that has lasted for more than a century. She trusted God for every meal for twenty-five years, and the meals came. She prayed for revival, and saw one that spread across India and beyond. She translated the Bible into the everyday speech of the people she loved. The Church of England remembers her every year on 30 April as “Pandita Mary Ramabai, Translator of the Scriptures,” and she appears on 5 April in some trial and supplementary calendars of the Episcopal Church in America, though not in its current official calendar. In 2018 the New York Times published an obituary of her in a series on remarkable people it had overlooked in their own time.

And the critics have a point that should not be dismissed. She did promise her Hindu supporters a neutral school, and that school did become a place where many girls became Christians. Most of the famine girls she rescued were children, who did not choose Mukti for its religion but because they were starving. She hoped they would become Christians, and most of them did. To those who believed that the Hindu tradition was the soul of India, this could only look like a loss. From 1897 on she made no secret of what she hoped for, and no source shows her compelling anyone to be baptised. But her Hindu critics believed in 1893 that she had concealed her aims, her own American committee feared the pledge had been broken, and the famine children at Mukti had little real choice about the teaching they received. But it is not surprising that those who did not share her faith saw her work differently.

One Woman

The truth is that all three portraits describe the same woman, and the threads cannot be separated. Her feminism and her faith were not two different things. She became a reformer because she read the Hindu law-books and found that they held out no hope for her as a woman. She became a Christian, in the deepest sense, when she discovered that in Christ there was hope for her as a woman, freely given. “What good news,” she wrote, “for me, a woman; a woman born in India among Brahmins, who hold out no hope for me and the like of me.” Her famine rescues were acts of faith and acts of social reform at once. Her Bible translation was for the women of the villages.

The words at the head of this chapter are Paul’s, written to the churches of Galatia, who were arguing about whether Gentile Christians must become Jews. “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus.” Ramabai summed up the same truth in her own words when she described her discovery of the gospel: “No caste, no sex, no work, and no man was to be depended upon to get salvation, this everlasting life; but God gave it freely to any one and every one who believed on His Son.”

No caste. In the community she founded, Brahman widows lived alongside the daughters of outcastes and prayed with them, and at her funeral high castes and outcastes stood together by her body. No sex. She taught that the Spirit of God was given to daughters as well as sons, to handmaidens as well as servants, and she sent young women out to preach across India. No work. She believed that salvation was not earned by pilgrimages or alms or fasting, as she had once believed, but freely given, and she gave freely in turn.

Mukti Today

The community she founded still exists. The Pandita Ramabai Mukti Mission still stands at Kedgaon, east of Pune. According to its own figures it is home to some fifteen hundred people, among them orphaned and abandoned girls, widows, elderly and disabled women, and boys, and it runs schools for more than two thousand pupils, a hospital, a farm, and a Bible school, on a site of some two hundred and forty acres. One of its schools is still called Sharada Sadan. Another is named after Manorama. Ramabai would not build the mission on an endowment, and it still relies on gifts.

Her other legacies are harder to measure. The revival of 1905 spread to many other places in India, and through Minnie Abrams’s little book it reached as far as Chile, where it helped to begin a Pentecostal movement. Her Marathi Bible was printed and given away at Mukti, in the plain speech she had chosen for the village women. The women she trained became teachers, nurses, and Bible-women across western India. And her life became a story that has been told in many languages, to many people who never heard of the Shastras or the famines of the 1870s, as an example of what one woman’s faith and courage could do.

The Fatherless and the Widow

This book began with a verse from the Psalms: “A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, Is God in his holy habitation.” The verse goes on: “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV). Ramabai was fatherless at sixteen and a widow at twenty-three, and she knew what it was to be solitary. She spent the rest of her life setting the solitary in families: child-widows whose families had cast them out, famine orphans who had lost everyone, women whom society called fallen, girls sold in the camps. At Mukti they found a family, and a mother.

She would not want to be remembered as a heroine. She described herself as a sweeper. She would want to be remembered, if at all, as a witness to the faithfulness of God. “I have come to believe the Word of God implicitly,” she wrote, “and I have found out by experience that it is true.” And near the end of her testimony she turned from herself to her readers: “I entreat you, my readers, to prove the Lord as I have proved Him.”

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of Pandita Ramabai
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. Pandita Ramabai called herself a sweeper, and would have been uncomfortable being held up as a model. She wanted her life to point to the faithfulness of God. Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on her example alone. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider how those who went before us lived and died, and to imitate their faith, not every detail of their lives.

1. Teach Your Daughters

Her father defied his caste to teach his wife and daughters, and everything Ramabai became grew from that. Children learn what their parents care enough to teach them. “Thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deuteronomy 6:7, ASV).

2. Love the Truth More Than Approval

At Dwarka, as a girl, she saw no golden city, and would not pretend she did. All her life she preferred the truth to the good opinion of others. “Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32, ASV).

3. Suffering Does Not Make Us Kind; Grace Does

She warned that hunger and grief had hardened her heart, not softened it, and that only God could give her a heart that cared for others. “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26, ASV).

4. God Draws Those Who Cannot Find Their Own Way

Widowed at twenty-three, before she knew Christ, she wrote that if she was to come to God, “He must Himself draw me.” “No man can come to me, except the Father that sent me draw him” (John 6:44, ASV).

5. Speak for Those Who Cannot Speak

She told a government commission that women were oppressed by men, when almost no Indian woman had a public voice. “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV).

6. Christ Receives the Outcast

She was drawn to Christ by seeing Christians care for women society had cast out, and by the story of the woman at the well. “Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4:14, ASV).

7. Religion Is Not the Same as Christ

For eight years after her baptism, she said, she had “found the Christian religion” but “had not found Christ.” Many people still stop where she stopped. “The people that sat in darkness Saw a great light” (Matthew 4:16, ASV).

8. Salvation Is a Gift

“No caste, no sex, no work, and no man was to be depended upon to get salvation.” What she had tried for years to earn, she found was freely given. “But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8, ASV).

9. Do Not Shut the Door

She would not hide her faith from those who wanted to hear, and in time she told her supporters plainly what her work had become. Honesty about faith can cost friends and still be right. “Am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God?” (Galatians 1:10, ASV).

10. Begin It Yourself

When she wished someone would start a work of faith in India, she heard God ask why she did not begin it herself. Wishing that others would act is easy. “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecclesiastes 9:10, ASV).

11. Love the Wanderer

She was ready to leave the runaway girl at the Herna river, until she remembered how God had loved her while she was still a sinner. Mercy that waits for repentance is not yet the mercy of God. “I have loved thee with an everlasting love” (Jeremiah 31:3, ASV).

12. Prove the Lord

She fed hundreds, and then thousands, without endowment, guaranteed income, or bank account, and found God faithful. She invited her readers to test him as she had. “Prove me now herewith, saith Jehovah of hosts” (Malachi 3:10, ASV).

13. Revival Begins with Ourselves

The prayer circle at Mukti prayed first for “the true conversion of all the Indian Christians, including ourselves.” “If my people, who are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven” (2 Chronicles 7:14, ASV).

14. Love Is the Sign

In the excitement of the revival she insisted that “love, perfect divine love, is the only and most necessary sign of the baptism of the Holy Spirit.” “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1, ASV).

15. Give the Word Freely

She spent her last years translating the Bible into the language of ordinary women, and never allowed it to be sold. “Freely ye received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8, ASV).

16. Be a Sweeper

One of the most learned women of her generation called herself a sweeper, and spent her life gathering up those whom others had thrown away. “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, And lifteth up the needy from the dunghill” (Psalm 113:7, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make Pandita Ramabai an object of admiration, but to let her life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Several chapters raise hard questions about women, caste, conversion, colonial rule, and the relationship between Christianity and other faiths. They are meant to be discussed honestly, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Pandita and Her Biographers

Central idea

Ramabai is remembered as a reformer, a saint, and a missionary; her own words are the surest guide to which she was.

Scriptures to revisit

John 8:32; Proverbs 18:17.

Reflection

1. Why do different groups remember the same person so differently? 2. What is the difference between finding a religion and finding Christ?

Chapter 1 - The Forest School

Central idea

A father who defied his caste to teach his wife and daughters shaped everything Ramabai became.

Scriptures to revisit

Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Proverbs 22:6.

Reflection

1. What did your parents teach you that has lasted? 2. Who in your community is being kept from learning?

Chapter 2 - Pilgrims

Central idea

A child who saw no golden city learned to prefer the truth to the approval of the crowd.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 115:4-8; Jeremiah 10:14.

Reflection

1. Have you ever pretended to see something you did not see? 2. How should Christians speak honestly but respectfully about other religions?

Chapter 3 - The Famine

Central idea

Her father gave her into the hands of the only God he knew, and she came to believe that God had heard him.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 27:10; Acts 17:23.

Reflection

1. What does it mean that God may answer prayers offered in ignorance? 2. What did pride of caste cost her family?

Chapter 4 - Four Thousand Miles

Central idea

Suffering does not of itself make people kind; Ramabai believed only grace can give a heart of flesh.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 107:4-6; Ezekiel 36:26.

Reflection

1. Has suffering made you harder or softer? 2. What changed Ramabai’s heart?

Chapter 5 - Pandita

Central idea

Honoured for her learning, she found that the sacred books held no hope for her as a woman.

Scriptures to revisit

Job 28:12-13, 28.

Reflection

1. Where do people look for wisdom today? 2. What did Keshab Chandra Sen’s smile give her?

Chapter 6 - Nineteen Months

Central idea

Widowed at twenty-three, she found that grief drew her nearer to a God she did not yet know.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 54:4-5; John 6:44.

Reflection

1. What did widowhood mean in Ramabai’s world? 2. How has God drawn you?

Chapter 7 - “Open Thy Mouth for the Dumb”

Central idea

She spoke publicly for India’s women when almost no woman had a public voice.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 31:8-9; Psalm 10:17-18.

Reflection

1. Who in your society has no voice? 2. What did it cost Ramabai to speak?

Chapter 8 - As Abraham

Central idea

Christians caring for outcast women, and the story of the woman at the well, drew her to Christ.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 11:8; John 4:1-26.

Reflection

1. Why did the rescue homes at Fulham move her so deeply? 2. What did Father Goreh’s book add?

Chapter 9 - The Religion Without Christ

Central idea

She refused to let others govern her conscience, and went to the Bible itself.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 5:21; Acts 17:11.

Reflection

1. Was Ramabai right to resist the Wantage sisters? 2. What is the difference between independence and pride?

Chapter 10 - The High-Caste Hindu Woman

Central idea

In America she pleaded for India’s widows, believing that the despised could redeem their nation.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 1:17; John 1:46.

Reflection

1. What did she mean by “out of Nazareth”? 2. Why did she criticise British rule even while seeking Western help?

Chapter 11 - Sharada Sadan

Central idea

She opened a home of learning for widows, and left the door of her room open.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 9:1-6.

Reflection

1. Was the promise of neutrality wise? 2. What would you have done about the open door?

Chapter 12 - The Storm of 1893

Central idea

Honest people on both sides clashed over her school, and she learned not to fear men.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 56:3-4; Isaiah 54:17.

Reflection

1. Were the reformers wrong to resign? 2. When is it right to keep a promise, and when to break it?

Chapter 13 - “I Had Not Found Christ”

Central idea

She surrendered to Christ and found salvation freely given to a woman.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 4:16; Romans 5:8; Galatians 3:28.

Reflection

1. Have you found the religion, or Christ? 2. Why was the gospel good news “for me, a woman”?

Chapter 14 - Remember the Days of Old

Central idea

Remembering her own famine, she went into the famine districts to rescue girls.

Scriptures to revisit

Deuteronomy 32:7; Esther 4:14; Romans 5:8.

Reflection

1. What do you need to remember about where God found you? 2. What does the story of Girija teach about mercy?

Chapter 15 - “My Great Sin”

Central idea

She exposed injustice in the poorhouses and the army, and was punished for saving starving girls.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 24:11-12; Deuteronomy 10:18.

Reflection

1. Was her anger righteous? 2. Where do we say “we knew not this” today?

Chapter 16 - Prove Me Now

Central idea

She began a work of faith herself instead of wishing others would, and proved God faithful.

Scriptures to revisit

Malachi 3:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:24.

Reflection

1. What are you wishing someone else would do? 2. What are the gifts and the costs of a faith mission?

Chapter 17 - The Sweeper

Central idea

She swept up the people India had thrown away, and gave them work and a home.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 113:7-9; Isaiah 9:6.

Reflection

1. What did it mean for a Brahman to call herself a sweeper? 2. How should Christians answer the charge of making “Christian outcasts”?

Chapter 18 - “Ramabai Is Dead”

Central idea

She told her American supporters plainly that her work had changed, and gave them back what was theirs.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 1:10; Matthew 9:38.

Reflection

1. Was Ramabai fair to her supporters? 2. What did she mean by “Ramabai is dead”?

Chapter 19 - Fire

Central idea

A prayer circle that began by praying for itself saw revival spread across India.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 2:17-18; 1 Corinthians 13:1.

Reflection

1. Why did they pray “including ourselves”? 2. How did Ramabai keep spiritual gifts in their place?

Chapter 20 - A Famine of the Word

Central idea

She translated the Bible into the plain speech of village women and gave it away.

Scriptures to revisit

Amos 8:11; Psalm 119:130; Zechariah 4:6.

Reflection

1. Why does plain language matter in Scripture? 2. Did she go too far in rejecting her Hindu heritage?

Chapter 21 - Manorama

Central idea

Her daughter gave her life to her mother’s work, and died before her.

Scriptures to revisit

Job 1:21; 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

Reflection

1. What might Manorama’s life have cost her? 2. How do Christians grieve with hope?

Chapter 22 - Having Nothing

Central idea

She died owning almost nothing, and left behind a community, a Bible, and thousands of lives restored.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Timothy 4:7.

Reflection

1. What does it mean to be “poor, yet making many rich”? 2. What did the old Brahman widow’s cry reveal?

Chapter 23 - No Caste, No Sex

Central idea

Her feminism and her faith were one, rooted in the freedom of the gospel.

Scriptures to revisit

Galatians 3:28; Psalm 68:5-6.

Reflection

1. Which of the three Ramabais do you find most compelling, and why? 2. Whom might God be calling you to set in a family?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of Pandita Ramabai
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Where Ramabai’s own writings, contemporary letters, or the records of the Ramabai Association give a date, it is given plainly. Where the sources disagree, the chronology gives the best-supported date and the disagreement is noted in the chapters or in Appendix D.

Before 1858 - Anant Shastri

Anant Shastri Dongre, a Brahman Sanskrit scholar from the Mangalore district, studies in Poona, resolves to teach his wife Sanskrit, and later marries Lakshmibai, aged nine. He teaches her, and makes a home in the Gangamul forest in the Western Ghats.

23 April 1858 - Birth

Ramabai is born in the forest, the youngest of three surviving children: Srinivas, Krishnabai, and Ramabai.

Late 1858 - The Pilgrim Life Begins

Ruined by hospitality, the family leave the forest when she is about six months old, and live for some fifteen years as Puranikas, reciting the Puranas at sacred places across India.

c. 1862-1873 - Education and Pilgrimages

Her mother teaches her Sanskrit from about eight to fifteen. Pilgrimages to Tirupati, Dakor, the Jumna, Dwarka, and Pandharpur. Her father refuses to marry her as a child.

c. 1874-1877 - Famine

As famine spreads in the Madras Presidency, the family spends its money on religious merit. Her father dies near Tirupati; her mother at Raichur; her sister soon after. She is about sixteen. The usual date of 1877 is probably too late.

c. 1875-1878 - Wandering

Ramabai and Srinivas walk, by her reckoning, more than four thousand miles, north to Kashmir and east to Calcutta.

1878 - Calcutta

She meets Keshab Chandra Sen, reads the Dharma Shastras, is given a Sanskrit Bible, and is acclaimed by the pandits with the title Sarasvati. She becomes known as Pandita Ramabai.

1880 - Bereavement and Marriage

Srinivas dies, probably at Dacca. In November she marries Bipin Behari Medhavi, a Bengali lawyer of non-Brahman caste, in a civil ceremony.

1881 - Manorama

Her daughter Manorama is born, probably in April, at Silchar in Assam. At Silchar she reads Luke’s Gospel in Bengali.

1882 - Widowhood and Poona

Her husband dies of cholera, probably in February. She moves to Poona, founds the Arya Mahila Samaj, publishes Stri Dharma Niti, and on 5 September gives evidence to the Education Commission.

1883 - England and Baptism

She sails for England in the spring with Manorama and a companion, Anandibai Bhagat, who later takes her own life. On 29 September she and Manorama are baptised at Wantage.

1884-1886 - Cheltenham

She studies and teaches Sanskrit at Cheltenham Ladies’ College under Dorothea Beale, while arguing with the Wantage sisters over doctrine and authority.

1886-1888 - America

She reaches Philadelphia in March 1886 and attends Anandibai Joshee’s graduation. The High-Caste Hindu Woman is published in June 1887. The Ramabai Association is formed in Boston on 13 December 1887. She lectures across the United States and sails from San Francisco in November 1888.

1 February 1889 - Return

She lands at Bombay.

11 March 1889 - Sharada Sadan

The school for high-caste widows opens at Chowpatty, Bombay. In December she speaks at the Indian National Congress.

November 1890 - Poona

The Sharada Sadan moves to Poona.

1891 - Finding Christ

By her own account, eight years after her baptism, she surrenders to Christ and finds peace. A press campaign in Poona attacks her school.

13 August 1893 - The Resignation

The Hindu advisory board resigns, charging proselytism. Thirty-one pupils are withdrawn. The Ramabai Association investigates and supports her.

1895 - Kedgaon and the Spirit

A farm is bought at Kedgaon. In April, at Lonavla, she seeks and receives the Holy Spirit. By July some girls of the Sharada Sadan have been baptised.

1896-1897 - Famine Rescues

She travels into the Central Provinces and brings back hundreds of famine girls. Plague restrictions in Poona force her to move them to Kedgaon in the spring of 1897.

1897 - Mukti

Minnie Abrams arrives in October. Many girls are baptised in the Bhima river in November. In December the settlement at Kedgaon is dedicated and named Mukti.

1898 - Boston and Keswick

On 16 March she addresses the Ramabai Association in Boston. The old Association dissolves and the property passes to her; she transfers it to the new American Ramabai Association. At the Keswick Convention she asks prayer for 100,000 men and 100,000 women to preach in India.

1899 - Kripa Sadan

The foundation stone of Kripa Sadan, the House of Grace for rescued women, is laid on 20 March.

1899-1900 - The Second Famine

Famine in Gujarat. By August 1900 more than 1,350 Gujarati girls are at Mukti. Manorama returns from America to lead the Sharada Sadan.

1901-1902 - Growth

Mukti shelters some two thousand women and girls. A home for boys opens in 1902.

1904 - Bible Translation

Work begins on a new translation of the Bible into colloquial Marathi.

1905 - Revival

A prayer circle of about seventy begins in January. Revival breaks out late in June. Praying bands go out across western India.

1906-1907 - Tongues and A Testimony

Speaking in tongues appears at Mukti in December 1906. In 1907 she publishes A Testimony and defends the revival in the Mukti Prayer Bell.

1912 - Gulbarga and the New Testament

Manorama begins Shanti Sadan at Gulbarga (1912-13). A tentative edition of the New Testament as far as Acts is printed.

1919 - Honour

She is awarded the Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal in the New Year Honours.

July 1921 - Manorama’s Death

Manorama dies at Miraj, aged forty.

5 April 1922 - Death

Ramabai dies at Mukti, aged sixty-three, shortly after completing the translation of the Bible. Lissa Hastie succeeds her.

1924 - The Marathi Bible

The complete Bible in her translation is published.

1989 - Stamp

India issues a postage stamp in her honour.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims have been corrected. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

Ramabai’s Own Writings

Wherever possible, this book lets Ramabai speak for herself. Her principal English writings, all now in the public domain, are these:

  • The High-Caste Hindu Woman (Philadelphia, 1887), her own book, with an introduction by Rachel Bodley that includes much biographical material told to Bodley by Ramabai, and her 1882 evidence to the Education Commission. When the book was reprinted in 1901, Ramabai asked for Bodley’s introduction to be left out. Where Bodley’s account of her childhood differs from Ramabai’s own, this book follows Ramabai.
  • Famine Experiences in India (1897), two letters written for the relief of the famine, containing her fullest account of her parents’ deaths and her own famine journeys.
  • A Testimony (Kedgaon, 1907, with later additions), her account of her spiritual journey. We have not found a copy of the original pamphlet. It survives in a condensation made with her permission by J. J. Lucas (Pandita Ramabai: A Wonderful Life, 1919) and in a fuller text printed by Helen Dyer (see below). The two differ: Dyer’s text omits the names of the Hindu reformers who helped her in Poona and of Father Nehemiah Goreh, and Lucas’s includes them. This book quotes both, and follows Lucas where Dyer has cut.
  • A short tract, Trying to be Saved by Their Own Merit, describing the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.
  • Her letters to the Ramabai Association in Boston, printed in its annual reports from 1890 to 1898, and other letters printed in Pandita Ramabai: The Widows’ Friend (Melbourne, 1903), whose later chapters were written by her daughter Manorama.

Her Marathi writings, including Stri Dharma Niti (1882) and her book on the United States (1889), and her correspondence with the Wantage sisters, edited by A. B. Shah as The Letters and Correspondence of Pandita Ramabai (1977), have been used only through what modern scholars report of them. The modern English translations of these works are in copyright.

The Early Biographers

  • Helen S. Dyer, Pandita Ramabai: The Story of Her Life (1900), and Pandita Ramabai: Her Vision, Her Mission and Triumph of Faith (London, after 1922), whose last chapter, on Ramabai’s death, was completed by another hand after Dyer’s own death. Dyer knew Ramabai and her circle, and her books contain many letters and first-hand accounts, especially of the revival. She wrote to inspire prayer and support, treats Hinduism with open contempt, and was herself a participant in at least one controversial episode (the hiding of a girl in 1893) that she describes approvingly.
  • Clementina Butler, Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati (1922), a memorial life by the chairman of the American Ramabai Association’s executive committee, valuable for its American documents and its account of Ramabai’s last years.
  • Nicol Macnicol, Pandita Ramabai (1926), in the series Builders of Modern India. The most careful of the early lives, it draws on the Marathi biography by D. G. Vaidya and the recollections of Ramabai Ranade, and is willing to criticise its subject.
  • Jennie Chappell, Women Who Have Worked and Won (1900), a popular account that adds romantic details found nowhere else. It has been used sparingly and never alone.

Modern Scholars

This book has drawn facts and interpretations, but not text, from modern scholarship, especially Meera Kosambi (Pandita Ramabai Through Her Own Words, 2000, and her edition of Ramabai’s American book, 2003), Uma Chakravarti (Rewriting History, 1998), Gauri Viswanathan (Outside the Fold, 1998), Antoinette Burton (At the Heart of the Empire, 1998), Robert Eric Frykenberg (ed., Pandita Ramabai’s America, 2003), Keith J. White (Let the Earth Hear Her Voice, 2022), Edith Blumhofer on the revival, and Gary B. McGee on the history of speaking in tongues at Mukti. Short phrases from their work are quoted and attributed in the text.

Corrections to Popular Accounts

  • Birthplace. She was born in a forest home at Gangamul in the Western Ghats, on the borders of Mysore State above her father’s native Mangalore district, not in the city of Mangalore. She never named the place herself.
  • The famine deaths. Her parents and sister are often said to have died in 1877. Her own account and her age (about sixteen) suggest about 1874-75, early in the famine.
  • Four thousand miles. The figure is her own, and refers to her wanderings with her brother after their parents’ deaths, not to the family’s pilgrimages.
  • Her titles. She was acclaimed with the title Sarasvati by the pandits of Calcutta in 1878; “Pandita” seems to have followed by popular use. Claims that she was the first or only woman to receive such titles cannot be verified.
  • Stories she did not tell. Keshab Chandra Sen gave her a Veda, by her own account, not a book of New Testament selections. The story of her brother exposing the “floating mountains” of a Himalayan lake, and the claim that she worked as a cook, appear only in later admiring accounts and are not used here.
  • Her marriage. Modern scholars date it to November 1880, and her husband’s death to February 1882. She remembered it as “nineteen months.” The two cannot both be exact.
  • The Education Commission. She gave evidence in Poona in September 1882, not 1883.
  • Her baptism. She was baptised at Wantage on 29 September 1883. The tradition that Canon William Butler baptised her has not been confirmed from the register.
  • Her return from America. She landed at Bombay on 1 February 1889, not at Calcutta and not in 1887 as two early accounts say.
  • George Müller. She read the life of George Müller, the Bristol orphanage founder, about 1895, not during her years in England. The Müller she knew in the 1880s was the Oxford Sanskrit scholar Max Müller.
  • The Marathi Bible. Hers was not the first Marathi Bible; William Carey and others had translated it earlier. Nor was she the first woman to translate the whole Bible; Julia Smith published an English translation in 1876. Hers was the first Bible in colloquial Marathi, and she was among the first women anywhere to translate the whole of Scripture from the original languages.
  • The revival and Azusa Street. The Mukti revival began in June 1905, before the Azusa Street meetings of April 1906. Speaking in tongues at Mukti came later, in December 1906, after news of Azusa Street had arrived.
  • Commemoration. The Church of England remembers her on 30 April. She appears on 5 April in some Episcopal Church resources, but not in that church’s current official calendar.
  • Her death. She died on 5 April 1922 at the age of sixty-three, not sixty-four. No reliable source gives a medical cause.
  • Mukti’s naming. Dyer places the dedication and naming of Mukti at the camp meeting of December 1897; Manorama dates the dedication of the “New Home” to 24 September 1898.
  • Manorama’s death. The early sources give July 1921; one modern scholar gives June 1921.

Language

The nineteenth- and early twentieth-century sources describe Hindu religion and Indian people in language that is often contemptuous and sometimes racist. Ramabai herself, as a Christian, wrote harshly about the religion of her childhood. This book quotes such language only where it shows what she or her contemporaries thought, and does not adopt it. It has tried to describe Hindu belief and practice fairly, and to treat Ramabai’s Hindu critics as people with real reasons for their views.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations in the book’s own voice are from the American Standard Version (1901). Where Ramabai quotes Scripture in her own words, usually from the Authorized Version, her wording has been kept.

Method

This book is not a work of original archival research. It tells a true story for general readers from the published sources. Where the sources are uncertain, it says so. Where they disagree, it has preferred Ramabai’s own contemporary writings to later recollections, and contemporary records to the embellishments of admirers. No conversations have been invented. Every quotation comes from the sources named above.

It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it. Ramabai’s Own Writings Wherever possible, this book lets Ramabai speak for herself. Her principal English writings, all now in the public domain, are these: The High-Caste Hindu Woman (Philadelphia, 1887), her own book, with an introduction by Rachel Bodley that includes much biographical material told to Bodley by Ramabai, and her 1882 evidence to the Education Commission. When the book was reprinted in 1901, Ramabai asked for Bodley’s introduction to be left out. Where Bodley’s account of her childhood differs from Ramabai’s own, this book follows Ramabai. Famine Experiences in India (1897), two letters written for the relief of the famine, containing her fullest account of her parents’ deaths and her own famine journeys. A Testimony (Kedgaon, 1907, with later additions), her account of her spiritual journey. We have not found a copy of the original pamphlet. It survives in a condensation made with her permission by J. J. Lucas (Pandita Ramabai: A Wonderful Life, 1919) and in a fuller text printed by Helen Dyer (see below). The two differ: Dyer’s text omits the names of the Hindu reformers who helped her in Poona and of Father Nehemiah Goreh, and Lucas’s includes them. This book quotes both, and follows Lucas where Dyer has cut. A short tract, Trying to be Saved by Their Own Merit, describing the pilgrimage to Pandharpur. Her letters to the Ramabai Association in Boston, printed in its annual reports from 1890 to 1898, and other letters printed in Pandita Ramabai: The Widows’ Friend (Melbourne, 1903), whose later chapters were written by her daughter Manorama. Her Marathi writings, including Stri Dharma Niti (1882) and her book on the United States (1889), and her correspondence with the Wantage sisters, edited by A. B. Shah as The Letters and Correspondence of Pandita Ramabai (1977), have been used only through what modern scholars report of them. The modern English translations of these works are in copyright. The Early Biographers Helen S. Dyer, Pandita Ramabai: The Story of Her Life (1900), and Pandita Ramabai: Her Vision, Her Mission and Triumph of Faith (London, after 1922), whose last chapter, on Ramabai’s death, was completed by another hand after Dyer’s own death. Dyer knew Ramabai and her circle, and her books contain many letters and first-hand accounts, especially of the revival. She wrote to inspire prayer and support, treats Hinduism with open contempt, and was herself a participant in at least one controversial episode (the hiding of a girl in 1893) that she describes approvingly. Clementina Butler, Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati (1922), a memorial life by the chairman of the American Ramabai Association’s executive committee, valuable for its American documents and its account of Ramabai’s last years. Nicol Macnicol, Pandita Ramabai (1926), in the series Builders of Modern India. The most careful of the early lives, it draws on the Marathi biography by D. G. Vaidya and the recollections of Ramabai Ranade, and is willing to criticise its subject. Jennie Chappell, Women Who Have Worked and Won (1900), a popular account that adds romantic details found nowhere else. It has been used sparingly and never alone. White (Let the Earth Hear Her Voice, 2022), Edith Blumhofer on the revival, and Gary B. McGee on the history of speaking in tongues at Mukti. Short phrases from their work are quoted and attributed in the text. Corrections to Popular Accounts Birthplace. She was born in a forest home at Gangamul in the Western Ghats, on the borders of Mysore State above her father’s native Mangalore district, not in the city of Mangalore. She never named the place herself. The famine deaths. Her parents and sister are often said to have died in 1877. Her own account and her age (about sixteen) suggest about 1874-75, early in the famine. Four thousand miles. The figure is her own, and refers to her wanderings with her brother after their parents’ deaths, not to the family’s pilgrimages. Her titles. She was acclaimed with the title Sarasvati by the pandits of Calcutta in 1878; “Pandita” seems to have followed by popular use. Claims that she was the first or only woman to receive such titles cannot be verified. Stories she did not tell. Keshab Chandra Sen gave her a Veda, by her own account, not a book of New Testament selections. The story of her brother exposing the “floating mountains” of a Himalayan lake, and the claim that she worked as a cook, appear only in later admiring accounts and are not used here. Her marriage. Modern scholars date it to November 1880, and her husband’s death to February 1882. She remembered it as “nineteen months.” The two cannot both be exact. The Education Commission. She gave evidence in Poona in September 1882, not 1883. Her baptism. She was baptised at Wantage on 29 September 1883.
